articles.title: P-doped Tubular g-C3N4 with Surface Carbon Defects: Universal Synthesis and Enhanced Visible-light Photocatalytic Hydrogen Production
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental
2.1 Preparation of phosphorus-doped tubular P-TCN with surface carbon defects
First, 1.26 g (10 mmol) melamine is dissolved in 100 ml deionized water under a water bath at 85
°C, then different amounts of sodium pyrophosphate were added into the solution with strong stirring for
30 min. Subsequently the mixture was transferred into an autoclave with Teflon liner and heated at 180
°C for 10 h. The mixture was centrifuged, washed with deionized water and dried in an oven at 60 °C.
Finally, the resultant solids were heated at 500 °C for 4 h under a flow of nitrogen at a heating rate of 2.5
°C/min. The sodium pyrophosphate modified samples were defined as CN-SP. Similarly, a series of
phosphorus-containing compounds, including ammonium phosphate, sodium hypophosphite and sodium
phosphite, were employed to react with melamine, and the corresponding calcination products were
denoted as CN-AP, CN-SH, CN-SPh.
For comparison, g-C3N4 was also prepared with melamine placed in a porcelain crucible and calcined
at 550 °C for 4 h in N2 atmosphere at a heating rate of 2.5 °C min-1, and then the product was ground to a
homogeneous powder.
2.2 Characterization
X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained by Bruker D8. Scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) micrographs were taken using a Hitachi S-4800 instrument operating at 15 KV.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed on a JEM-2100 electron microscope (JEOL,
Japan) with an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) was
recorded on a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One spectrometer using KBr pellets. Photoluminescence spectra
(PL) were recorded with a Hitachi F-4600 fluorescence spectrophotometer at room temperature. The
specific surface area was determined according to the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method using a
Tristar II 3020 surface area and porosity analyzer (micromeritics). UV-visible absorption spectroscopy
was recorded using a UV-visible spectrophotometer (Shimadzu UV-2550). X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was performed on a VG ESCALAB MK II with an Mg Kα (1253.6 eV)
achromatic X-ray source. The thermal stability of the as-prepared samples was verified using a
thermogravimetric analyzer (SDT Q600).
2.3 Photocatalytic hydrogen production
The photocatalytic hydrogen production experiment was conducted in an on-line photocatalytic
hydrogen production system (AuLight, Beijing, CEL-SPH2N) at an ambient temperature of 20 ºC. 0.1g
catalyst was suspended in a mixture of 80 mL distilled water and 20 mL methanol in the reaction cell with
magnetic stirring. 1 wt. % Pt loaded photocatalysts were prepared by a known standard in-situ photo-
deposition method using H2PtCl6 aqueous solution. A Xenon 300 W lamp (Oriel, USA) equipped with a
420-nm cut-off filter was used as the light irradiation source. Gas evolution was observed only under
irradiation, being analyzed by an on-line gas chromatograph (SP7800, TCD, molecular sieve 5 Å, N2
carrier, Beijing Keruida Limited). Once the photocatalytic reaction of a testing cycle of 3 h was
completed, the reactor was replenished with 1 mL of methanol and degassed in a vacuum before starting
the subsequent cycle.
2.4 Photoelectrochemical characterization
Electrochemical measurements were conducted with a BAS Epsilon Electrochemical System in a
conventional three-electrode cell, using a Pt plate as the counter electrode and a
saturated calomel electrode as the reference electrode. The working electrode was prepared by spreading
aqueous slurries of as-synthesised samples (50 μL) over FTO glass substrate. The suspension was
prepared by dispersing samples (20 mg) with Nafion solution in ethanol (1 wt. %, 2 ml). The electrodes
were then dried in an oven, and calcined at 400 ºC for 30 min under a flow of N2 gas. The working
electrode was irradiated from its reverse side. The supporting electrolyte was an aqueous solution of
Na2SO4 (0.2 M) and purged with nitrogen for 1 h before measurement.
2.5 Density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations
The density of states (DOSs) of g-C3N4 and P-doped g-C3N4 were calculated by using the CASTEP
code. To deal with the exchange-correlation energy, Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional form with
a generalized gradient approximation (GGA-PBE) was adopted. Furthermore, a scissor operator
contributing about 1.226 eV was introduced to correct the well-known band gap problem. To avoid the
pseudo-interactions between periodic images along z axis, a vacuum region with a length of 15 Å was
introduced into the 2D slabs, as shown in Figure 7(a). The lattice constants for the (2×2×1) hexagonal
supercell were optimized to be a = 16.7 Å and b = 12.4 Å, respectively. With the application of Ultrasoft
pseudo-potential, the plane wave cut-off was determined to be 340 eV, and the sampling over the
Brillouin zone was treated by a (3×3×4) supercell. This set of parameters guarantees that the energy
tolerance is within 1.0×10-5 eV per atom.

articles.title: Engineering carbon-defects on ultrathin g-C3N4 allows one-pot output and dramatically boosts photoredox catalytic activity
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental section
2.1. One-pot construction of porous ultrathin g-C3N4 nanosheets
The synthesis of the ultrathin g-C3N4 nanosheets was proposed with 
extremely facile means, compared to those known tactics. In a typical 
procedure, 20 g urea was firstly dissolved into 20 mL deionized water to 
form a transparent solution A under 50 ◦C. Then, solution A was trans­
ferred into a covered ceramic crucible (100 mL) and calcined at 550 ◦C 
for 4 h. Finally, a light yellow product of ultrathin g-C3N4 nanosheets 
was obtained with a yield of about 5.7 % (Fig. S1), which is denoted as 
U1W1-CNS. Furthermore, two compared g-C3N4 photocatalysts of U1WX- 
CNS were synthesized by varying the mass ratio of urea to water in so­
lution A (Urea: Water = 1: 0.5 and 1: 0), and the resulted corresponding 
products were labeled as U1W0.5-CNS and U1W0-CNS, respectively.

2.2. Construction of bulk g-C3N4
The bulk g-C3N4 was prepared according to the reported literature 
[22]. In brief, 3 g melamine was directly heated to 550 ◦C for 4 h. The 
obtained product was named Bu-CNS.
2.3. Characterizations
The morphology structure of samples Bu-CNS, U1W0-CNS, U1W0.5- 
CNS, and U1W1-CNS were observed with transmission electron micro­
scopy (TEM, JEM-2010 EX, 200 kV), scanning electron microscopy 
(SEM, S4800, 5 KV, 10 μA) and atomic force microscopy (AFM, Autop­
robe CpResearch). The Powder X-ray radiation diffraction (XRD) was 
recorded on a Smartlab TM 9 KW (Cu Kα radiation, λ = 0.154178 nm). 
The surface porosity information of samples Bu-CNS, U1W0-CNS, 
U1W0.5-CNS, and U1W1-CNS were collected on the BELSORP-MINI in­
strument at 77 K. The chemical compositions of different samples were 
analyzed by X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS, ULVAC-PHI) and 
Fourier Transform Infrared Measurements (FTIR, Nicolet Nexus 470). 
The steady-state Photoluminescence spectra and time-resolved Photo­
luminescence decay spectra of samples Bu-CNS, U1W0-CNS, U1W0.5- 
CNS, and U1W1-CNS were collected using F-4600 FL Spectrophotometer 
and FLS920 time-resolved Spectrofluorometer, respectively. The visible 
light absorption information was collected with UV–vis diffusion- 
reflectance spectra (UV–vis DRS, Perkin-Elmer Lambda 35 Spectropho­
tometer, 200 nm – 800 nm). The electron paramagnetic resonance 
spectra of different samples were recorded using Bruker ESR JESFA200 
spectrometer. The ⋅O2
−-DMPO and ⋅OH-DMPO trapping measurements 
were collected by the Bruker ESR JESFA200 spectrometer under visible 
light irradiation (λ > 400 nm). The static water contact-angle instrument 
was performed to investigate the hydrophilicity of different samples. 
Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed using Netzsch 
STA449F3 (Ar flow) with mass spectroscopy (MS, QMS403C).
2.4. Photocatalytic hydrogen evolution rate measurement
The H2 evolution activity of different samples was tested using 
Labsolar-III AI photoreactor (Beijing Perfectlight Technology Co., Ltd, 
300 W xenon lamp, λ > 400 nm). Typically, 50 mg photocatalysts were 
firstly dispersed into 100 mL of 10 vol% triethanolamine aqueous solu­
tion (here, 2 wt % Pt were severed as a cocatalyst), and then is purged 
with nitrogen for 30 min to ensure the remained O2 eliminated. The 
production of H2 was analyzed with online gas chromatography (GC 
9890A, TCD).

Rhodamine B (RhB, 30 ppm), Tetracycline (TC, 30 ppm), levo­
floxacin (LEX, 20 ppm), norfloxacin (NOR, 20 ppm), and ciprofloxacin 
(CIP, 20 ppm) were chosen as the target contaminant to test the photo- 
degradation activity of different samples under visible light irradiation 
(300 W xenon lamp, λ > 400 nm). Typically, 50 mg photocatalysts were 
firstly dispersed into 30 ml of organic contaminant solution (RhB or TC) 
and stirring in the dark for 30 min. The time-depended degradation ef­
ficiency of RhB and TC were analyzed by a PerkinElmer Lambda750

2.6. Photo-electrochemical measurements
the meantime, urea molecule would also be converted to form cyanic 
acid and melamine, and then polymerizes to bulk g-C3N4 (Fig. S2a). 
However, note that, under the assistance of water molecules (the 
aqueous solution state of urea), more endogenous gaseous species 
(Fig. S2b and S2c) could be in-situ generated compared to the solely 
thermal polymerization of urea. These large amounts of endogenous 
gaseous species could easily crash into the g-C3N4 layer, and subse­
quently, alter the local packing and connectivity of building motifs in g- 
C3N4 frameworks (Scheme 1b). As a result, under the assistance of the 
thermal gas-shocking exfoliation effect of endogenous gas, ultrathin g- 
C3N4 nanosheets could be in-situ obtained. Ulteriorly, those carbon- 
defects on the ultrathin g-C3N4 nanosheets would be in-situ formed 
during these gas-shocking processes, which could be verified by later 
characterization evidence. 
To identify the in-situ bottom-up exfoliation process, Thermogravi­
metric Analysis-Mass Spectroscopy (TGA-MS) experiment was con­
ducted to provide the key evidence (Fig. S3, S4, and S5). As for the 
precursor urea solution and urea powders, three sections of weight loss 
could be observed in the range 150−225 ◦C, 225−375 ◦C, and 
375−500 ◦C (Fig. S3a and S4a), indicating three types of phase trans­
formation had occurred during the whole polymerization process. Ac­
cording to the previous report, the first and second dramatic weight loss 
can be ascribed to the transformation from urea to cyanamide and 
subsequently condensed into melamine [25]. The third slight weak 
weight loss accounts for the formation of the covalent carbon-nitride 
skeleton by further copolymerized melamine units (Fig. S2a). Corre­
spondingly, a continuity of released gaseous species could be detected 
(including NH3, CO2, and H2O) from mass-spectroscopy (150−500 ◦C) 
during the temperature programming process, which provides further 
evidence for these proposed reaction paths (Fig. S3b and S4b). Notably, 
the precursor of urea solution (final sample U1W1-CNS) presents an 
additional weight loss in the range of 100–150 ◦C except another three 
similar weight loss (stage 0), which could be attributed to the reaction of 
urea and water and the vaporization of water (Fig. S2b and S2c). And 
the precursor urea solution (final samples U1W1-CNS) exhibited a more 
weight loss and the strongest relative ion current of NH3, H2O, and CO2
The photo-electrochemical information of the samples was collected 
by using CHI660C electrochemical workstation which employed a 
standard three-electrode system (Pt foil, Ag/AgCl, and working elec­
trodes, 0.5 M Na2SO4 solution). Working electrodes prepared methods: 
5 mg of the photocatalysts were dispersed into 5 ml ethyl alcohol solu­
tion which contains 0.5 μL Nafion and 0.5 μL distilled water and soni­
cated for an hour. Then, 1 mL of the resulting slurry was spread on a 
3 × 1.0 cm FTO glass and dried in air.
2.7. Calculations of Density functional theory (DFT)
DFT calculations were performed using the Dmol3 package of Ma­
terials Studio (Accelrys Inc) with generalized-gradient approximation 
(GGA) and Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation func­
tional [23,24]. The atomic orbitals were treated by the double numerical 
plus polarization (DNP) basis set and the core electrons were treated by 
semi-core pseudopotential. Real-space global cutoff radius: 4.0 Å. The 
optimization geometrical convergence tolerances: energy change was 
2.0 × 10−5 Hartree; gradient was 4.0 × 10-3 Hartree/Å; maximum 
displacement was 5.0 × 10-3 Å. All calculations are spin-polarized.

articles.title: Ultrathin g-C3N4 with enriched surface carbon vacancies enables highly efficient photocatalytic nitrogen fixation
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental
2.1 Synthesis of bulk g-C3N4 and g-C3N4-V
The bulk g-C3N4 was synthesized by polycondensation of dicyandiamide.
Dicyandiamide (Sinopharm, Chemically Pure, ≥ 98 %) of 6 g was calcined in a tube
furnace with a covered semi-closed crucible. The samples were treated by
temperature-programming step. It was smoothly heated to 350 ℃ for 1.5 h and hold
for 2 h, next heat up to 600 ℃ in 1.5 h and maintain for 2 h. Then cooled down and
ground to yellow powders as g-C3N4.[46]
The g-C3N4-V with enriched surface carbon vacancies was synthesized by two-
step calcination. Within 100 min, 2.4 g bulk g-C3N4 was heated to 500 ℃ and kept for
2 h in muffle furnace. The obtained sample of 1.2 g was calcined under 530 ℃ in a
muffle furnace for 2 h (heating rate of 5 ℃ min-1). Finally, the porous white powders
with surface carbon vacancies were obtained, denoted as g-C3N4-V.
2.2 Sample Characterization
X-ray diffraction (XRD, Shimadzu XRD-6000 X-ray diffractometer) (Cu K
radiation, λ=1.5406 Å) was used to determine the composition of the materials in the
range of 10-70 °. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL JSM-7001F) was
obtained to characterize the morphologies. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM,

JEM-2100) was applied to explore the fine structure of the sample. The Tristar II
2030 analyzer was applied to determine the specific surface and porosity of the
sample. The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, VG MultiLab 2000 system),
equipped with a monochromatic Mg-K source, was performed to analyze the
compositions and elemental states. The Fourier transform infrared (FTIR)
spectrometer (Avatar 470, Thermo Nicolet) was used to record the FTIR spectra of
samples. The UV-vis spectrophotometer (Shimadzu, UV-2450) was obtained to
record the DRS curves. The Varian Cary Eclipse spectrometer was performed to get
the photoluminescence (PL) spectra. The Bruker ESR JES-FA200 spectrometer was
employed to obtain the electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra. The CHI
760B electrochemical system with a three electrode system was used to record the
electrochemical experimental results. 5 mg as-prepared sample was dispersed in 1mL
ethylene glycol to produce a suspension. Then 20 μL of the prepared sample paste
was applied to an ITO glass plate (as the working electrode). A platinum wire and an
Ag/AgCl/sat. KCl electrode were used as counter electrode and reference electrode,
respectively. The analysis of electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was
tested in the phosphate buffer solution (PBS, 0.1 M, pH 7.0) mixed in KCl (0.1 M)
solution and Fe(CN)63-/Fe(CN)64- (5 mM). Liquid to solid contact angle was obtained
by contact angle measuring instrument (Attention, KSV CM200).
2.3 Nitrogen absorption and desorption experiment
The sample was dried in a vacuum oven to remove the organic solvent. First, the
empty mass tube was weighed, and then the sample was put in and degassed. After
cooling to room temperature, the total mass was recorded, meanwhile the mass of the
sample was calculated. The quality tube was loaded into ratio surface and porosity
analyzer surrounded by liquid nitrogen. Finally the appropriate data was achieved
after program running.
2.4 Photocatalytic nitrogen fixation measurement
Photocatalytic nitrogen fixation experiments were carried out in a 100 mL quartz
reaction flask around with external cooling water jacket at ambient temperature and
atmospheric pressure. A 300 W Xe lamp was used as light source. In experimental

Typically, 50 mg of as prepared samples was added into 100 mL water, and
ultrasonically dispersed. Before the reaction, the solution was passed through N2
(purity ≥ 99.999 %) in the dark and bubbled for 30 min to establish an adsorption-
desorption equilibrium. High purity Ar (purity ≥ 99.999 %) was used for the control
experiment and bubbled in the dark for 12 h. The photoreactor was sealed and
illuminated internally with the light source. During the photocatalytic reaction, about
8 mL of the suspension was withdrawn from the reaction flask for a fixed period of
time for subsequent NH4+ concentration analysis.
The Nessler’s method was used to analyzed NH4+ content. First, the suspension
was filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane filter, and 1 ml was taken up in a 5 mL
colorimetric tube and diluted with water to a specific ratio. Then, a sodium potassium
tartrate solution and a Nessler’s reagent were added, mixed and set for a period of
time to develop a color reaction. Finally, the concentration of NH4+ was measured at λ
= 420 nm by UV-Vis spectrophotometer (UV-2450, Shimadzu) using water as a
reference solution.
2.5 Water contact angle measurement
A certain quality sample was taken onto the glass piece and pressed into about
1mm thick plane. The water contact angle was measured by contact angle measuring
instrument. The angle between the liquid and the solid surface was recorded with a
high-speed camera for a certain period of time, and the same time scale image for
different samples was compared for research.

cyanuric acid, leading to the NO photoreduction into N2 with
larger efﬁciency and conversion rate [40]. Hence, the con-
struction of suitable carbon vacancies in g-C3N4 framework
was also identiﬁed as a promising and effective strategy to
improve photocatalytic activity.

Introduction
Photocatalysis technology using solar energy is recognized as
one of promising approaches to solve the worldwide energy
crisis and environmental pollution issues [1e4], driven by the
pioneering works about photocatalytic H2 generation [5] and
photocatalytic elimination of organic pollutants [6] over TiO2-
based photocatalysts. However, traditional TiO2-based pho-
tocatalysts have a lower utilization efﬁciency of solar energy
due to the unsuitable band gap (Eg~3.2 eV) [7,8]. Alternatively,
visible-light-response photocatalysts are desirable for the
photocatalysis reactions because the visible light has a larger
proportion in solar energy (~43%) [9]. Graphitic carbon nitride
(g-C3N4), a metal-free polymer semiconductor, has been
widely investigated in recently years for a variety of photo-
catalysis applications, such as the photocatalytic H2 evolution
from water splitting [10,11], photocatalytic elimination of
organic pollutants [12,13],

2. Experimental
2.1. Materials
The chemicals used in the experiments were ammonium thiocyanate 
(NH4SCN), ammonium thiosulf ((NH4)2S2O3), ateammonium sulfate 
((NH4)2SO4), dicyandiamide (D), thiourea (T) and melamine (M), all 
purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., LTD.
2.2. Characterization
A DX-2700 X-ray diffractometer (XRD; Dandong Fangyuan Instru­
ment Co., LTD.) was used to characterize the phase composition and 
crystallization degree of the synthesized samples. The scanning speed 
was 8◦/min, and the investigated scanning range was 5–50◦. Fourier 
transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) measurements were carried out 
using a Vertex 70-type device to characterize the chemical bonds or 
functional groups in the 400–4000 cm−1 range. Specific surface area, 
average pore diameter and pore volume of the samples were measured 
by a 3H-2000PS2-type analyzer by the static volume method. A Tescan 
Mira 3 high resolution field emission scanning electron microscope 
(SEM) was used to observe the morphology of the samples. A Thermo 
ESCALAB 250 Xi X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (XPS) was used to 
investigate the surface and the valence state of the C, N, O and S ele­
ments in the samples. For the quantitative analysis of C, H, N and S a 
Thermo Fisher FlashSmart analyzer was used, while for the determina­
tion of O the difference subtraction method was applied. The photo­
luminescence (PL) spectra were recorded with a Shimazu RF-6000 
fluorescence spectrophotometer, using λ = 400 nm as excitation wave­
length in the 350–700 nm range. The UV–vis diffuse reflectance spectra 
(DRS) of the samples were measured with a U-3900 UV–vis spectro­
photometer in the 200–800 nm range. Electron paramagnetic resonance 
(EPR) measurements were carried out using a Bruker A300-type device. 
Temperature program desorption (TPD) tests were carried out with a 
Contador chemosorption unit using NO and O2 for the measurements 
and He as carrier gas.
2.3. Sample synthesis
Eight kinds of starting materials, which were the mass of 20 g
Chemical Engineering Journal 411 (2021) 128551
dicyandiamide, 20 g thioureas, 20 g melamine and the mass of NH4SCN 
+ (NH4)2S2O3 + (NH4)2SO4 were 20 + 0 + 0, 20 + 0 + 3, 20 + 1 + 1, 20 
+ 3 + 3, and 20 + 5 + 5 (the mass fraction of the last three mixed salts 
was 20:1:1; 7:1:1; 4:1:1) were prepared in a corundum crucible and put 
in a high temperature cracking furnace. The samples were heated from 
room temperature to 550 ◦C under argon atmosphere using 3 ◦C/min 
heating rate, then they were cooled down to room temperature in 3 h. 
Then, the yellow block-shaped samples were collected and ground into 
powder in a mortar. The samples were named as CN-D, CN-T, CN-M, CN- 
AT, CN-ATAS, CN-MIX-1, CN-MIX-3, and CN-MIX-5, respectively 
(graphitized carbon nitride-CN; ammonium thiocyanate-AT; ammonium 
thiocyanate + ammonium sulfate-ATAS; ammonium thiocyanate +
ammonium thiosulf + ammonium sulfate-MIX).
2.4. Electrochemical characterization
Transient photocurrent response tests of the samples was carried out 
in a three-electrode system, in which the counter electrode was a plat­
inum electrode, the reference electrode was a Ag/AgCl electrode and the 
working electrode was an indium tin oxide (ITO) electrode. A 0.5 mol/L 
sodium sulfate solution was used as electrolyte during the measurements 
applying a xenon lamp (>420 nm) as light source. The illumination time 
interval was 20 s (20 s to turn on the lamp, 20 s to turn off the lamp), and 
the test lasted for more than 4 cycles. Electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were carried out in the 0.1–100 kHz 
frequency range, in 0.5 mol/L sodium sulfate solution, and 5 mV voltage 
amplitude was measured.
2.5. Photocatalytic NO removal test
The NO removal experiments were carried out in a continuous flow 
reactor at room temperature under visible light irradiation. First, 100 
mg catalyst was dispersed in 20 mL deionized water by ultrasonication 
for 15 min. The obtained suspension was poured into a circular glass 
reactor and dried at 105 ◦C. The reaction vessel containing the catalyst 
was sealed, and NO gas in low concentration (about 200 ppm) was 
introduced into it until reaching adsorption-desorption equilibrium (by 
the concentration of the gas reaching its maximum level and remaining 
constant). Then, a Xe lamp (Beijing Porfilai Technology Co., LTD. Pls- 
sxe300, 300 W) with a 420 nm filter was turned on to illuminate the 
cylindrical reactor vertically for the photocatalytic reaction. Samples 
were taken every 30 min for 3 h, and the absorbances of NO and NO2 
were detected and recorded. Finally, the concentration of NOx was 
calculated by the N-(1-naphthyl)-ethylenediamine dihydrochloride 
spectrophotometric determination method. (Standard ID: HJ 479-2009). 
The NO removal rate (η) can be calculated using the following 
formula:
η(%) = (1 −
C/C0) × 100
where, C0 represents the concentration of NO in equilibrium before 
illumination (mg/m3), and C represents the concentration of NO in 
equilibrium after illumination (mg/m3).

articles.title: Effective Photocatalytic H2O2 Production under Visible Light Irradiation at g-C3N4 Modulated by Carbon Vacancies
Carbon Vacancy Regulated Photoreduction of NO to N2 over Ultrathin g-C3N4 Nanosheets
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental Section
2.1 Preparation of Catalysts. All chemicals used in this study were analytical-grade
reagents without further purification. Nanosheet structure graphitic carbon nitride
(Ns-g-C3N4) was synthesized by mixing melamine (1 g) with cyanuric acis (2 g) in 20
mL of ethanol with stirring at 333 K to remove the ethanol. The resultant mixture was
put into an alumina crucible with a cover and then heated to 550 oC for 4 h in air to
obtain the final samples. The bulk graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) was prepared by
heating melamine (3 g) in 20 mL of ethanol using the same heating procedures as just
described.
2.2 Sample characterization. The crystal structures of the final samples were
analyzed by Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation at
40 KV and 40 mA. The morphology of the final samples was analyzed by
transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL JSM-2010). Surface electronic states
were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Perkin-Elmer PHI 5000C,
Al KR). All of the XPS spectra were calibrated to the C 1s peak at 284.6 eV of the
surface adventitious carbon. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signals were
recorded at room temperature (298 K) with a Bruker ESR A300 spectrometer. The
UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) were obtained using a UV-vis spectrometer
(Shimadzu UV-2550) by using BaSO4 as a reference and were converted from
reflection to absorbance by the Kubelka-Munk method. Photoluminescence spectra
(PL) of the final samples were obtained using a ﬂuorescence spectrometer (Hitachi
F-4500) at 293 K. The nitrogen adsorption and desorption isotherms at 77 K were
measured using Micrometrics ASAP2020 system after samples were vacuum dried at
180 °C overnight. Fourier transform infra red spectroscopy (FT-IR) spectra were
obtained using a FT-IR spectrophotometer (Nicolet iS50, Thermo) with KBr as the
reference sample.
2.3 Photocatalytic activity measurement. The experiments of photocatalytic NO
removal on g-C3N4 and Ns-g-C3N4 were carried out in a continuous flow reactor. In
the experiment, 50 mg of g-C3N4 or Ns-g-C3N4 was added to 10 mL of H2O and
ultrasonicated for 15 min. The aqueous suspension was then cast onto the glass dish (R
= 3 cm), followed by drying at 60 °C until the water was completely removed. The
glass dish was placed in the middle of the reactor. A 300 W Xe lamp with a 420 nm
cutoff filter was vertically placed above the quartz window, so that the incident light can
irradiate directly on the sample dish. Compressed NO (10 ppm, balance with Ar) was
used as the NO source. NO concentration was diluted to about 600 ppb by air stream.
The flow rate was controlled at 1 L/min by a mass flow controller. The change in NO
concentration was continuously measured by using a chemiluminescence NO analyzer
(Thermo Scientific, 42i).
NO removal efficiency (η) was calculated as follows:
η (%) = (1 − [NO]f / [NO]i) × 100%
where [NO]f and [NO]i are the concentrations of NO in the outlet stream and feeding
stream, respectively.
2.4 Anaerobic photocatalytic NO removal. In the anaerobic photocatalytic NO
removal, a 0.1 g amount of photocatalyst was uniformly dispersed on a glass reactor
with an area of 4.2 cm2. The volume of the reaction system was about 230 mL. The
reaction setup was vacuum-treated several times, and then 1500 ppb NO (Banlance
with Ar) was introduced into the reaction to achieve ambient pressure. During the
irradiation, about 1 mL of gas was taken from the reaction cell at given intervals for
subsequent N2 concentration analysis with a gas chromatograph (GC-14B, Shimadzu
Corp., Japan).
The selectivity of N2 (SN2) was calculated as follows:
SN2 = ([N2] / [N2]+[NO2]) × 100%
2.5 Electrochemical and Photoelectrochemical experiments. Electrochemical and
photoelectrochemical measurements were performed in a three-electrode cell with a
platinum plate (1 × 1 cm2) as the auxiliary electrode and a saturated calomel electrode
(SCE) as the reference electrode on a CHI 660C workstation. The working electrode
(photoelectrode) was immersed in a 0.1 M KCl aqueous solution. Time dependent
photocurrent curves were measured with amperometric i–t curve method. A 300 W Xe
lamp with a 420 nm cutoff filter was chosen as a visible light source. Nyquist plots
were obtained by using the AC impedance method.
The photoelectrodes were prepared as described in our previous report.31 Typically,
the aqueous slurries of g-C3N4 and Ns-g-C3N4 were spin-coated on ITO glass
substrate at a spin rate of 3000 rpm for 30 s under low vacuum. The films on ITO
glass substrate were dried in air and annealed at 200 oC for 1 h as the final
photoelectrodes.

articles.title: 3D macropore carbon-vacancy g-C3N4 constructed using polymethylmethacrylate spheres for enhanced photocatalytic H2 evolution and CO2 reduction
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental
2.1. Synthesis of catalysts
3DM C/g-C3N4: PMMA spheres were prepared using a reported method [27].
Cyanuric acid (4 g) and melamine (2 g) were dissolved in PMMA (100 mL) solution
(3 mg mL-1). The mixture was stirred for 20 min and then dried at 80 °C. The obtained
sample was calcined at 500 °C for 2 h, and the product was defined as 3DM C/g-C3N4.
Reference cyanuric acid and melamine (CM) /g-C3N4 were synthesized using a
solvent containing cyanuric acid (4 g), melamine (2 g), and ethanol (40 mL) without
PMMA. The solution was stirred at 60 °C until ethanol evaporated, and the deposit
was calcined at 550 °C for 4 h. The reference g-C3N4 was synthesized using melamine
(g-C3N4), cyanamide (g-C3N4-C), dicyandiamide (g-C3N4-D) and thiourea (g-C3N4-T)
at 550 °C for 4 h.
2.2. Characterization
The specific characteristics of the samples are illustrated in the supporting
information.
2.3. Photocatalytic activity
2.3.1. Photoelectrochemical measurement
A three-electrode cell was subjected to electrochemical measurements. Ag/AgCl
and Pt plate served as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively, and the
electrolyte solution was 0.1 mol L-1 Na2SO4. The working electrode was fabricated
using slurries of samples on the FTO glass, and the film area was 1 cm2. The light
source was a solar simulator (AM 1.5, NEWPORT).
2.3.2. Photocatalytic H2 evolution
Photocatalytic H2 evolution was conducted in an online test system (Prefect Light,
Labsolar–6A). In brief, 100 mg of catalysts were dispersed in triethanolamine (10
vol%) aqueous solution (100 mL) in a glass reaction cell under magnetic stirring. Pt
nanoparticles (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, and 1 wt.%) were loaded on the catalysts via
photo-deposition using a H2PtCl6•6H2O precursor. The air in the system was fully
removed before irradiation with a 300 W Xe lamp. Cold-water circulation was
performed to maintain the temperature at 7.5 ± 2.5 °C. The gas produced was tested
using gas chromatograph with a TCD detector (Agilent GC-7890B).
2.3.3. Photocatalytic CO2 reduction
Photocatalyst of 0.5 g was placed in an online closed system to analyze the CO2
reduction rate. Air discharged by the CO2 gas were supplied prior to the light
irradiation by using a 300 W Xe lamp. CO2 and H2O mixtures were introduced into a
photoreactor with a quartz window. The photoreactor was cooled by circulating water
at 20 °C. After 4 h of reaction, the reaction system was evacuated and refilled with
CO2 and H2O. The product was analyzed by a gas chromatograph with an FID
detector (Agilent GC-7890B).

2. Experimental Section
2.1 Sample preparation
The fabrication of hydrothermal feedstock: 4.28 g urea and 3 g melamine were dissolved into 50
mL of deionized water and then stirred for 40 min. Subsequently, the above mixture was subjected to
hydrothermal treatment at 180 ℃ for 24h. After that, the reaction product was centrifuged, washed
with deionized water and dried in an oven at 60 ℃ for 10h.
The synthesis of tubular C3N4: 19.5 g of resultant solids were placed into 200 mL of porcelain
crucible and calcined at 400 ℃, 450 ℃, 500 ℃, 550 ℃ and 600 ℃ for 4h in nitrogen gas with a heating
rate of 5 ℃/min, the corresponding end-products were labelled as TN 400, TN 450, TN 500, TN 550
and TN 600, respectively. Bulk C3N4 (denoted as T 500) was also obtained by annealing 19.5 g of
hydrothermal precursor at 500 ℃ without the introduction of nitrogen gas for comparison purposes,
2.2 Sample characterization
The crystal structures of the as-made photocatalysts were analyzed by Bruker D8 Advance X-ray
diffractometer (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation at 40 KV and 40 mA. The morphology of the
as-prepared samples was analyzed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL JSM-2010)
Journal Pre-proof
and scanning electron microscope (SEM, JEOL JSM-6490). Surface electronic states were analyzed
by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Perkin-Elmer PHI 5000C, Al KR). All the XPS spectra
were calibrated to the C 1s peak at 284.6 eV of the surface adventitious carbon. Electron
paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signals were recorded at room temperature (298 K) with a Bruker
ESR A300 spectrometer. The UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) were obtained using a UV-vis
spectrometer (Shimadzu UV-3600) by using BaSO4 as a reference and were converted from
reflection to absorbance by the Kubelka-Munk method. Photoluminescence spectra (PL) of the final
samples were obtained using a ﬂuorescence spectrometer (Hitachi F-4500) at 293 K. The nitrogen
adsorption and desorption isotherms at 77 K were measured using Micrometrics ASAP2020 system
after samples were vacuum dried at 180 °C overnight. IR spectra were recorded on a Nicolet iS50
spectrometer (Thermo) equipped with a liquid nitrogen cooled MCT detector. In-situ diffuse
reflectance infrared fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) for NO photo-oxidation measurement
was carried out on a TENSO II FTIR spectrometer (Bruker, Germany) equipped with an in-situ
diffuse-reflectance cell (Harrick, USA), and the photocatalyst pre-treatment and the measurement
procedure was followed Zhou et al.’s work [31]. The treatment processes of photocatalytic activity
measurements and trapping active species experiments as well as photoelectrochemical experiments
were in line with our previous work [32].
2.3 Photocatalytic activity measurement
The ppb level NO photo-oxidation of C3N4 specimens was executed in a continuous flow reactor
at ambient temperature. Constructed of stainless steel, the rectangular reactor with a volume of 4.5 L
(30 cm × 15 cm × 10 cm, L × W × H) and covered with quartz glass. Visible-light source was derived
from an LED lamp (λ≥448 nm), which was put above the reactor perpendicularly. 0.2 g of the
Journal Pre-proof
as-obtained sample was added into 30 mL of deionized water and sonicated for 30 min; whereafter,
the suspension was poured into a glass dish (12 cm in diameter), which was pre-treated at 60 °C to
completely evaporate water from suspension and then cooled to indoor temperature before
photo-oxidation evaluation. NO gas can be acquired from a compressed NO gas cylinder with 50
ppm. Initial concentration of NO was diluted to approximately 600 ppb by using air stream supplied
from a zero-air generator (Advanced Pollution Instrumentation, Teledyne Technologies Company,
Model 701). The gas stream was premixed fully by a gas blender, and a mass flow controller can
control the flow rate at 1.0 L/min. After reaching the adsorption–desorption equilibrium, switching
on the lamp. To monitor NO and NOx (NOx represents NO + NO2) at a sampling rate of 1.0 L/min,
NO concentration was continuously measured by a chemiluminescence NOx analyzer (Advanced
Pollution Instrumentation, Teledyne Technologies Company, Model T200). The removal ratio (η) of
NO was calculated as η (%) = (1–C/C0) × 100, where C and C0 are the concentrations of NO in the
outlet and feeding streams, respectively.
2.4 Calculations of DFT
The theoretical calculations of as-obtained samples were employed by exploiting the Vienna ab
initio simulation package (VASP code 5.4.1) with a generalized gradient correlation functional
[33-36]. Cut-off energy and Gaussian trailing width were set to be 400 eV and 0.2 eV, respectively.
The Bril-louin zone was adopted by a 3×3×1 Monkhorst Pack grid. All structures and energy were
converged to below 0.01eV. A 2×2×3 supercell of bulk g-C3N4 was ﬁrst relaxed.

articles.title: Robust Photocatalytic H2O2 Production over Inverse Opal g-C3N4 with Carbon Vacancy under Visible Light
articles.experimental_text:
2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
2.1. Preparation of Ordered Silica PCs (SiO2 PCs).
Monodispersed SiO2 microspheres were prepared by the Stöber
method. Brieﬂy, TEOS (8 mL) was dropped into ethanol (92 mL),
and then the mixed solution was agitated to form liquor A.
Meanwhile, EtOH (56.6 mL), DI water (29.4 mL), and NH3·H2O
(14 mL) were added to a round-bottom ﬂask (250 mL) for the
formation of liquor B. Liquor A was quickly dropped into liquor B,
and then the round bottom ﬂask was sealed with a frosted hollow
plug. After constant stirring for 1 min, the mixed liquor was
decelerated to bubble-free stirring. Afterwards, the liquor was stirred
for 24 h under an oil bath at 25 °C. After the reaction, the prepared
silica spheres were washed with water by centrifugation three times.
Later, the dried silica spheres were fully ground and dissolved in water
(5 wt % concentration relative to the mass of the silica spheres) and
the mixed solution were then allocated into vials. At last, the vials
were put on the oven with a heating temperature of 110 °C and the
silica PCs can be found on the wall of the vials.
2.2. Preparation of IO CN-Cv. DCDA (0.6 g) and 1.0 g of SiO2
PCs were fully ground and calcined in an Ar atmosphere under the
temperature programming of 520 °C for 120 min. The ﬁnished
temperature programming was 550 °C for 120 min. The formed
yellow powder was then cooled. NH4HF2 (4 M) liquor was
subsequently used to etch the silica templates thoroughly. Two days
later, the yellow liquor was centrifuged to remove vestigial NH4HF2,
and then the samples were ﬁnally dried at 60 °C. Finally, the yellowish
powder was obtained.
2.3. Preparation of Bulk CN, Bulk CN-Cv, and Nanosheet
CN. Bulk CN and bulk CN-Cv were obtained via calcining DCDA
both in air and Ar atmospheres. The temperature program is the same
as that of IO CN-Cv. The obtained sample was designated as bulk CN
and bulk CN-Cv.
Nanosheet CN was prepared as follows: the bulk CN was ﬁrst
under the temperature programming of 500 °C and the ﬁnished
temperature programming was 500 °C for 120 min. The prepared
yellow powder was designated as nanosheet CN.
2.4. Characterization. An X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) instrument
was applied to record the XRD data. A scanning electron microscopy
(SEM) was applied to obtain the SEM data. A surface area analyzer
was used to obtain the Brunauer−Emmett−Teller (BET) data. An X-
ray photoelectric spectrometry (XPS) was applied to obtain the XPS
data. An UV−vis spectrophotometer was applied to obtain the UV−
visible absorption spectra. Barium sulfate was used as a reference. A
ﬂuorospectrophotometer was applied to obtain the photolumines-
cence (PL) spectra. A ﬂuorospectrophotometer was applied to obtain
the time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) spectra. An electron
spin resonance (ESR) spectrometer was applied to obtain the ESR
data. An electrochemical workstation was applied to obtain the
electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), photocurrent (POL),
and Mott−Schottky data.
An electrochemical workstation (Zahner, Zennium) was used to
analyze the electrochemical properties. To obtain the working
electrode, the sample was coated on a ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide
glass. The sample (0.005 g) was dissolved in EtOH (500 μL) and
subsequently 20 μL of liquor was covered on the glass. The area
covered was almost 1 cm2. To obtain the POL intensity of our
photocatalysts, 0.5 M sodium sulfate liquor was applied and the
experiments were performed under a 300 W xenon lamp without the
ﬁlter. To obtain the impedance of our photocatalysts, 25 mM
potassium ferricyanide, 25 mM potassium ferrocyanide, and 100 mM
potassium chloride were mixed for the working solution.
2.5. Photocatalytic Experiments. A sample (20 mg) was
dissolved in liquor (20 mL) including DI water (19 mL) and ethanol
(1 mL, 5% EtOH). Then O2 was bubbled for 30 min to make the
system equilibrated with O2. Afterward, a 300 W xenon lamp with a
420 nm cutoﬀﬁlter was applied to stimulate the photocatalytic
reaction and the H2O2 production experiment was performed for 2 h.
An iodometric method was used to calculate the production of H2O2.
In detail, 100 mM potassium iodide (2000 μL) and 10 mM
ammonium molybdate tetrahydrate (50 μL) were added in the
reaction liquor. Then the mixed liquors made to stand for a long time,
and the absorbancy of iodine in 352 nm was applied to obtain its
concentration by using a UV−vis spectrophotometer.
To create an oxygen-free environment, ﬁrst, the photocatalyst (20
mg) was dissolved in liquor (20 mL) including DI water (19 mL) and
5% EtOH (1 mL). Second, the mixed solution was heated for 1 h to
remove the dissolved oxygen as far as possible. Third, the mixed
solution was bubbled with N2.
2.6. Active Species Trapping Experiments. To reveal the
inﬂuence of •O2
−on H2O2 production, BQ (1 mM) was used as a
scavenger for •O2
−. The experiments were similar to the photo-
catalytic experiments.
2.7. Determination of Reactive Species. To detect the
generation of active species, ﬁrst, DMPO •O2
−species was collected
under visible light irradiation for 15 min with the photocatalyst.

articles.title: H2+CO2 Synergistic Plasma Positioning Carboxyl Defects in g-C3N4 with Engineered Electronic Structure and Active Sites for Efficient Photocatalytic H2 Evolution
articles.experimental_text:
3. Materials and Methods
3.1. Materials
Analytical grade urea obtained from Aladdin Industrial Corp. (Shanghai, China)
was used as the precursor of g-C3N4 and used without further puriﬁcation. High-purity
hydrogen gas (containing 95% Ar as safety carrier gas) and high-purity carbon dioxide gas
were purchased from Qingkuan Corp. (Shanghai, China).
3.2. Preparation of Raw g-C3N4 and Carboxyl-Defective g-C3N4
Raw g-C3N4 was synthesized by direct thermal polycondensation of 10.0 g of urea,
which was put in a covered crucible and placed in mufﬂe furnace at 560 ◦C for 4 h at a
heating rate of 5 ◦C·min−1. The resulting light-yellow powder after natural cooling to
room temperature was ground to a ﬁne powder in an agate mortar and marked as g-C3N4.
Plasma-treated modiﬁed g-C3N4 samples were all synthesized by plasma immersion in a
sample chamber for 3 min. The plasma-treated g-C3N4 samples were named according to
the used plasma source (H2-pCN, CO2-pCN, H2+CO2-pCN).
3.3. Plasma Equipment and Process
The plasma technique is well recognized to be able to generate very highly ionized
reactive plasma species (e.g., electrons, ions, excited atoms), and to enable reactions that
cannot be achieved by conventional methods. For decades, CO2 plasma has been used
as a soft oxidation approach to generate the surface carboxyl group of carbon materials
to achieve hydrophilicity or improved electrochemical activity. Besides, dielectric barrier
discharge plasma was used to prepare N/C vacancy-embedded g-C3N4 catalysts in situ
under H2 atmosphere. These generated plasma species further interact with the polymer
surface through possible reactions such as etching, cross-linking, and chemical modiﬁcation.
As a consequence, functional groups with desired surface properties are generated on the
surface of polymers, such as –OH, –CO, –NH and –COOH. To date, many plasma processes
have been developed. Among them, CO2 plasma is capable of adhesion promotion as it can
form –COOH on polymer surface, and is somewhat less destructive to polymer backbone
chains than conventional oxygen-based plasma. To achieve large-area uniform plasma
surface modiﬁcation in industry, the demand for plasma source is increasing. Due to high
dissociation, large area and uniformity, electrodeless microwave plasma is promising in
industry, although the equipment is expensive.
For this purpose, we developed a microwave surface wave plasma device shown in
Figure 9 to achieve uniform plasma surface modiﬁcation. The 2.45 GHz microwave was
employed as a source to generate surface wave plasma under a quartz window via slot
antenna cut on the bottom of waveguide [41]. The working gas system was determined
by a vacuum system, cut-off valves, a gas mass ﬂow controller and a gas tank together to
create a necessary environment in the processing chamber. When microwave energy was
applied, uniform plasma was formed within 1 s. On the sample state, we set an electrode
to apply bias voltage to form an accelerating ﬁeld, which can be used to control the ion
energy bombing to the sample.

2.1Materials
Manufacturers of melamine (C3H6N6), cyanuric acid (C3H3N3O3), sodium salt of
tetraiodofluorescein (C20H6I4Na2O5), polyethylene glycol (HO(CH2CH2O)nH) and

(H2PtCl6), isopropanol (C3H8O) and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (CHN2O8) are all
Sinopharm; none of the drugs have been further purified; deionised water is
homemade in the laboratory.
2.2 Preparation of photocatalysts
S-doped honeycomb nanosheets of g-C3N4 were prepared mainly by thermal
polycondensation. In particular, firstly, 3g of melamine (C3H6N6) and 3g of cyanuric
acid (C3H3N3O3) were placed in a 50ml beaker, 40ml of deionized water was added
and then stirred vigorously for 30min at 75°C in a water bath, followed by pouring

white suspension, which was then continued to be stirred until dry, and finally placed
in a drying oven and continued to dry for 12h. It was thoroughly dried, then the
thiourea-modified precursor was obtained by grinding it to a powder in an agate
mortar. At a ramp-up temperature of 5°C·min-1 , the resultant precursor was
immediately put into a closed crucible and heated to 550°C while being kept for 4h.

Experimental
The atmospheric pressure air-plasma reactor consists of two
electrodes and a glass beaker containing 40 mg of bulk g-C3N4
(CN) in 100 mL de-ionized water. The stainless-steel electrode
(grounded) is submerged in water, while the copper electrode
placed at a distance of 2 mm above the water surface is used for
plasma generation. For the generation of plasma, a high AC
voltage of 5 kV is applied to the copper rod. Plasma is generated
for 30 min to 150 min above the liquid surface. During this
time, the aqueous dispersion of CN is continuously stirred. The
exfoliated products are named CN30, CN60, CN90, CN120, and
CN150. The exfoliated nanosheets are separated from unexfo-
liated CN through centrifugation. Starting with 40 mg of pris-
tine CN, the yield aer 30 min plasma-treatment (CN30) is 50–
55% (20–22 mg). As the plasma exfoliation time increases, the
amount of exfoliated CN nanosheets in the dispersion also
increases. Hence, the yield is high for the sample CN150, which
is nearly 75% (30 mg). Of note, there was a mass loss of 3–5%
during recovery of exfoliated nanosheets aer centrifugation.
The nal product aer washing is dried in an oven to obtain the
exfoliated nanosheets in a powder form.
The crystalline structure of the prepared photocatalysts is

used for imaging the morphology of the nanosheets. UV-visible

articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental section
2.1. Photocatalyst preparation
A bifunctional carbon nitride based photocatalyst (BaCN-C3N4) co- 
modified with Ba2+ and cyano group was successfully synthesized by 
doping Ba2+ to construct cyano group defects in g-C3N4 framework, 
using a salt-assisted method. Specifically, 10 g of C3H6N6 and a certain 
amount of BaCl2 (0.5 g, 0.7 g and 0.9 g) were placed in a 100 mL ceramic 
crucible, and 20 mL of deionized water was added and fully stirred. The 
mixture was then sonicated in an ultrasonic cleaner for 20 min, and
Chemical Engineering Journal 423 (2021) 130278
further dried overnight in a blast drying oven to obtain a precursor. 
Thereafter, the precursor was raised from room temperature to 600 ◦C in 
a muffle furnace at a heating rate of 5 ◦C/min, and maintained at this 
temperature for 4 h. After cooling to room temperature, the calcined 
material was fully ground to obtain a powder sample. Further, 1 g of the 
powder sample was placed in 250 mL of deionized water and ultrason­
ically washed for 3 h to fully remove water-soluble impurities. Finally, 
after centrifugation at 5000 r/min, the sample m-BaCN-C3N4 was dried 
and labeled, where m (5%, 7%, and 9%) refers to the relative content of 
BaCl2. Pure g-C3N4 was prepared by directly calcining 10 g of melamine 
(without BaCl2), labeled as g-C3N4. The preparation process of BaCN- 
C3N4 is shown in Scheme 1.
2.2. Characterization
The phase structure, functional groups and element composition of 
the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) (XRD-6100, 
Shimadzu, Japan), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR, 
IRPrestige-21, Shimadzu, Japan) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy 
(XPS, Thermo Scientific, ESCALAB 250xi, USA). The content of the 
doped Ba2+ was determined by inductively coupled plasma optical 
emission spectrometry (ICP-OES, Spectro genesis, Germany). Trans­
mission Electron Microscopy (TEM, FEI, Tecnai G2F20, USA), N2 
adsorption–desorption apparatus (BET, ASAP 2020, USA) and Energy 
Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS SU1510, Hitachi, Japan) were used 
to observe the morphology, physical properties and element distribution 
of the catalyst. The optical properties and catalytic mechanism were 
studied by UV–visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (UV–vis DRS, 
Shimadzu, Japan), Photoluminescence (PL, F-7000, Hitachi, Japan), 
Electron spin-resonance spectroscopy (ESR, Hitachi, FA200, Japan), LC- 
MS/MS with a combination of 1260 Infinity HPLC (Agilent, USA) and a 
mass spectrometer (6420 Triple Quadrupole LC/MS, Agilent, USA).
2.3. DFT calculations
The calculations of geometry configurations and the band structures 
were carried out by the Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP), 
taking advantage of the density functional theory (DFT) with the Pro­
jected Augmented Wave (PAW) method. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof 
(PBE) function was employed to illustrate the exchange and correla­
tion effects. SCF convergence criteria was set to be 10-5 eV in the 
calculation. Gaussian smearing with 0.1 eV width was adopted in the 
geometry optimization. The relaxation convergence criteria was set to 
be 0.03 eV/Å. The cut-off energy was set to be 400 eV. The Γ-centered 
Monkhorst-Pack grids were set to be 1 × 1 × 1 for performing the

calculations. As for band structure and electronic configuration calcu­
lation, tetrahedron method with Bl¨ochl corrections was adopted. The 
energy cutoff was set to be 600 eV and a denser k-point mesh of 2 × 2 × 1 
was adopted. We firstly constructed a single-layer g-C3N4 system (g- 
C3N4). Then, Ba2+ was introduced into part of the heptazine ring cavity 
(Ba-C3N4) to study the influence of Ba2+ on the CN structure framework 
and energy band. Lastly, a part of Ba2+ doping and cyano (-C≡N) co- 
modified g-C3N4 (BaCN-C3N4) was also constructed to reveal their syn­
ergism effect on the band structure and electronic configuration of the g- 
C3N4 system. For all the systems, a ~ 20 Å vacuum thickness was added 
in the z-direction of the simulation box, preventing the interactions 
between the adjacent surfaces.
2.4. Photocatalytic test
25 mg photocatalyst powder, 50 mL TEOA aqueous solution (45 mL 
deionized water and 5 mL TEOA) and 2 mL chloroplatinic acid (1 g/L, 
~3 wt% Pt) jointly constitute the reaction system in a 100 mL gas-closed 
Pyrex reactor. Subsequently, the reaction system was connected to a 
glass closed gas circulation system and a continuous circulation cooling 
tank was used to control the temperature (15 ◦C). A 300 W Xe lamp 
matched with a 420 nm cut-off filter (λ > 420 nm) was used as the light 
source, and the average light power obtained by CEL-NP2000 spec­
troradiometer (Education Au-light, China) was about 300 mW/cm2. 
Before the light irradiation, the whole reaction system was evacuated. 
Finally, the amount of generated hydrogen (GC 7920, Beijing) was 
analyzed by gas chromatograph. The apparent quantum efficiency 
(AQE) of the synthesized photocatalyst was obtained by Equation (1):

It is important and valuable that the hydrogen evolution and 
degradation efficiency of BaCN-C3N4 were simultaneously investigated 
in wastewater. Only by replacing the deionized water in the above in­

2.5. Photoelectrochemical analysis
3 mg of the catalyst was dispersed in a mixed solution of 250 μL of 
water, 250 μL of absolute ethanol, and 10 μL of Nafion, and the mixed 
solution was further ultrasonically dispersed for 30 min to obtain a 
dispersion. This dispersion was uniformly deposited on a 15 cm × 15 cm 
ITO conductive glass, then dried under vacuum at 60 ◦C for 30 min. The 
photocurrent was estimated in a three-electrode battery connected to

2. Experimental
2.1. Chemical materials
Nafion solution (5 wt%), NaSO4, isopropanol, triethanolamine, thiourea, KCl, and
chloroplatinic acid hexahydrate (>99%, H2PtCl6·H2O) were all obtained from Sinopharm
Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd and used without further purification. Ultrapure (Milli-Q) water
was used to prepare all solutions and in the photocatalytic hydrogen production tests.
2.2. Synthesis of g-C3N4 and CCN photocatalysts
Pristine g-C3N4 was prepared by thiourea thermal polymerization. Briefly, 10 g of
thiourea was calcined at 600°C in a tube furnace for 2 h at a heating rate of 2.5°C min-1.
Cyanamide defects-grafting carbon nitride (CCN) were synthesized as follows: 10 g of
thiourea was dissolved into aqueous KCl solutions (KCl 0.005, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05 and 0.1 g in
10 mL H2O), the resulting solution was heated at 160°C for 1 h, and the solution was rapidly
frozen to -80°C and kept for 4 h. The solid was then calcined in a tube furnace at 600°C for 2
h at a heating rate of 2.5°C min-1. All samples were washed with deionized water to remove
any residual alkali salt. The products were denoted as CCN-M (M = 0.005, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05

Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were collected on a Bruker DAVINCI D8
ADVANCE diffractometer equipped with Cu-Kα source. The morphology of samples was
examined using transmittance electron microscopy (TEM) (JEOL, JEM-2100F) and a field
emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) (FEI XL-30E) at an accelerating voltage of 10
kV. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were recorded on a Perkin Elmer GX

Advantage 200A Raman spectrometer with a 632.8 nm laser (Delta Nu, USA). Zeta potentials
were measured on a Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS. The C, N and O contents were measured via

at room temperature. Diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) were measured using a Cary 5000
spectrophotometer fitted with an integrating sphere attachment from 200-800 nm with BaSO4
as the reference. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were performed on a
Quantum 2000 Scanning ESCA Microprobe (Physical Electronics) using monochromatic Al
Kα radiation (1486.7 eV) as the X-ray source. The specific surface area was determined by
the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method with N2 adsorption at 77 K (BELSORP-mini II).
The photoluminescence (PL) spectra were recorded with Hitachi F-7000 fluorescence

The photoelectrochemical properties were investigated in a three-electrode cell by using
an electrochemical analyzer (CHI Inc., USA). An ITO glass coated with catalyst, a Pt foil and

working electrode, the counter-electrode and the reference electrode, respectively. A 300 W
Xe arc lamp equipped with a 420 nm cutoff filter was utilized as a light source. The

fabrication of the photoanode, ITO were cleaned by ultrasonication in distilled water, absolute
ethanol, and isopropanol for 15 min sequentially, and then dried in vacuum. 5 mg of

homogeneous catalyst colloid. Then, 110 μL of the catalyst colloid was deposited onto the

The catalyst-coated ITO was dried in air to form the working electrode.
2.5. Photocatalytic Activity Measurements
The photocatalytic H2 production was carried out in a Pyrex glass reaction cell containing 80

articles.title: Salt-template-assisted construction of honeycomb-like structured g-C3N4 with tunable band structure for enhanced photocatalytic H2 production
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental section
2.1. Synthesis of pristine g-C3N4
In a typical procedure, 4.5 g dicyandiamide (DCDA) was placed into
a crucible with a cover and calcined at 550 °C for 2 h with a ramping
rate of 5 °C /min. The as-obtained product was named as PCN.
2.2. Synthesis of honeycomb-like structured g-C3N4 with tunable band
structure
4.5 g dicyandiamide was dissolved into 500 mL ethanol and a cer-
tain amount of NaCl saturated aqueous solution was then injected drop
by drop into dicyandiamide ethanol solution under constant stirring
vigorously. The ethanol and water were removed by rotary evaporation
and the obtained powder was calcined at 550 °C for 2 h with a ramping
rate of 5 °C/min. After the calcination, the samples were added into
deionized water under constant stirring. After the mixture was stirred
for 1 h, the product was collected through centrifugation, washed with
deionized water several times to remove any water-soluble impurity
and dried in vacuum. The samples synthesized with various amounts of
NaCl (the molar ratio of NaCl: DCDA = 1:1, 3:1, 5:1, 10:1, and 15:1)
were noted as CN-1, CN-3, CN-5, CN-10, and CN-15, respectively. The
m-CN-10 as a control was prepared by just mixing DCDA with NaCl (the
molar ratio of NaCl: DCDA = 10) and heating to 550 °C for 2 h with a
ramping rate of 5 °C /min. After the calcination, the sample was treated
by the same procedure for CN-10 mentioned above.
2.3. Characterization
X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) measurements were carried out on a Bruker
D8 Focus Diﬀraction System with Cu Kα radiation. Scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) images were obtained using a Hitachi S-4800 scan-
ning electron microscope at an accelerating voltage of 3 kV and energy
dispersive spectrometer (EDS) mapping was measured using a Thermo
Scientiﬁc energy dispersive spectroscopy. UV–vis diﬀuse reﬂectance
spectra (DRS) were obtained on a UV–vis spectrometer (UV-2700,
Shimadzu, Japan) using BaSO4 as the reference. X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS) examinations were carried out to analyze the
composition, chemical state and valence band position of the samples
on a PHI-1600 X-ray photoelectron spectrometer using Al Kα radiation.
The steady photoluminescence (PL) spectra and time-resolved ﬂuores-
cence spectra were recorded on a Jobin Yvon Fluorolog 3–21 ﬂuores-
cence spectrometer. The speciﬁc surface area was measured at 77 K
using an Autosorb-iQ2-MP apparatus. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR)
spectra were measured on a Thermo Scientiﬁc Nicolet 6700 spectro-
photometer. The solid 13C MAS nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)
spectra of PCN and CN-10 were recorded on an Inﬁnity Plus 300
spectrometer.
2.4. Fabrication of electrodes and photoelectrochemical tests
Before fabricating working electrodes, the F-doped tin oxide (FTO)
substrates were cleaned through ultrasonication in absolute ethanol,
acetone and absolute ethanol for 20 min sequentially. To fabricate
working electrodes, 4 mg of sample was dispersed in 4 mL absolute
ethanol and the as-prepared slurry was spread on a FTO substrate
(1 × 1 cm2) and subsequently calcined at 300 ℃for 2 h. The working
electrodes studied are with a similar loading amount. The electro-
chemical impedance spectroscopies (EIS) and transient photocurrent
response studies were investigated in a conventional three-electrode
cell with an Ag/AgCl reference electrode, a working electrode, and a Pt
counter electrode. Na2SO4 aqueous solution (0.5 M) was used as the
electrolyte solution. A 300 W Xenon lamp with a UV-cutoﬀﬁlter
(λ > 400 nm) was used as the light source. The Nyquist plots were
recorded at 1.0 V bias potential versus Ag/AgCl over the frequency
range from 1 MHz to 0.1 Hz. The transient photocurrent response tests
were performed at an applied 1.0 V potential versus Ag/AgCl.
2.5. Photocatalytic activity tests
The photocatalytic H2 production tests were performed in a Pyrex
glass reaction cell connected to a gas-closed system. In a typical pro-
cedure, 50 mg of photocatalysts was added into 270 mL 25 vol% of
lactic acid aqueous solution. 3 wt% Pt was in situ photodeposited on the
surface of photocatalysts by irradiation with a 300 W Xenon lamp for
2 h. Prior to the irradiation, the reaction cell was evacuated several
times to remove the air completely. Then the aqueous dispersion of
photocatalysts was irradiated under a 300 W Xenon lamp equipped
with a UV-cutoﬀﬁlter (λ > 400 nm). The evolved H2 was analyzed by
an online Shimadzu GC-2014C gas chromatograph equipped with a
thermal conductivity detector. The apparent quantum yield (AQY) was
measured by using 300 W Xenon lamp with a water ﬁlter and bandpass
ﬁlter (420 nm). A radiant power energy meter (AvaSolar-1) was used to

2. Experimental
2.1. Synthesis process
Cyano group modiﬁed graphitic carbon nitride (CG-CN) was de-
signed as follows: 5 g melamine was added to an alumina boat and
sintered at 600 °C at a heating rate of 5 °C/min for 2 h under N2 ﬂow.
Then, 0.6 g graphitic carbon nitride produced from the previous step
mixed with a certain melamine and LiCl/KCl salt. The mixture was
transferred into an alumina boat and sintered at 550 °C at the heating
rate of 5 °C/min for 2 h in an air atmosphere. The mass ratios of mel-
amine: g-C3N4 was 1:10, 3:10, and 5:10 (labeled CG-CN-1, CG-CN-3 and
CG-CN-5), respectively. CN was prepared by heating melamine at
600 °C at a heating rate of 5 °C/min for 2 h in a N2 atmosphere and then
calcined at 550 °C at the heating rate of 5 °C/min for 2 h in an air
atmosphere.
2.2. Photocatalytic measurements
The photocatalytic nitrogen ﬁxation experiment was carried out in
quartz photochemical reactor. 100 mL diluted hydrochloric acid con-
taining 50 mg photocatalyst was magnetic stirred for 30 min in the dark
with the high-purity N2 bubbled in the solution. Then the 300 W Xe
lamp (PLS-SXE300/300UV) with a cutoﬀﬁlter (λ > 400 nm) was
turned on. 2 mL mixture was collected and centrifugalized from the
suspension after 1 h irradiation. The concentration of ammonia was
measured by the indophenol indicator spectrophotometry method with
an ultraviolet–visible spectrophotometer (the details of NH3/NH4
+
concentration analysis are presented in the Supporting Information).
2.3. Characterization
The crystal structure of samples was characterized using a powder
X-ray diﬀractometer (XRD) with Cu-Kα radiation. A ﬁeld-emission
scanning electron microscope (FESEM) was employed to observe the
morphology of the samples. Transmission electron microscope (TEM,
FEI Tecnai G2) working at 300 kV was employed to characterize the
chemical composition of the samples. Ultraviolet–visible diﬀuse re-
ﬂectance spectra (UV–vis DRS) were carried out on a HITACHI UH-
4150 spectrophotometer. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectro-
scopy was detected employing IR Aﬃnity-1 FT-IR spectrometer. X-ray
photoelectron
spectroscopy
(XPS)
was
performed
on
a
Thermo

excitation source (1486.6 eV). The photoluminescence (PL) were car-
ried out using HORIBA FluoroMax-4 spectrometer. Time-resolved PL
spectra were measured on a FluoroMax-4 spectrometer. Nitrogen
temperature programmed desorption (N2-TPD) measurements were
performed using the Quantachrome Autosorb-iQ-C chemisorption ana-
lyzer. In situ Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy for the
coadsorption of N2 and H2O before and after simulated sunlight irra-
diation was performed on Nicolet IS50 spectrometer (MCT detector).

2. Experimental section
2.1. Materials and reagents
Dicyandiamide (DCDA) and acetonitrile were purchased from
Tianjin Guangfu Fine Chemical Research Institute, China. NH4Cl
was supplied by Tianjin Bodi Chemical Engineering Co., Ltd., China.
Benzylamine was obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co.,
Ltd. 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO), benzotriﬂuoride,
4-methoxybenzylamine, 4-ﬂuorobenzylamine, 2-methoxybenzylam-
ine, 4-chlorobenzylamine and 4-bromobenzylamine were provided
by
Aladdin.
4-methylbenzylamine,
3-methylbenzylamine
and
2,4-dichlorobenzylamine were obtained from Macklin. Terpineol
was supplied by Tianjin Damao Chemical Reagent Factory. Ultrapure
O2 gas (purity 99.999%) was purchased from Dalian Guangming
Special Gas Co., Ltd., China. All reagents used in this study were at
least in analytical grade without further puriﬁcation. De-ionized
water was used for all experiments.
2.2. Preparation of photocatalysts
g-C3N4 nanosheets (CNNS) was prepared according to a previ-
ously reported procedure [1], with slight modiﬁcations. In detail,
2 g DCDA and 10 g NH4Cl were added into 160 mL de-ionized
water, and the mixture was placed into a sonic bath for 5 min to
obtain a homogeneous solution. The solution was kept in a drying
oven to evaporate the water at 105 C. To increase the surface area
of CNNS, the obtained dried mixture was put in a crucible with a
semi-open cover and heated at 550 C for 4 h with a rate of 3 C/
min
in
a
mufﬂe
furnace.
Cyano-groups
decorated
g-C3N4
nanosheets (DCNNS) was prepared by thermally treating CNNS in
N2 atmosphere. In detail, 0.2 g as-prepared CNNS was heated in a
nitrogen atmosphere at different temperature of 450, 500, 550
and 600 C for 4 h with a rate of 20 C/min. According to the differ-
ent heating temperature, the ﬁnal samples were denoted as
DCNNS-450, DCNNS-500, DCNNS-550 and DCNNS-600. For com-
parison, bulk g-C3N4 (BCN) was synthesized by directly heating
DCDA (2 g) in a crucible with a semi-open cover at 550 C for 4 h
with a rate of 3 C/min in a mufﬂe furnace. Bulk cyano-groups dec-
orated g-C3N4 (BDCN-550) was prepared as follows: 0.2 g as-
prepared bulk g-C3N4 was heated in a nitrogen atmosphere at
550 C for 4 h with a rate of 20 C/min.
2.3. Photocatalyst characterizations
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were obtained
by using a Tecnai F30 TEM instrument (FEI). X-ray powder diffrac-
tion (XRD) patterns were taken on a Rigaku Corporation SmartLab
X-ray
diffractometer
equipment
using
Cu Ka
source
(k = 1.5406 Å).
Fourier
transform
infrared (FTIR)
spectroscopy
characterization of catalysts was performed on using a Bruker
EQUINOX55 infrared spectrometer. X-ray photoelectron spec-
troscopy (XPS) measurements were obtained using an ESCALAB
250 XPS system with a monochromatized Al Ka X-ray source
(15 kV, 150 W, 500 mm, pass energy = 50 eV). All binding energies
were calibrated to the C 1s peak at 284.6 eV of the surface adven-
titious carbon. Nitrogen adsorption and desorption isotherms were
measured on a Beishide apparatus of model 3H-2000PS1 system at
77 K. Before the measurement, all samples were degassed at 130 C
for 8 h. The speciﬁc surface areas were calculated via the BET
method, and the pore size distributions were calculated from an
adsorption branch of the isotherm via the BJH model. The UV–Vis
diffuse reﬂectance spectra (DRS) were recorded on a UV–Vis spec-
trometer (JASCO V-550) and were converted from reﬂection
to
absorbance
by
the
Kubelka–Munk
method.
The
room-
temperature photoluminescence (PL) spectra were investigated
using a ﬂuorescence spectrometer (Hitachi F-7000) equipped with
a 150 W Xe lamp with an excitation wavelength of 370 nm. The C/
N atomic ratio was determined using an elemental analyzer (Vario
EL, Germany) with speedy quantitative analysis of CHNS. The
room-temperature electron spin resonance (ESR) spectra were
collected with a Bruker A200 spectrometer. A microwave bridge
frequency of 9.5 GHz and 100.0 kHz modulation frequency.
2.4. Photoelectrochemical measurements
The photoelectrochemical investigations were performed on a
CHI660E
workstation
(Chenhua,
China)
with
a
conversional
three-electrode cell. In this electrochemical system, the sample
coated indium tin oxide (ITO) glass, a Pt pole, an Ag/AgCl electrode
(saturated KCl solution) and 0.5 mol L1 Na2SO4 aqueous solution
were used as the working electrode, the counter-electrode, the ref-
erence electrode, and the electrolyte, respectively. For fabricating a
working electrode, an ITO glass (2.0  2.0 cm2) was coated by as-
synthesized sample slurry, which had been prepared by mixing
10 mg photocatalyst with 500 lL terpilenol with the assistance of
sonication. Speciﬁcally, the slurry was dipped (50 lL) and spin-
coated (2000 r min1, 30 s) onto an ITO glass followed by the dry-
ing at 100 C for the next coating. The whole coating process was
repeated ﬁve times.

and dicyandiamide in static air condition. Then, the CNNS was
re-heated at different target temperature under inert atmosphere.
After cooling naturally, the DCNNS was successfully synthesized.
The as-obtained materials are designated as DCNNS-x, in which x
denotes the corresponding post-treating temperature (C). The
morphology of DCNNS-550 was analyzed by TEM. From Fig. 1a,
DCNNS-550 features a crinkly nanosheet structure with a size of
several micrometers. To examine the crystal structure of CNNS
and DCNNS, X-ray diffraction (XRD) characterizations were con-
ducted, all samples display two typical diffraction peaks, which
locate at 13.0 and 27.3, attributed to in-planar structural arrange-
ments of heptazine units and interlayer stacking motif, respec-
tively (Fig. 1b) [14]. Compared to the parent CNNS, the two
peaks of DCNNS gradually became weaker with the treatment tem-
perature increases, indicating the loss of ordered structures within
the framework. Moreover, the chemical structures of all the sam-
ples were analyzed by Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spec-
troscopy (Fig. 1c). The pristine CNNS features adsorption peaks
located at 810, 900–1800 and 3000–3500 cm1, ascribed to the
out-of-plane breathing mode of heptazine rings, skeletal stretching
modes of NAC@N heterocycles and the vibrational modes of NAH
bonds, respectively [18]. For the DCNNS, a new absorption band at
2178 cm1 related to the asymmetric stretching vibration of
AC„N groups [34,35], indicating the presence of AC„N groups.
Interestingly, the peak intensity of the AC„N group gradually
increases along with the increasing treatment temperature.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements (Sup-
porting Information, Fig. S1) were applied to determine the surface
chemical states, and the analysis results are listed in Table S1 and
S2. In the C 1s spectrum, three peaks centering at 284.6, 286.2 and
288.1 eV are assigned to standard reference carbon, carbon atom
attached to ANHx on the edges of heptazine units and sp2-
hybridized carbon in NAC@N, respectively. Notably, the 286.2 eV
peak of DCNNS-550 shows increased intensity in comparison with
that of CNNS, further conﬁrming the formation of AC„N groups
because AC„N groups possess similar binding energies to C-NHx
in C 1 s spectrum [34]. Correspondingly, the peak-area percentage
of 286.2 eV peak increases from 3.30% to 7.48%, while the peak-
area percentage of 288.1 eV peak decreases from 63.67% to
59.04%, clearly conﬁrming that the generation of cyano groups is
most likely due to the breakage of NAC@N heterocycles during
thermal treatment process [35]. Elements analysis (EA) was con-
ducted to investigate the elemental compositions. As listed in
Table S3, atomic ratio C/N for DCNNS-550 is 0.661, slightly higher
than that of CNNS (0.648), and this weak increase could be ascribed
to that the removal of nitrogen atoms is slightly higher than that of

. In detail,
5 mg of photocatalyst was dispersed in 2.5 mL of methanol with
the assistance of ultrasound. The mixture was bubbled with oxy-
gen for 0.5 h followed by the addition of 14 lL of DMPO. Finally,
the mixture was irradiated under a Xe lamp for 0.5 min, and then
was analyzed by ESR.
2.6. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations
The electron band structures of CNNS and DCNNS were carried
out using Dmol3 module in Material Studio 6.5 software package. A
two dimensional (2D) melon sheet was constructed to represent
the incomplete polycondensation of melon, with a large vacuum
space of 15 Å to separate two neighboring 2D melon sheets. A cubic
cell was adopted for the carbon nitrides materials with experimen-
tal lattice constants of a = 16.7 Å and b = 12.4 Å. The generalized
gradient
approximation
(GGA)
with
Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof
(PBE) function was employed for the DFT exchange correlation
energy, a 340 eV cutoff was assigned to the plane-wave basis set,
and the Brillouin zone was sampled by 3  3  4k-points.
2.7. Photocatalytic measurements for oxidative couplings of amines
The photocatalytic oxidative coupling of amines were carried
out in acetonitrile (CH3CN) solution in O2 atmosphere (1 atm)
under visible light irradiation (k > 420 nm). Typically, 10 mg photo-
catalyst, 0.1 mmol benzotriﬂuoride and 0.1 mmol substrate were
dispersed into 5 mL CH3CN solution in a 10 mL round-bottom ﬂask.
Prior to illumination, the reaction system was saturated with
ultrapure O2 gas, followed by illumination with a 300 W Xe lamp
(PLS-SXE300/300UV,
PerfectLight,
Beijing)
equipped
with
a
420 nm cut-off ﬁlter. The temperature of the reaction solution
was carefully maintained at 25 C during the entire experiment
with a homemade thermostatic control device. After the irradiation,
the photocatalyst was removed by centrifugation, the remaining
liquid was examined by GC and GC–MS. The conversion and selec-
tivity were determined using benzotriﬂuoride as internal standard.

2. Experimental section
2.1. Preparation of photocatalysts
All reagents used in this work were of analytical reagent grade and without further
purification. In a typical process, 1 g melamine was fully ground together with 5 g of
eutectic mixture of LiCl and KCl (in molar ratio of 59:41, with the eutectic point of
Journal Pre-proof
352 °C [48]) in an agate mortar more than 15 min to obtain a homo-disperse mixture.
After that, the grinded mixture was placed in an alumina crucible which covered and
wrapped with aluminium-foil paper, and then annealed in a muffle furnace at different
temperatures (450 °C, 500 °C, 550 °C and 600 °C) for 4 h with a heating rate of
5 °C/min. After cooling down naturally to room temperature in the furnace, the
obtained samples were washed with hot deionized water and ethanol for several times,
and then dried at 80 °C overnight. Finally, these as-prepared samples were uniformly
denoted as MS-CN. In detail, the samples synthesized at different temperatures were
labeled as MS-450, MS-500, MS-550, and MS-600, respectively.
For the sake of comparison, the bulk g-C3N4 was also prepared by a conventional
thermal polymerization route. Briefly, 1 g melamine was placed in the crucible with a
ceramic lid and heated at 520 °C for 4 h with a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The resultant
product was simply designated as B-CN.
2.2. Characterization
Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) data of the as-prepared samples were collected on an
X-ray diffractometer (D8-FOCUS, Bruker, Germany) with Cu Kα radiation (λ =
1.5418 Ǻ). Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra in the wavenumber range of
4000-500 cm-1 were recorded on a Nicolet 6700 spectrometer with KBr pellet
(Thermo scientific, USA). The morphology and microstructure observation were
examined by field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, SU8010, Hitachi,
Japan) and transmission electron microscope (TEM, Tecnai G2 T20, FEI, America).
Meanwhile, the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) spectra and elemental
Journal Pre-proof
mapping images were collected in an EDAX Genesis, which was attached to the
FE-SEM. The N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms at 77 K were conducted on an
automatic surface area analyzer (MicroActive for ASAP 2460, America), and the
specific surface areas of as-prepared samples were measured using the
Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
measurement was performed on a Thermo Scientific Escalab 250X spectrometer
equipped with an Al Kα X-ray source. UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) were
tested on an UV-2550PC spectrophotometer (Shimadzu Corporation, Japan), using
BaSO4 as the reflectance standard. The photoluminescence (PL) spectra of
photocatalysts were measured by a fluorescence spectrometer (Fluoromax-4P, Horiba
Jobin Yvon, New Jersey, USA), which was equipped with a 150 W xenon lamp as the
excitation source. The photoluminescence decay curves were performed from the
Fluorescence Spectrometer (FLS 920, Edinburgh Instruments, Livingston, UK).
2.3. Photocatalytic H2 evolution
The photocatalytic H2 production experiments were conducted in a sealable quartz
reactor with top visible light irradiation. A 300 W Xe lamp with a cut-off filter (λ >
420 nm) was used as the visible light source, and the fixed light-to-liquid distance was
10 cm. In detail, 100 mg of the as-prepared sample was dispersed in 100 mL aqueous
solution containing 10 vol% triethanolamine (TEOA) as the sacrificial agent for the
holes, and 3 wt% Pt as the cocatalyst was loaded on the surface of catalyst by the
conventional in situ photodeposited method using H2PtCl6·6H2O. The mixture
solution was continuously stirred by a magnetic stirrer. Before visible light irradiation,
Journal Pre-proof
the reactant system was purged by N2 for 30 min to remove air. The amount of H2
evolution was analyzed by a gas chromatograph (GC7900, Techcomp) equipped with
a thermal conductivity detector.
The apparent quantum efficiency (AQE) of the as-prepared photocatalyst was
determined by photocatalytic water-splitting H2 evolution under the monochromatic

2.4. Electrochemical measurements
The photocurrent response spectroscopy, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
(EIS) and Mott-Schottky plots were collected on a standard three-electrode
electrochemical analyzer (CHI760E, Shanghai). The as-prepared sample coated onto
the FTO electrode was served as the working electrode, an Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl)
Journal Pre-proof
as the reference electrode, and a Pt foil as the counter electrode. The Na2SO4 (0.1 M)
solution and 300 W Xe lamp were employed as electrolyte and light source,
respectively. The working electrodes were prepared according to previously reported
method [33]: 5 mg of photocatalyst powder and 10 μL of Nafion solution (5 wt%)
were dispersed into 100 μL isopropanol and 300 μL water, and then ultrasonic
treatment for 1 h to prepare a homogeneous catalyst colloid. Finally, the resultant
catalyst slurry was coated onto the precleaned FTO glass surface with an active area
of ca. 1.00 cm × 1.00 cm and then dried in air.

articles.title: Synthesis of synergetic phosphorus and cyano groups (C≡N) modified g-C3N4 for enhanced photocatalytic H2 production and CO2 reduction under visible light irradiation
