2. Experimental Section
2.1. Synthesis of pristine g-C3N4
Pristine g-C3N4 was prepared by traditional thermal polycondensation. Briefly, 6 g
of urea and 6 g of dicyandiamide were grounded in an agate mortar for 20 min. Then,
the mixture was calcined at 550 °C in a muffle furnace for 4 h using a heating rate of

5 °C min-1 in air. After cooling naturally, the yellow product was grounded for 30 min
to obtain a powder sample. The obtained product was 4.8 g and the yield was 40 %.
2.2. Preparation of phosphorus and cyano groups (−C≡N) modified g-C3N4
Briefly, the as-prepared g-C3N4 (0.4 g) was mixed with NaH2PO2 (0.2 g) at a
weight ratio of 2:1, grounded in a mortar sufficiently, and then calcined in a tube
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
furnace under Ar atmosphere at different temperatures ( 300 °C, 350 °C, 400 °C,
425 °C, 450 °C and 500 °C ) for 60 min using a heating rate of 10 °C min-1. Residual
PH3 was very dangerous, so strong oxidizing sodium hypochlorite solution (1 mol/L)
was used to absorb the residual PH3 at the end of the vent. After cooling naturally, the
resultant products were washed with water, NaOH (0.1 mol/L), HCl (0.1 mol/L) and
water again to remove any unreacted and potentially detrimental surface species. The
achieved products were denoted as g-C3N4 –x, x indicated the heating temperature. By
contrast, the preparation process of g-C3N4 treated by Na2HPO4 was the same as
g-C3N4 treated by NaH2PO2 except replacing NaH2PO2 by Na2HPO4.
2.3. Material characterization
X-ray diffraction patterns (XRD) were recorded on a Bruker AXS D8
diffractometer equipped with Cu Kα radiation (λ=0.154056 nm). Diffuse reflectance
UV−vis absorption spectroscopy was recorded using Shimadzu UV-2550
spectrophotometer, with BaSO4 performing as a reference. Morphologies and
microstructures of the products were characterized by scanning electron microscopy
(Hitachi S-4800) equipped with an Energy Dispersive Spectrometer (EDS) and
transmission electron microscopy (JEOL JEM-2100F). X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Fisher Scientific Escalab 250 spectrometer) with
monochromatized Al Kα excitation was used to analyze quantitatively the chemical
composition of the products and C 1s (284.8 eV) was used to calibrate the peak
positions. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were recorded using the FT-IR
spectrometer (Nicolet Nexus 670). The PL measurement was analyzed on a Hitachi
F-4500 fluorescence spectrophotometer at room temperature and obtained with
excitation wavelength at 360 nm. The time resolved fluorescence spectra were
recorded at 460 nm using a 377.8 nm excitation by Edinburgh FLS920 PL, decay

curves were fitted by using a biexponential decay function to obtain deconvolution of
the instrument response function. The Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) specific
surface area was measured by a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 apparatus. Isotopic
experiment was performed using 13CO2 (purity: 99%), and the produced CO was
analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS).
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
2.4. Photoelectrochemical measurement
Photocurrent response and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)
measurements were measured by a Princeton Applied Research EG&G 263A
electrochemical analyzer using a standard three-electrode mode with 0.2 M Na2SO4
(pH = 6.8) solution as the electrolyte, the catalyst-coated FTO glass as the working
electrode, a Pt sheet as the counter electrode and Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode.
The light source was a 300W Xe arc lamp coupled with an AM1.5 global filter. The
photocurrent response was measured at 1.0 V. To prepare the working electrodes, 50
mg of the as-prepared samples were dispersed in absolute ethanol and grounded for
30 min, the suspension was spin-coated on cleaned fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO)
glass and then calcined at 450 °C for 60 min in a muffle furnace.
2.5. Photocatalytic test
Photocatalytic hydrogen production was performed in a Pyrex top-irradiation
reaction vessel connected to a glass closed gas circulation system and kept at 15 °C
during reaction. 100 mg of catalyst powder was well dispersed in a 100 mL mixed
solution containing triethanolamine (10 vol.%) as a sacrificial agent. 1 wt% Pt was
photo-deposited on the catalysts through photo-reduction of H2PtCl6 dissolved in the
reactant solution. The system was evacuated several times to remove air completely
and then irradiated by a 300 W Xe lamp equipped with a 420 nm cut-off filter (λ≥ 420
nm) as the light source. The distance between the light source and the solution was
about 14 cm, and the average power energy density of the irradiation was about 200
mW/cm2 measured by PL−MW2000 spectroradiometer (PerfectLight, China). The gas
production in the reaction system was sampled and measured with a gas
chromatograph (GC-7806, Shiweipx). In order to investigate the stability of the
product, cycling experiment was taken out. The detailed procedures were as follows:

after irradiation for 3 h, the produced H2 was removed by a vacuum pump. Then, the
next cycle began under the same condition. And the action spectra were measured
under the same conditions with band-pass monochromatic filters centered at 420, 450,
520 and 600 nm, respectively. The quantum efficiency (QE) for H2 production was
measured with a 300 W Xe-lamp equipped with a 420 nm (±10 nm) monochromatic
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
filter as the light source. The irradiation area was 4 cm2 and the average energy
density was 55 mW/cm2. The QE was calculated using the following equation:

Photocatalytic CO2 reduction was performed in a 250 mL Pyrex top-irradiation
reactor at ambient temperature and atmospheric pressure. The opening of the reactor
was sealed with silicone rubber plug to form a closed system, and a 300 W Xe lamp
equipped with a 420 nm cut-off filter (λ≥ 420 nm) as the light source. Before reaction,
1 wt% Au was deposited on the catalysts through chemical reduction of HAuCl4 using
NaBH4 as reductant. 100 mg of as-prepared product was well dispersed in a 100 mL
solution containing 1 M NaHCO3, and the system was bubbled with high purity CO2
for 10 min. And the contrast experiment was carried out without adding NaHCO3 and
bubbling high purity CO2, before irradiation, the system was vacuumed by pump and
high purity Ar gas was bubbled for 30 min to ensure that almost no CO2 took part in
the reaction. The gas production in the reaction system was sampled and measured
with a gas chromatograph (GC-7920, CEAULIGHT, Beijing) equipped with a flame
ionized detector. In order to study the stabilities of the products, cycling experiment
was taken out. The detailed procedures were as follows: after irradiation for 3 h, the
produced CO was removed by blowing high purity CO2. Then, the next cycle began
under the same condition. And the isotopic experiment was performed using 13CO2
(purity: 99%), and the produced CO was analyzed by gas chromatography-mass
spectrometry (GC-MS).

articles.title: Metal organic framework derived heteroatoms and cyano (CN) group co-decorated porous g-C3N4 nanosheets for improved photocatalytic H2 evolution and uranium(VI) reduction
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental section
2.1. Synthesis of pristine g-C3N4 nanosheets (CNNS)
Generally, 15 g of urea was heated at 550 C in an alumina cru-
cible with a cover for 2 h (2.3 C min1) in a mufﬂe furnace. The
resultant yellow product was collected for further use.
2.2. Synthesis of Zn-MOFs precursor
Typically, zinc nitrate (Zn(NO3)26H2O) and hexamethylenete-
tramine (HMTA) with molar ratio of 5:1 were dissolved in ethanol,
respectively. Then, the Zn(NO3)26H2O solution was added to the
HMTA solution. Afterwards, the precipitates were obtained after
stirring for 30 min, centrifugation and washed repeatedly with
ethanol, and dried at 80 C.

H. Gao et al. / Journal of Colloid and Interface Science 570 (2020) 125–134
2.3. Synthesis of heteroatoms (Zn + C) and cyano (AC„N) group co-
decorated g-C3N4 nanosheets (DCNNS)
A series of DCNNS photocatalysts were prepared through direct
calcination of urea and Zn-MOFs precursor. Typically, 15 g of urea
was ground with Zn-MOFs precursor, and then the solid mixtures
were calcined at 550 C for 4 h (2.3 C min1) in a mufﬂe furnace.
The obtained samples were ground for ﬁne powders and marked as
DCNNS-x (where x = 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3, and x corresponds
to the mass (g) of Zn-MOFs precursor used).
2.4. Characterization
The morphologies were studied by scanning electron micro-
scope (SEM, JSM-7500) and transmission electron microscope
(TEM, JEOL-2100F). The crystal structures were investigated by
X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D8 Advanced) equipped with a Cu
Ka radiation. The chemical states were learned by X-ray photoelec-
tron spectroscope (XPS, Thermo Fisher ESCALAB 250Xi). Fourier
transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were recorded on a Nicolet-
Nexus 670 infrared spectroscopy. Nitrogen adsorption/desorption
measurements were conducted with an Autosorb-IQ2 (Quan-
tachrome Corporation) through nitrogen sorption. The speciﬁc sur-
face areas of the samples were calculated using the Brunauer-
Emmett-Teller (BET) method. Photoluminescence (PL) data were
collected on a Hitachi F4600 Luminescence Spectrometer. UV–vis
diffuse reﬂectance spectra (DRS) were performed using a Shimadzu
UV-3600 UV–vis spectrophotometer. Solid electron spin resonance
(ESR) signals of samples were investigated by a Bruker model A300
spectrometer at room temperature.
Fig. 1. (A) XRD patterns, (B) FTIR spectra of pristine CNNS and DCNNS-x, (C) N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms and the BJH pore size distribution curves (inset), and (D) EPR
spectra of pristine CNNS and DCNNS-0.1.
2.5. Photocatalytic H2 evolution
Typically, photocatalysts (10 mg) were suspended in tri-
ethanolamine (TEOA) aqueous solution (10 vol%). ~3 wt% Pt was
loaded on the photocatalysts by an in situ photo-deposition
method using H2PtCl6. The suspension was vacuumed thoroughly,
and then exposed to a 300 W Xenon lamp ((PLS-SXE, Perfectlight,
China)) equipped with a UV cutoff ﬁlter (k  420 nm). The amount
of evolved H2 was determined by an online gas chromatography
using argon as the carrier gas.
2.6. Photocatalytic U(VI) reduction
Typically, photocatalysts (100 mg) were added in UO2
2+ solution
(0.12 mM, 200 mL, containing 2.5 mL methanol as sacriﬁcial
agent). A 300 W Xeon-lamp with a cutoff (k  420 nm) was used
as the light source. And then, the solution was stirred in the
anaerobic-dark environment for 2 h to achieve adsorption/desorp-
tion equilibrium. At certain time intervals, 4 mL of the suspension
was analyzed to remove the photocatalyst by centrifugation. The U
(VI) concentrations were detected by Shimadzu UV-2600 UV–vis
spectrophotometer at 650 nm wavelength.

2. Experimental methods
2.1 The synthesis of catalysts
4 g dicyandiamide was firstly added in 20 mL deionized water. Subsequently, 2
g silicon dioxide (15 nm) was added under persistently stirring. After 2 h. Then
deionized water was removed at 80 oC by evaporation. The mixture were stayed in a
covered crucible and heated at 550 oC for 2 h to gain SiO2/g-C3N4.
1g of SiO2/g-C3N4 was adequately ground with various mass KCl and LiCl
Journal Pre-proof
molten salt (the weight ratio of KCl and LiCl was 11:9) in agate mortar for 20 min.
Then, the mixture were treated at 550 oC for 2 h under nitrogen atmosphere. After
cooling down, molten salt was washed by plenty of hot deionized water. Silicon
dioxide was removed by etching with hydrofluoric acid solution (60 mL, 7 wt%) for
24 h. According to the added mass of molten salt (1 g, 3 g and 5 g), the samples were
marked as mDCN-M-1, mDCN-M-2 and mDCN-M-3. As compared sample, the
Journal Pre-proof
preparation of the mesoporous g-C3N4 (mDCN) was obtained using the same
procedures except the addition of KCl and LiCl. Bulk g-C3N4 was produced via
heating 4 g dicyandiamide at 550 oC for 120 min and marked as DCN.
2.2 Characterizations and H2 evolution
The details were supplied in Supporting Information.

2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
2.1. Sample Preparation. 2.1.1. Preparation of Bulk g-C3N4.
Bulk g-C3N4 was synthesized by direct thermal polymerization of
dicyandiamide in a chemical vapor deposition furnace.2 Typically, 5 g
of dicyandiamide in sealed ceramic crucibles was calcined at 550 °C
for 4 h with 2 °C/min heating rate under an Ar atmosphere. The
brilliant yellow product was naturally cooled down to ambient
temperature and ground into powder for later use. The product is
denoted as B-g-C3N4.
2.1.2. Preparation of Atomic-Layered g-C3N4. The samples of
atomic-layered g-C3N4 were synthesized by the two-step thermal
exfoliation method. Typically, 500 mg of B-g-C3N4 was ﬁrst put into
the ceramic crucibles and heated at 550 °C for 1 h with a ramp rate 5
°C/min. After natural cooling, the samples were further heated at 500
°C for 2 h with a ramp rate of 2 °C/min. Finally, the sample was
collected and denoted as A-g-C3N4.
2.1.3. Preparation of Defect Engineering-Modiﬁed Atomic-
Layered g-C3N4. Defect engineering-modiﬁed atomic-layered g-
C3N4 was synthesized using high-temperature treatment and the
two-step thermal exfoliation process. Typically, 5 g of dicyandiamide
in sealed ceramic crucibles was calcined at 650 °C for 4 h with 2 °C/
min heating rate under an Ar atmosphere. The obtained orange red
product was ground into powder. Then, 500 mg of the product was
put into the ceramic crucibles and heated at 550 °C for 1 h with a
ramp rate of 5 °C/min. After being naturally cooled, the samples were
further heated at 500 °C for 2 h with a ramp rate 2 °C/min. Finally,
the sample was collected and denoted as A-V-g-C3N4.

articles.experimental_text:
4. Experimental Methods
4. 1 Material Preparations
5 g of melamine and 5 g of dicyanamide were carefully ground together for 30 minutes
to obtain a homogeneous mixture prior to transferring to a crucible, and 5 ml of solvent was
added to create a slurry-like composite. The mixture was directly calcined at 550°C for 4 hours.

After cooling to room temperature, the yellow samples were collected, ground, washed multiple
times with distilled water and ethanol, and stored for further use. The obtained materials were
labeled as HCN, MCN, ECN, ICN, and TCN, corresponding to using H2O, methanol (MeOH),
ethanol (EtOH), isopropanol (IPA), and tetrahydrofuran (THF) as modified factors. The control
sample, g-C3N4, named CN, was synthesized by the identical procedure without the addition of
any solvent.
4.2 Piezo-photocatalytic Evaluations
The piezo-photocatalytic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) generation was evaluated as
follows. First, 1 mg of the piezo-photocatalyst powder was dispersed in 50 mL of distilled water
in a 100 ml two-neck round-bottom flask. This mixture was placed in a custom-built
piezoelectric photocatalytic reactor equipped with an ultrasonic generator operating at an output
power of 60 W and a frequency of 40 kHz. The piezo-photocatalytic reaction was initiated by
irradiating the suspension with a 120 W full-spectrum LED light source. During the reaction
process, the system temperature was regulated by cooling water while ultrasonication was
continuously applied. After 30 minutes of irradiation, 1.5 mL of the solution was withdrawn,
filtered through a 0.22 μm syringe membrane filter, and analyzed for H2O2 concentration using
an iodometric method. This involved mixing 1mL sample with 1mL of 0.4 M potassium iodide
and 1mL of 0.1M potassium hydrogen phthalate solutions, followed by monitoring the
absorbance after incubating for 30 minutes by UV-Vis spectroscopy at ambient conditions at
350 nm. The absorbance values were correlated to the concentration of generated H2O2 via the
standard curve of H2O2.
4.3 Au Deposition Procedures
The modified g-C3N4 sample, which exhibited optimal catalytic performance, was
selected for the photo, piezo, and piezo-photo depositions of Au. For the depositions of Au (2%
wt), a suitable amount of HAuCl4 and 200 mg of the optimal sample were dispersed in 200 mL
 ORCID:  Content not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv. License: CC BY-NC 4.0

of an aqueous solution. The solution was irradiated under a 300 W Osram Ultra Vitalux lamp
and placed in an ultrasonic cleaner (60 W, 40 kHz) with continuous nitrogen bubbling into the
reactor for 30 minutes. Additionally, to maintain a constant reaction temperature of 25 °C, a
water cycling system was employed throughout the deposition process. The resulting product
was collected, ground, and washed several times with pure water and denoted as 2%Au-X-LU,
with X as the optimal sample's name. The comparison samples, 2%Au-X-U and 2%Au-X-L,
were synthesized using the same procedures but without light or ultrasound exposure,
respectively. Furthermore, the sample 0.2%Au-X-LU was prepared under the same conditions
as the 2%Au-X-LU sample but with a modified amount of the Au precursor.
4.4 Characterizations
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was employed to analyze the chemical
component of materials, while Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and 13C solid-
state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) were used to the chemical structure of
the catalysts. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) technique was applied to study the material
crystallinity and defects. Solid-state electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) and positron
annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) were used to study nitrogen defects in the materials. Scanning
electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was applied to evaluate
the bulk components of the prepared catalysts. High-resolution (HR-TEM/TEM) and EDS
studies were carried out using a Talos F200i transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher
Scientific) operating at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. N2 adsorption-desorption
measurements were applied to determine the prepared materials' specific surface area and
porosity. Besides, UV-Vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (UV-DRS), photoluminescence
(PL), and time-resolved PL (TRPL) measurements were also performed to analyze the optical
properties. XPS-Valance Band (XPS-VB) and Mott-Schottky plots were applied to describe the
valence band (VB) and conduction band (CB) positions of materials. In-situ EPR measurements
were also conducted to validate the formation of oxygenic radicals. Piezo-response force

2. Experimental
Preparation of MCS crystal. The MCS complexes were prepared as 
in our previous work [14] . In detail, Melamine (1 g) and cyanuric 
acid (1 g) were dissolved in deionized (50 mL) water at 80 °C, re- 
spectively. The MCS complexes were obtained by mixing the above 
two solutions. The MCS complexes were centrifuged and dispersed 
in 100 mL deionized water (the concentration of MCS complexes 
is 20 mg/ml). Then, 50 mL of the above solution was hydrother- 
mally treated at 150 °C for 12 h in a Teﬂon-lined stainless-steel 
autoclave of 100 mL. The MCS crystals were obtained after clean- 
ing and drying. The inﬂuence of hydrothermal treatment tempera- 
ture, hydrothermal treatment time, and concentration of MCS com- 
plex on the yield and morphology of the samples was investigated. 
In terms of concentration control, the other concentrations of MCS 
complexes are 10 mg/mL and 40 mg/mL, respectively. For the hy- 
drothermal treatment time, the MCS complex solution (20 mg/mL) 
was hydrothermally treated at 150 °C for 4 h, 6 h, and 12 h. For 
the hydrothermal treatment temperature, the MCS complex solu- 
tion (20 mg/mL) was hydrothermally treated at 120 °C, 150 °C, and 
180 °C for 12 h. 
Preparation of CNT, B-CNT, P-CNT, and S-CNT. (a) CNT: 1.5 g of 
MCS crystal was added to an alumina crucible (25 mL) and placed 
into an oven at 520 °C for 2 h to convert to CNT. (b) B-CNT: The 
B-CNT was prepared by adding boric acid (2.4 g) under the opti- 
mal conditions for the preparation of MCS crystal (150 °C, 12 h).

vert to B-CNT. Moreover, the B 0.6 -CNT and B 1.2 -CNT were prepared

of boric acid and MCS in 50 mL water is 0.6 and 1.2, respectively.

dihydrogen phosphate was used as the P source. The P 0.45 -CNT,

articles.title: Boron-Decorated Graphitic Carbon Nitride (g‑C3N4): An Efficient Sensor for H2S, SO2, and NH3 Capture

articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental methods
2.1. Materials and synthesis
All chemicals were of analytical grade and used as received without 
further purification. Dicyandiamide, C2H4N4 (99 %), and boric acid, 
H3BO3 (99.5 %) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. Deionized water 
(resistivity ≥18 MΩ cm) generated using ELGA LabWater water puri­
fication system was used during all experiments. In a typical procedure, 
4 g dicyandiamide and a certain amount of boric acid (H3BO3) were 
dispersed in 50 mL deionized water under magnetic stirring at 80 ◦C to 
form a homogenous solution. When the water was evaporated, the white 
solid was dried in an oven at 60 ◦C overnight. Subsequently, the solid 
was ground to get a uniform precursor. The obtained precursor was 
calcined at 650 ◦C for 4 h with a ramping rate of 2.5 ◦C min−1 under N2 
atmosphere. After cooling to room temperature, the obtained sample 
was ground, washed several times with deionized water and dried at 
60 ◦C in an oven. The B-doped atomic-thin g-C3N4 samples were denoted 
as B-ATCN-1, B-ATCN-2, and B-ATCN-3 for added H3BO3 mass of 0.45 g, 
0.90 g, and 1.35 g, respectively. The schematic illustration on the syn­
thesis protocol is shown in Fig. S1. In addition, two control samples were 
also fabricated, in which the atomic-thin g-C3N4 was prepared by cal­
cinating the precursor without the addition of H3BO3 at 650 ◦C for 4 h
within 100 min without any sacrificial agent by introducing C vacancies 
[44]. Yang et al. fabricated g-C3N4 nanosheets with controllable C
J. Lee et al.
with a ramping rate of 5 ◦C min−1 under N2 atmosphere and the sample 
was marked as ATCN. Similarly, pristine g-C3N4 was prepared with an 
analogous procedure but with a calcination temperature of 550 ◦C and 
the sample was labelled as CN.
2.2. Characterization
The surface morphology and elemental composition of the samples 
were recorded by field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) 
using a Hitachi SU8010 microscope equipped with energy-dispersive X- 
ray (EDX). Transmission emission microscopy (TEM) images were taken 
using FEI Tecnai G2 20 S-TWIN operated at 200 kV. Meanwhile, the 
thickness of the prepared semiconductors was measured using a Bruker 
Multimode 8 atomic force microscopy (AFM). The crystallographic 
structures of the samples were studied via X-ray diffraction (XRD) 
measurement on a Bruker D8 Discover X-ray diffractometer with Ni- 
filtered Cu Kα radiation at a scan rate of 0.02◦s−1. Elemental analysis 
for the determination of CHNS content of material was carried out on a 
Perkin Elmer 2400 Series II Elemental Analyser. The Brunauer-Emmett- 
Teller (BET) surface area and pore distribution of the prepared samples 
were measured through multipoint of N2 adsorption-desorption using 
Micrometrics ASAP 2020. To study the chemical states and composition 
of the constituent elements in the samples, a Phoibos 100 spectrometer 
(SPECS, Germany) with monochromatic Al-Kα X-ray source was applied 
for X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements. All binding 
energies were referenced to adventitious carbon signal (C 1 s peak) at 
284.6 eV prior to deconvolution. Besides, Fourier transform infrared 
(FT-IR) spectra of the samples were analysed on a Thermo-Nicolet iS10 
infrared spectrometer to identify the functional groups on surface of all 
samples. UV–Vis diffused reflectance spectra of the samples were eval­
uated using a Cary 100 UV–vis spectrophotometer (Agilent) equipped 
with an integrated sphere and BaSO4 was employed as a reflectance 
standard. 
Photoluminescence 
(PL) 
and 
time-resolved 
photo­
luminescence (TRPL) spectra were acquired using the LS-55 Fluores­
cence Spectrometer (PerkinElmer, Inc.) at an excitation wavelength of 
350 nm and HORIBA DeltaPro-DD time-resolved spectrofluorometer 
with a laser excitation wavelength of 317 nm, respectively.
2.3. Photoelectrochemical analysis
Photoelectrochemical measurements were conducted using an elec­
trochemical workstation (Autolab) with a standard three-electrode cell. 
The three-electrode cell system is composed of Ag/AgCl saturated with 
3 M KCl as the reference electrode, a Pt rod as the counter electrode and 
a working electrode. The working electrode was fabricated by spray 
coating an ethanol suspension of photocatalyst samples onto a fluorine- 
doped tin oxide (FTO) glass slide with a fixed area of 1 cm × 1 cm. With 
0.5 M Na2SO4 aqueous solution serving as the electrolyte, the mea­
surements were acquired under light illumination supplied by a 500 W 
xenon arc lamp (CHF-XM-500 W). The transient photocurrent responses 
were recorded at a bias voltage of 0.2 V while electrochemical imped­
ance spectroscopy (EIS) was obtained at an applied bias of −0.6 V in the 
frequency range of 10−2 to 105 Hz. Mott-Schottky plots were measured 
in the −
1 to 1 V potential range at frequencies of 1, 2 and 3 kHz.
2.4. Photocatalytic nitrogen fixation experiments
The photocatalytic N2 fixation performances of the photocatalysts 
were evaluated in a photocatalytic reactor with a quartz glass window 
under atmospheric pressure and ambient temperature, using a 500 W 
xenon arc lamp (CHF-XM-500 W) as the light source. The light source 
was assembled with a UV cut-off filter (λ > 400 nm) and positioned at a 
distance of 15 cm to the reactor. To eliminate the interferences of 
possible NH3 from environment towards the NH3 generation by photo­
catalytic NRR, the N2 feeding gas was first pre-purified by bubbling it 
through 0.01 M H2SO4 solution. The outlet gas is also purged through
Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering 11 (2023) 109511
0.01 M H2SO4 to retain any NH3 in the tail gas. The experimental setup 
and schematic diagram are as shown in Fig. S3. Typically, 30 mg of 
photocatalyst was dispersed in 80 mL of deionized water and the 
resulting solution mixture was sonicated for 10 min to achieve uniform 
dispersion. The reactor was sealed and purged with purified N2 (99.9995

articles.title: Novel carbon and defects co-modified g-C3N4 for highly efficient photocatalytic degradation of bisphenol A under visible light
articles.experimental_text:
2.1. Chemicals
Melamine (C3H6N6, Aladdin Chemistry, ≥99%), and oxalic acid
(C2H2O4, Aladdin Chemistry, ≥99%) were used without any puriﬁca-
tion. Ultrapure water with the speciﬁc resistance of 18.2 MΩ cm was
obtained by reversed osmosis followed by ion-exchange and ﬁltration.
2.2. Preparation of carbon and defects co-modiﬁed g-C3N4
Pure CN powder was synthesized as follows: melamine (10 mmol,
1.274 g) was put into a covered crucible and heated at 550 ℃in a
furnace for 4 h in static air (ramp rate: 1℃min−1), then the obtained
powder was grinded with a mortar. CxCN samples were synthesized
using new precursors. Typically, C1.0CN was prepared as below: oxalic
acid (10 mmol, 0.99 g) and melamine (10 mmol, 1.27 g) were added
into 100 mL ultrapure water, which was placed in a beaker (200 mL)
with stirring at 50 ℃for 5 h. Then the above precipitate was collected
after water washing for 3 times and then freeze-dried for two days.
Then, the obtained powder was put into a covered crucible and heated
following the similar procedure of CN. Diﬀerent oxalic acid: melamine
molar ratios (0.5:1, 1.5:1, and 2.0:1) were used and the samples were
calcined to obtain other C0.5CN, C1.5CN, and C2.0CN, respectively.
2.3. Photocatalytic test
A photocatalyst (20 mg) was put into a 200 mL beaker containing
100 mL BPA solution (10 mg L−1), where a light source was placed
20 cm above the solution surface. The reaction started with magnetic
stirring under a Xenon lamp (300 W, Microsolar 300) irradiation with a
420 nm cutoﬀﬁlter. After a certain reaction interval, 3 mL of BPA re-
action solution was collected for evaluating the photocatalytic de-
gradation activities. Related adsorption experiment was operated under
dark condition, and the test process is similar to photocatalytic reac-
tion. Cycling experiment was conduct as follows: after degradation of
BPA, the photocatalyst was collected with water washing for 2 times,
and then used for the next cycle experiment. The trapping experiment
was carried out to analyze main active species, where three types of
scavengers [tert-butyl alcohol (TBA, 10 mM), disodium ethylenediami-
netetraacetate (EDTA-2Na, 10 mM) and benzoquinone (BQ, 10 mM)]
were used for the active species [hydroxyl radicals (%OH), holes (h+)
and superoxide radicals (%O2-), respectively] [Wu et al., 2018a; Liu
et al., 2019] identiﬁcation during photocatalytic degradation of BPA
under visible light irradiation.
2.4. Catalyst characterization
Powder X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) patterns were performed on a D/
Max-Ultima ⅣX-ray diﬀractometer with Cu Kα irradiation (λ = 1.5406
Å) by a scan rate of 8°/min. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
was operated by a Talos F200s with an accelerating voltage of 100 kV.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) data were obtained by an
ESCALABMk 250Xi spectrometer with a C 1s reference peak at 284.6
eV. UV–vis diﬀuse reﬂection spectra of the samples were recorded on an
Agilent 300 spectrophotometer. The photoluminescence (PL) spectra of
the samples were tested on a PL-4500 ﬂuorescence spectrophotometer.
The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface areas were determined by
N2 sorption using a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 Plus HD88 analyzer.
Mineralization rate of BPA after photocatalytic reaction was de-
termined by total organic carbon (TOC), which was measured on a
M. Wu, et al.
Journal of Hazardous Materials 384 (2020) 121323
TOC-L CPH Total Organic Carbon Analyzer (SHIMADZU). The thermal
analysis of samples was operated on Mettler Toledo TGA2 under N2
atmosphere. An electrochemical workstation (CHI650E) equipped with
a standard three-electrode system was used for testing the photoelec-
trochemical performance. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) was
operated on */EMXplus-10/12 (Bruker).
2.5. Density functional theory calculations
All the calculations were performed based on density functional
theory (DFT), and the DMOL3 modulus was implemented for the cal-
culations of geometry optimization and band structure. The exchange-
correlation interactions were described by generalized gradient ap-
proximation (GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) function.
Spin-polarization was included in all calculations, a damped van der
Waals correction was incorporated using Grimme’s scheme to describe
the non-bonding interactions and 0.005 Ha smearing was used in the
calculations. The Brillouin zone was sampled with the Monkhorst-Pack
mesh with K-points of 6 × 6×1 grid in reciprocal space during elec-
tronic structure calculations. CN of 4 × 4×1 supercell containing one
single atomic layer with a vacuum width of 15 Å was used in our si-
mulation. The vacuum width is considered to be big enough to elim-
inate the interaction between the layers. All atoms are allowed to relax
in all energy calculations.

articles.title: Band structure engineering and efficient injection rich-π-electrons into ultrathin g-C3N4 for boosting photocatalytic H2-production
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental section
2.1. Synthesis of g-C3N4 and CNA
Urea (99%) and 2-Aminopyrimidine (98%) were purchased from Sinopharm
Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd (Shanghai, China) and without other purification. The
C-substitution for N in ultrathin g-C3N4 was synthesized by urea and
2-Aminopyrimidine copolymerization. Typically, urea (20 g) was transferred into the
beaker, and then heated at 150 °C (oil bath) until melting state. Afterward, different
quality of 2-Aminopyrimidine was added to melting urea liquids under magnetic
stirring. After cooling to room temperature, the obtained samples were placed in a
crucible with cover and calcined at high temperature in a muffle furnace (600 °C, 3h
and 5 °C min-1). The as-prepared catalysts were marked as CNAx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.4
and 0.6), in which x (g) represents the quality of 2-Aminopyrimidine added. In
comparison, the single g-C3N4 was prepared by thermal polycondensation of
melamine (bulk g-C3N4) and urea (g-C3N4) under the same experimental conditions.
2.2. Characterization
The chemical structure of g-C3N4 and CNAx were investigated by X-ray
diffraction (XRD, D/MAX-2500 diffractometer), Fourier transforms infrared (FTIR,
Nexus 470) and the solid-state 13C NMR information (Agilent 600 DD2 spectrometer),
respectively. The morphology and microstructure were analyzed by transmission
electron microscope (TEM, Tenai G2 F30 S-Twin) and atomic force microscope
(AFM, MFP-3D, America). The SBET were measured by N2 adsorption-desorption at
ASAP 2020 (Micromeritics America). The chemical composition and contact angles
were researched by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB250XI) and
contact angle goniometer (CAs, KSV CAM 200). And UV-vis diffuse reflectance
spectra (DRS) of the samples were obtained from a UV-2450 using BaSO4 as a
reflectance standard. The photoelectric performance of as-prepared samples was
measured by photoluminescence (FL, FLS 1000), transient photocurrent (TPC) and
electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS, CHI 660 C), respectively.
2.3. Photoelectrochemical measurements
This part is in the Supplementary Information.

2.4. PHE activity evaluation
The photocatalytic activity of the g-C3N4 and CNAx were evaluated by PHE
under visible light (300 W Xe lamp, λ > 420 nm). Briefly, 0.05 g of catalysts was
uniformly dispersed into 100 mL triethanolamine (TEOA, 20 vol%) containing
H2PtCl6·6H2O aqueous solution (1.5 mL, 0.1 mg/mL). Before the visible irradiation,
the PHE reaction system passes 20 min of Ar gas to exhaust the air inside. And the
temperature of the PHE reaction system was maintained at 20 °C through the
circulating water during the whole reaction time. The obtained H2 was analyzed by an
online gas chromatography system (GC-2030, Ar and N2 as the carrier gas, 5 Å
molecular sieve column, and TCD detector).
The apparent quantum efficiency (AQE) for PHE was investigated by the same
experimental setup. The light densities of incident light were 6.14 mW cm-2, 3.06 mW
cm-2, 8.70 mW cm-2, 9.54 mW cm-2, 11.02 mW cm-2 and 9.72 mW cm-2 for the 400
nm, 420 nm, 450 nm, 500 nm, 550 nm and 600 nm filters, respectively. And the
irradiated surface area was about 21 cm2. Additionally, the AQE was calculated

2.5. DFT Calculations
The structural optimization and transition states have been calculated using
DMol3 code [38, 39]. The generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the
Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional [40] and all-electron double numerical
basis set with polarized function (DNP) have been employed. The convergence
tolerance of energy, maximum force and maximum displacement are 1.0x10-5 Ha,

atom is absorbed on the surface of CN and CN-C, respectively. The Grimme method

for DFT-D correction is considered for all calculations. Each atom in the storage
models is allowed to relax to the minimum in the enthalpy without any constraints.
The adsorption free energy of an H atom on sample was calculated based on

articles.title: Facile synthesis of carbon-rich g-C3N4 by copolymerization of urea and tetracyanoethylene for photocatalytic degradation of Orange II

Urea were purchased from Kermel (99%, Tianjin, China), and

Graphitic carbon nitride was prepared by a thermally induced

ground to a powder for further use.

articles.title: Fabrication of alveolate g-C3N4 with nitrogen vacancies via cobalt introduction for efficient photocatalytic hydrogen evolution
articles.experimental_text:
Experimental
Preparation of alveolate -like g-C3N4 (ACN)
Alveolate-like g-C3N4 was prepared using SiO2 microspheres
as hard template. SiO2 microspheres were prepared by sol-gel
method using tetraethyl orthosilicate as raw materials. Firstly,
3.8 mL tetraethyl orthosilicate, 7.5 mL ammonia water (28 wt
%), 18 mL deionized water and 120 mL absolute ethanol were
accurately measured and mixed completely, the SiO2 emul-
sion was obtained for 24 h at room temperature. Then washed
to neutral with deionized water, and the resulting white
sample is dried at 60 C, SiO2 microspheres are obtained.
890 mg SiO2 microspheres were uniformly dispersed into
50 mL ethanol, then 1.25 g dicyandiamide was added after
ultrasound for 30 min, stirred for 24 h, and dried in an oven at
60 C. The dried solid was transferred to the crucible and put
into the mufﬂe furnace. The bright yellow product was ob-
tained by holding at 550 C for 2 h. Finally, the SiO2 nano-
spheres were removed with 20 wt% HF, washed to neutral

i n t e r n a t i o n a l j o u r n a l o f h y d r o g e n e n e r g y 4 5 ( 2 0 2 0 ) 2 4 7 9 2 e2 4 8 0 6
with deionized water, dried to obtain alveolate-like g-C3N4
(named ACN). In addition, bulk-like g-C3N4 (BCN) could be
easily synthesized by thermal polymerization of dicyandia-
mide at 550 C for 2 h.
For comparison, the ACN with different blending amount
of SiO2 microsphere (222.5 mg, 445 mg, 890 mg, 1.78 g) were
prepared, and name them ACN-0.25, ACN-0.5, ACN and ACN-
2.
Preparation of X%Co/ACN composite powder
Typically, 90 mg of the prepared ACN and the quantitative
Co(NO3)2$6H2O were dispersed in deionized water, and ultra-
sonically shaken for 2 h to obtain a suspension. Then, it was
dried at 50 C under a collector magnetic stirring (rotation
speed of 15 r/min). Finally, the dried solid is transferred to the
crucible, as well as the furnace temperature is increased to
500 C in 48 min under the ﬂowing nitrogen atmosphere,
maintaining at 500 C for 3 h, then cooled and ground to obtain
the dark gray solid powder. 5% Co/ACN, 10% Co/ACN, 15% Co/
ACN and 20% Co/ACN composites were prepared by adjusting
the initial Co(NO3)2$6H2O mass to 23.61, 49.82, 79.13 and
112.10 mg respectively.
Physicochemical characterization
Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were carried
out under Cu Ka radiation with D/max-2500/pc from 10 to 90.
The FTIR of the sample in the range of 400e4000 cm1 was
measured on the EQ55þFRA106 infrared spectrometer to
obtain the functional group. The morphology and structure of
the prepared catalysts were analyzed via using ﬁeld emission
scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, Hitachi S-4800) and
transmission electron microscopy (JEOL-2010) with a working
voltage of 200 kV. In addition, in order to explore the thermal
stability and composition analysis of the sample, thermogra-
vimetric analysis (DSC/TG, 449C, NETZSCH, SELB, Germany)
were carried out at a heating rate of 5 C/min from 20 to
1000 C in air. The chemical status of the samples was deter-
mined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) on an
ESCALAB 250XI instrument with an Al Ka monochromatized
source. The surface areas were determined by N2 adsorption/
desorption analysis on a Micrometrics ASAP2020 surface area
analyzer. Pore volumes and sizes were reckoned from the
pore-size distribution curves from the desorption isotherms
using
the
Barrett-Joyner-Halenda
(BJH)
method.
The
ultravioletevisible diffuse reﬂection spectra (UVevis DRS)
were obtained via a Shimadzu UV-2550 spectrophotometer
using BaSO4 as the reference in the wavelength region
200e800 nm. The photoluminescence (PL) spectra and time-
resolved PL spectra were recorded using the FLS-980 Edin-
burgh Fluorescence Spectrophotometer with an excitation
wavelength of 360 nm. Electrochemical impedance spectros-
copy (EIS) testing, Mott-Schottky plots testing and Transient
photocurrent-time (i-t) response testing were obtained using
an electrochemical work station (CHI760e Shanghai CH In-
strument Company). In order to further prove the existence of
nitrogen vacancies, the electron paramagnetic resonance
(EPR) spectrum was measured with Bruker A300-10/12 spec-
trometer. The amount of H2 was measured by an online gas
chromatograph (Beijing GC7900) equipped with a thermal
conductivity detector with nitrogen as the carrier gas.
Photocatalytic experiment
In the photocatalytic hydrogen evolution experiment, 25 mg
of the prepared sample was added to a mixed solution con-
taining 80 mL of water and 20 mL of triethanolamine (TEOA,
20% by volume as an auxiliary reagent). 3 wt% of Pt light was
deposited on the sample using H2PtCl6 dissolved in the reac-
tant solution. A 300 W Xe lamp (PLS-SXE300/300 UV) with a
cut-off ﬁlter (420 nm) was used, which was 10 cm from the
reactor, and the measured reaction system had a focusing
intensity of about 100 mW/cm2. After evacuating for 30 min to
remove air, the reaction cell was irradiated at room temper-
ature under magnetic stirring. In addition, the production test
of H2 was carried out for 5 h each and was repeated four times
to check the stability.
Electrochemical characterization
Photochemical tests were carried out on a typical three-
electrode electrochemical workstation (CHI 618E, Chenhua
Instruments Co., Shanghai, China) with Pt wire as the working
electrode and Ag/AgCl (built-in saturated KCl) electrode as the
reference electrode. Generally, the working electrode was
prepared as follows: 5 mg of the prepared photocatalyst was
dispersed in 3 mL of absolute ethanol, and 50 ml of Naﬁon was
added using a micro-injector. After the suspension was soni-
cated for 30 min, 10 mL of the ink suspension was dropped on a
3 mm diameter GC electrode, dried at room temperature for
2 h, and a 0.5 M Na2SO4 solution was used as the electrolyte. In
the photoelectrochemical measurement, a 300 W xenon lamp
with a cut-off ﬁlter (l  420 nm) was used as an excitation light
source, and irradiate the visible light under the bias voltage of
0.4 V. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) test
was carried out at an open circuit potential in the frequency
range of 1 Hze10 MHz, with an AC voltage range of 5 mV. Mott-
Schottky curve was obtained at room temperature with a
potential range of 2.0e1.0 V, a frequency of 1000 Hz, and AC
voltage amplitude of 10 mV. For electrocatalytic HER, the
electrochemical HER experiment was performed in a similar
typical three-electrode device with a bias scan range of 0.61
to 2.10 V vs Ag/AgCl in 5 mV steps.

It can be seen from the above reaction formula that the active
species in CO2 plasma are: CO, O, O, CO, CO2þ, C, etc.
In the as-developed equipment, the microwave surface wave
discharge mode was employed to generate CO2 plasma, which has
many advantages over traditional dielectric barrier discharge in the
material treatment process, including almost eliminated electrode
pollution, as well as much higher plasma density and richer active
component species. Therefore, the is in-depth carboxyl “defect” can
be developed by involving the regulation of the basic framework
structure of polymer semiconductors, rather than the conventional
plasma induced surface carboxyl groups adsorption modiﬁcation
[30].
2.2. Preparation of surface carboxyl defects and single atom Cu dual
endowed g-C3N4
Surface carboxyl defects and single atoms Cu endowed g-C3N4
nanosheets were prepared via a simple microwave surface wave
plasma technology by using CO2 gas as the working gas. In detail,
5 g of urea placed in a covered alumina crucible was heated at
550 C for 2 h at a rate of 10 C$min1. The yellow raw products
were ground into powder and named g-C3N4 for further use.
Then 5 g of raw g-C3N4 was well mixed with 0.1 g of
CuSO4$5H2O, put onto the sample stage in the plasma equipment
and treated using CO2 plasma for 3e12 min. The resulting samples
with 3, 6 and 12 min of plasma treatment were denoted as
CueCNeCO2-3min, CueCNeCO2-6min and CueCNeCO2-12min,
respectively. The Ar plasma treated sample was obtained using the
same equipment and conditions except for changing the carrier gas
source form CO2 to Ar. A raw CN þ CuSO4$5H2O mixture (mc-CN)
was synthesized by directly grinding at room temperature and used
as another control.
2.3. Material characterization
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded on a Bruker D8
Advance diffraction meter at 40 kV and 40 mA with Cu K radiation.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out using
Thermo Scientiﬁc escalab 250xi in Al Ka monochromatization.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were obtained
using JEM-2200F at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV. Spherical
aberration corrected transmission electron microscope test was
performed on a FEI Theims Z，Titan Cubed Themis G2300，JEM-
ARM200F platform. The nitrogen adsorption-desorption measuring
and Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) calculation was carried out on a
Micromeritics Tristar 3000 analyzer. UVeVis diffuse reﬂectance
spectra (DRS) were obtained under a Shimadzu UV-2600 spec-
trometer. Elementar Vario EL elemental analyzer was used to
perform elemental analysis. Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR)
spectra were collected was collected by a Thermo Scientiﬁc Nicolet
iS50 FTIR spectrometer. Solid-state 13C nuclear magnetic resonance
(NMR) spectra were acquired on a Bruker Avance III 400 NMR
spectrometer. Transient photocurrent curves and electrochemical
impedance spectra (EIS) were recorded by a ChI660C electro-
chemical workstation based on a conventional three-electrode
system. Photoluminescence (PL) spectra of samples were detected
by a Hitachi F-8000 ﬂuorescence spectrophotometer under exci-
tation at 367 nm. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signals
were investigated on a Bruker model EPR A300 spectrometer. X-ray
absorption spectroscopy (XAS) was employed to obtain the valence
state and structural information of the proposed monatomic
copper.
2.4. DFT calculation
Spin-polarized DFT calculations were performed using the
CASTEP package with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof generalized
gradient
approximation
exchange-correlation
functional.
The
CueCNeCO2 samples containing 48 atoms (including 1 H,18 C, 27 N
and 2 O atoms) were used as models. The core electrons were
treated with Ultrasoft pseudopotentials. Given the calculation cost,
geometrical optimization was conducted only at the gamma point.
The convergence criteria for the geometrical optimization were a
maximum force of 0.05 eV Å1 and a maximum displacement of
0.002
Å. The k-point meshes were 2  2  1 with the
MonkhorstePack method since the supercell was large enough.
After the optimization, the total density of states and differential
charge density of the different surface carboxyl defects and single
Cu atom endowed g-C3N4 systems were calculated with a cutoff
energy of 340 eV and a self-consistent-ﬁeld tolerance of 1  106 eV
per atom.
2.5. Photocatalytic performance test
To show the diversity and availability of the as-developed
photocatalysts, we performed photo-Fenton experiments and
photocatalytic hydrogen production analysis. The photo-Fenton
degradation of the RhB dye experiments was employed as a
model of practical refractory organics treatment, which was per-
formed under visible light irradiation (300 W Xe lamp with 420 nm
cutoff ﬁlter, radiation intensity about 50 mW/cm2) [31]. In a typical
process, 10 mg of a sample was dispersed in 50 mL of RhB dye
aqueous solution (20 mg L1) ﬁlled in a transparent quartz test tube
and stirred in the dark for 60 min for adsorptionedesorption
equilibrium. 250 ml of a H2O2 solution (10 wt%) was added to the
suspension to induce potential Fenton degradation reaction. Then
the Xe lamp was turned on, 1 mL of the suspension sample was
taken out every 30 min and measured by using UVeVis spectro-
photometer (Shanghai LG Technology Co., China, UV 752S14026).
The possible residual photocatalysts were removed by centrifuga-
tion at 7500 rpm for 10 min. Then we further evaluated the pho-
tocatalytic performance of the samples (30 mg) by testing the
hydrogen production activity by using MilliQ water and trietha-
nolamine (TEA) sacriﬁcial agent. Then ~1 wt% Pt was loaded as co-
catalyst via a conventional photo-deposition approach using
H2PtCl6. The light source was a 500 W Xe lamp with 420 nm cutoff
ﬁlter, provided a 60 mW/cm2 radiation. Hydrogen production was
obtained by gas chromatography (Shimadzu, GC-2014C) using
thermal conductivity detector.

articles.title: Defects remodeling of g-C3N4 nanosheets by fluorine-containing solvothermal treatment to enhance their photocatalytic activities
articles.experimental_text:
2.1. Materials
All chemicals in this work were analytical grade and used with-
out further puriﬁcation. Dicyandiamide (C2H4N4; 99.5%) was pur-
chased from Aladdin. Ammonium chloride (NH4Cl; 99.5%) was
obtained from Xilong Chemical Co., Ltd. Hydroﬂuoric acid (HF;
40%) was supplied by Shanghai Shenbo Chemical Co., Ltd.
2.2. Synthesis of pure g-C3N4 nanosheets (CNS) and bulk g-C3N4 (BCN)
The pure CNS were prepared referring to a previously report
[24], in which dicyandiamide was a precursor and NH4Cl acts as
a dynamic gas template to yield g-C3N4 nanosheets. The schematic
representation of NH4Cl mediated synthesis process of CNS is
shown in Schema S1. To be speciﬁc, 6 g dicyandiamide powder
and 30 g NH4Cl were dissolved in 200 ml deionized water and
evaporated at 80 C to obtain the dried mixture. Then the mixture
was placed in the crucible with cover and calcined at 550 C for 4 h
a heating rate of 1 C/min. Herein, the heating rate and semi-sealed
environment is important for introducing some defects in the
framework of g-C3N4 nanosheets. The BCN sample was obtained
by direct pyrolysis of dicyandiamide powder under the same con-
dition without the addition of NH4Cl.
2.3. Preparation of ﬂuorine modiﬁed g-C3N4 nanosheets
Fluorine modiﬁed CNS were synthesized as followed: 0.5 g
hydroﬂuoric acid was added into 30 ml ethanol and stirred for
30 min, then 0.25 g as prepared CNS were added into the above
mixture solution under vigorous stirring for 60 min until homoge-
neous dispersion. The resulting mixture were transferred into a
Teﬂon-lined stainless steel autoclave, which was kept at 140 C
for 6 h. Till air-cooled to room temperature, the light yellow pre-
cipitates were collected, washed with ethanol for three times,
and dried in vacuum at 60 C to obtain ﬂuorine modiﬁed CNS.
The sample was named as F-CNS. g-C3N4 nanosheets prepared by
the same solvothermal processing without adding hydroﬂuoric
acid were noted as Et-CNS.
2.4. Characterization
The X-ray diffractions (XRD) pattern were obtained on a Smar-
tLab X-ray diffractometer using Cu Ka radiation (k = 0.154168 nm)
at 40 kV and 40 mA. High-resolution transmission electron micro-
scopy (HRTEM) images were taken on a JEM-2010 EX microscope
operating at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. UV–Vis diffuse
reﬂectance spectra proﬁles were recorded in the range of 200–
700 nm with BaSO4 as reference by a Lamda 950 spectrophotome-
ter. Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) spectra were obtained
on a Bruker EMX-10/12 EPR spectrometer with X-band at 110 K.
The X-ray photoelectron spectra (XPS) measurement was carried
out using a PHI 5000 Versa Probe with monochromatic Al Ka exci-
tation, and all the bonding energies were calibrated to the C1s peak
at 284.6 eV. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) was
recorded on a Nicolet 5700 FT-IR instrument running at 2 cm1
resolution. Samples were mixed and ground with KBr followed
by pressing into ﬂake for IR measurement in the range of 4000–
400 cm1. The speciﬁc surface area was calculated by the BET
(Brunauer-Emmet-Teller) method from N2 (77.4 K) adsorption–
Please cite this article in press as: W. Lin et al., Defects remodeling of g-C3N4 nanosheets by ﬂuorine-containing solvothermal treatment to enhance their
photocatalytic activities, Appl. Surf. Sci. (2018), 
desorption data obtained from BELSORP-cMINI instrument. Photo-
luminescence (PL) spectra was collected at room temperature
using a ﬂuorescence spectrophotometer (Hitachi F-4600) with
excitation wavelength of 325 nm. Elemental analyses were per-
formed on an Elementar (Vario ELcube).
2.5. Photodegradation of rhodamine B
Photocatalytic degradation of rhodamine B (RhB) under visible
light was utilized to evaluate the photocatalytic activity of the
samples in a Pyrex photocatalytic reactor with a cooling water cir-
culating jacket ((BLV-GHX-V, Shanghai Bilang Instrument Co. Ltd)).
30 mg of catalyst was added into 50 mL of RhB aqueous solution
(10 mg/L). Prior to irradiation, the suspension was sufﬁciently stir-
red in the dark for 1 h to obtain the equilibrium adsorption state,
and followed by irradiation with a 500 W Xe lamp ﬁltered with
an 420 nm cutoff ﬁlter to reduce the fraction of UV light. At given
irradiation time intervals, 4 ml specimens were withdrawn and
centrifuged to remove photocatalyst particles. The concentration
of RhB solution was analyzed by ultraviolet spectrophotometer.
2.6. Photocatalytic hydrogen evolution
The H2 evolution test was conducted in Labsolar-III AI photore-
actor (Beijing Perfectlight Technology Co., Ltd). Brieﬂy, 50 mg pho-
tocatalysts were dispersed in 100 ml aqueous solution containing
10vol% triethanolamine. The photodeposition of 3wt% Pt on the
surface of as-prepared photocatalyst was carried out by adding H2-
PtCl6 to the reaction solution. A 300 W Xe lamp (PLS-SXE
300/300UV) with 400 nm cutoff ﬁlter was used as the visible light
source. Before irradiation, the above reaction system was evacu-
ated to remove air completely. The temperature of the system
was maintained at room temperature during the reaction. The
yield H2 was analyzed by an online gas chromatograph (GC
9890A) equipped with a TCD detector.

articles.title: One-step synthesis of iodine-doped g-C3N4 with enhanced photocatalytic nitrogen fixation performance
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental
2.1. Preparation of bulk g-C3N4 and iodine-doped g-C3N4
All chemicals were analytical-grade reagents purchased from Sigma-
Aldrich, Inc. and used without further puriﬁcation. Iodine-doped g-
C3N4 was synthesized by an in-situ decomposition-thermal poly-
merization method with dicyandiamide and KIO3 as the precursors. In a
typical procedure, 2 g of dicyandiamide with a certain amount of KIO3
was grounded carefully in an agate mortar and calcined at 823 K for 4 h
with a heating rate of 5 K/min under nitrogen atmosphere in a tube
furnace. The weight percent of KIO3 to dicyandiamide was controlled as
2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 15%. The corresponding samples were marked as
CNIX, and X represents the weight percent of KIO3 to dicyandiamide.
Pure g-C3N4 was prepared under the same condition but in the absence
of KIO3, and the sample was marked as CN.
2.2. Characterization
The obtained CN and CNIX were characterized by powder X-ray
diﬀraction (XRD, Rigaku D/max-2200/PC), transmission electron mi-
croscopy (TEM, FEI Tecnai G2 F30), UV/vis spectrophotometer (UV/
vis, Shimadzu UV-2500), X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (XPS,
Thermo Fisher, Al Kα, λ = 0.84 nm), Fourier transform-infrared spectra
(FT-IR, Bruker VECTOR 22), N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms
(Micromeritics ASAP 2020 apparatus), Fluorescence spectrophotometer
(PL, Hitachi F-7000) with an excitation wavelength of 365 nm, Time-
resolved PL spectra (Horiba Scientiﬁc), and Elemental analysis (EA,
Elementar Vario MACRO cube) to determine the phase structure,
morphology, UV/vis diﬀuse reﬂectance spectra, elemental composi-
tions and chemical states, speciﬁc surface area, photoluminescence
spectra and lifetime, and atomic ratio of carbon to nitrogen. The
thermal property of KIO3 was tested by TGA-DSC (Netzsch STA 449 F3).
2.3. Photocatalytic nitrogen ﬁxation
The photocatalytic N2 ﬁxation was conducted in a 50 mL jacketed
beaker with an external cooling water system. Typically, 20 mg of CN/
CNIX powder was dispersed in 30 mL of aqueous solution containing
5 vol% methanol (scavenger) by ultrasound. To remove the gas im-
purity, N2 was bubbled to the suspension with a ﬂow rate of 50 mL
min−1. Before irradiation, the mixture was stirred 30 min in dark with
bubbled N2 to establish equilibrium. The reactor was irradiated using a
300 W Xe lamp (PLS-SXE300D, Beijing Perfectlight Technology Co. Ltd)
with a power density of 191.2 mW/cm2 measured by an optical power
meter (model: CEL-NP2000, Beijing China Education Au-light Co., Ltd),
while the power density of natural sunlight outside was 76.8 mW/cm2.
At a certain time-interval, 2 mL of suspension was taken out for the
following NH3/NH4
+ concentration analysis.
Nessler’s reagent method was conducted to analyze the concentra-
tion of NH3/NH4
+. First, 1 mL of the suspension was centrifuged and
diluted by 4 mL of DI water in a 10 mL sample tube. Second, potassium
sodium tartrate solution (l mL) was added to the sample tube. Third,
Nessler’s reagent (1 mL) was injected and the system was stood for
10 min for full color processing. Finally, UV–vis spectrophotometer was
applied to measure the NH3/NH4
+ concentration at 420 nm.

2. Experimental and characterization methods
2.1. Reagents
Analytical grade melamine, lanthanum nitrate (La(NO3)3· 
6H2O), and other chemicals were purchased from Sigma-
Aldrich, (Hamburg, Germany) and were used without fur-
ther purification. In order to avoid contamination, deionized 
water was used for the preparation and washing of materials 
at a resistivity of ~18 MΩ cm.
2.2. Preparation of pure porous graphitic-C3N4 and La-doped C3N4
Pure graphitic-C3N4 was prepared through the air atmo-
spheric pyrolysis of melamine. Urea (8 g) was ground in a 
crucible, heated to 550°C at a rate of 5°C/min, finally, tem-
pered in the flowing air at 550°C for 2 h. The sample was 
then allowed to cool down to room temperature. The result-
ing powder was then ground with a mortar pestle. Residues 
absorbed on the porous g-C3N4 surface were removed by 
deionized water. In order to synthesize the doped sample, 
La(NO3)3·6H2O was added to melamine in the first stage, 
and the other procedures for pure C3N4 were then repeated.
2.3. Characterizations
The structural analysis of pure C3N4 and La-doped C3N4 
was performed by XRD. The XRD analysis was carried out 
by an X-ray diffractometer (Shimadzu LabXRD-6000, Tokyo, 
Japan) under Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 Å) at 30 kV and 30 mA.
The morphologies of the samples were observed by 
SEM (Model: JSM-6360) at an operating voltage of 20 kV.
The optical diffused reflectance spectra of the samples 
were detected by a UV-vis-NIR spectrophotometer (JASCO 
UV-vis-NIR-V-57, Easton, USA) in the wavelength range of 
200−800 nm.
The samples were irradiated under visible light to 
observe their photocatalytic degradation activities toward 
phenol and MB aqueous solutions in a handmade pho-
to-reactor. This photo-reactor was composed of two parts: 
the outer part was a wooden box of 100  cm height and 
65 cm width, whereas the inner part contained eight visi-
ble lamps, each one of 18 W, 60 cm length, emitting light at

A. Bouzidi et al. / Desalination and Water Treatment 204 (2020) 136–143
425–600 nm. The samples were put in a beaker with 50 mL 
of MB (20  mg/L) and were exposed to darkness to study 
the chemisorption for 30  min. Phenol (100  mL, 300  ppm) 
was exposed to light in the presence of the samples. The 
samples were then irradiated under visible light, and their 
activities were noted for every 15 min. The samples were 
finally analyzed by a 160 A UV-vis-spectrophotometer.

articles.title: Nitrogen vacancy and hydrogen substitution mediated tunable optoelectronic properties of g-C3N4 2D layered structures: Applications towards blue LED to broad-band photodetection
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental
2.1. Synthesis of variety of g-C3N4 samples
We have used Melamine (C3H6N6, Sigma-Aldrich) powder as the 
starting material and followed previously prescribed thermal poly­
condensation protocols with little modification for the synthesis of 
graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) [41,42,45]. 12 gm of Melamine pow­
der placed in an alumina crucible with lid was heat-treated inside a 
muffle furnace at ≈550 ◦C for 4 h with a ramping rate of 7 ◦C/min in 
static air atmosphere. After the furnace naturally cooled to room tem­
perature, the resultant whitish-yellow product was collected and prop­
erly grinded into powder using agate mortar. From various 
characterizations, it has been found that this powder grown in air 
ambiance has significant nitrogen vacancies. We have named this ni­
trogen deficient g-C3N4 sample as Nd-gCN. To modify the properties of 
this Nd-gCN via hydrogen substitutions at the nitrogen vacancy sites, we 
have further annealed previously collected powder inside a horizontal 
tube furnace at ≈530 ◦C with a slow ramping rate (2 ◦C/min) for 4 h 
under H2 ambiance with a flow rate of 100 sccm. Final brownish-red 
color product was collected and milled into fine powder. We
A. Ghosh et al.
designated this hydrogen substituted reduced g-C3N4 sample as H-gCN. 
Nd-gCN and H-gCN both are non-stoichiometric g-C3N4 samples. For a 
better understanding on structural properties relation of g-C3N4, we also 
have synthesized stoichiometric g-C3N4 sample through similar thermal 
polycondensation of Melamine powder inside horizontal tube furnace at 
≈550 ◦C for 4 h (ramping rate was 7 ◦C/min) in N2 atmosphere with a 
constant flow of 100 sccm. The resultant perfect yellow color product 
was collected after the furnace reached room temperature and properly 
grinded into powder using agate mortar. This stoichiometric g-C3N4 
sample grown in N2 ambiance was denoted as gCN. 
2D layered sheets of these three different types g-C3N4 samples (Nd- 
gCN, H-gCN, and gCN) were obtained via ultrasonic assisted liquid- 
exfoliation of the respective bulk powders in a water solvent. In detail, 
5 mg of each type of g-C3N4 bulk powder was dispersed in 10 mL of 
water and then ≈24 h of ultrasonication was done for a good exfoliation. 
After that, each of the suspensions was centrifuged at ≈3000 rpm for 2 
min to discard the unexfoliated g-C3N4 bulk particles and final 2D sheets 
containing suspensions were spin-coated on glass and silicon substrates 
at ≈800 rpm and dried on a hot plate at ≈100 ◦C for further charac­
terizations and studies.
2.2. Device fabrication
Electroluminescent device (LED) with highly luminescent nitrogen 
deficient g-C3N4 (Nd-gCN) as active emissive material, was fabricated on 
indium tin oxide (ITO) coated (thickness: 150 nm; resistivity ≈20 Ω-cm) 
glass substrates. First, we patterned the ITO/glass substrates having ITO 
strips of dimension 2 cm in length and 2 mm in width by masking with 
sellotape followed by etching in aqua regia (a mixture of HNO3 and HCl 
with a molar ratio 1:3) solution. Then patterned substrates were cleaned 
by ultrasonication in acetone, 2-propanol (IPA) and deionized water 
sequentially for 20 min in each solution followed by drying on a hot plate 
at ≈100 ◦C. We have purchased Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-poly 
(styrenesulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS, 3–4 wt% dispersion in H2O) from 
Sigma-Aldrich and used for this work after further diluted in ethanol with 
a volume ratio of 1:4, followed by stirring and ultrasonication for 30 min 
each. This diluted solution of PEDOT:PSS was spin-cast on the ITO strip/ 
glass substrates with a speed of 500 rpm for 30 sec and 1000 rpm for 30 
sec sequentially, followed by air annealing on a hot plate at ≈110 ◦C for 
15 min to get a film thickness of ≈100 ± 10 nm. This PEDOT:PSS film on 
ITO strip/glass substrate is utilized as a hole transporting layer in the LED 
device. Then emissive layer was spin-cast at 1500 rpm from the final 
suspension of Nd-gCN 2D sheets (previously described) on PEDOT:PSS 
film and dried at ≈110 ◦C in air atmosphere for 15 min, resulting in a film 
thickness of ≈80 ± 5 nm. Finally, Al as the cathode of ~ 200 nm-thick was 
thermally evaporated at the base pressure of ≈5 × 10−6 mbar using a 
shadow mask to define the device active area of 4 mm2. 
Broad-band photodetector device was realized by fabrication of H- 
gCN + PEDOT:PSS blend/p-type Si(100) vertical heterojunction device 
with top gold (Au) and bottom aluminum (Al) contacts. For the device 
fabrication, boron doped p-type Si(100) substrates (resistivity ~ 10 
Ω-cm) were taken and cleaned under ultrasonication in acetone, 2-prop­
anol (IPA) and DI water for 20 min in each solution sequentially, fol­
lowed by blow-dry with pure N2. Even though PL emission was 
quenched significantly in hydrogen substituted g-C3N4 (H-gCN) 2D 
sheets compared to Nd-gCN sheets, still H-gCN sample exhibits poor 
electrical conductivity. So, before using H-gCN sample in the photode­
tector, we have mixed H-gCN suspension with a diluted solution of 
PEDOT:PSS (described in the previous sections) with a volume ratio of 
3:1 under vigorous stirring, in order to ensure perfect blending. Finally 
H-gCN + PEDOT:PSS blend was spin-coated on cleaned p-Si(100) at 
1500 rpm and dried on a hot plate at ≈110 ◦C in an air atmosphere for 
15 min. The average thickness of the active blend layer on p-type Si was 
found to be ≈200 ± 10 nm. Then photodetector device fabrication was 
completed by depositing top Au and bottom Al contacts using a thermal 
evaporation technique at the base pressure of ≈5 × 10−6 mbar.
Applied Surface Science 556 (2021) 149773
2.3. Characterization and measurements
The morphological and structural characterizations on the different 
kinds of g-C3N4 samples were done using two different transmission 
electron microscopy (TEM) facilities rigorously; HRTEM, JEOL JEM- 
2010 and TEM, FEI - TECNAI G2 20S – TWIN equipped with energy 
dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDX), both operated at 200 keV. For TEM 
analyses, the as-prepared final suspensions of respective samples were 
drop-casted on carbon-coated copper grid separately and dried in a 
vacuum. X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements on the three different 
kinds of g-C3N4 samples spin-coated on glass substrates, were performed 
using Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ =
0.15406 nm). The ground state absorption spectra from the respective 
samples in suspension were recorded using UV–Vis-NIR spectropho­
tometer (Model: Avaspec-3648). The chemical composition and stoi­
chiometry of the samples were investigated using PHI 5000 Versa Probe- 
II (ULVAC–PHI, INC, Japan) system equipped with a micro-focused 
(100 µm, 25 W, 15 kV) monochromatic Al-Kα source (hν = 1486.6 
eV), a hemispherical analyzer and a multichannel detector. The room 
temperature photoluminescence (PL) properties of the spin-coated 
samples were studied using a PL setup with an excitation wavelength 
of 325 nm (He-Cd laser) and liquid samples (i.e., 2D sheets in water 
suspension) were examined using LifeSpec II fluorescence spectropho­
tometer (Edinburg Instruments) with an excitation wavelength of 375 
nm (diode laser). Raman spectra were recorded at room temperature 
using micro-Raman spectrometer (In Via Renishaw) equipped with a 
diode laser of 750 nm (IR), focused through a 50 × objective lens. 
The specific surface area and pore structures of the samples were 
determined following the Brunaeur-Emmett-Teller (BET) nitrogen 
adsorption/desorption and Barrett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) method at 77 
K using Quanta chrome Instruments (version 5.21). The photocurrent 
measurement has been performed in a three-electrode electrochemical 
set up with a computer controlled Biologic (SP-200) electrochemical 
workstation. Here, the sample modified indium tin oxide (ITO), bare 
platinum wire, and saturated calomel electrode used as working, 
counter, and a reference electrode, respectively, and the measurement 
was carried out in 0.1 M phosphate buffer solution (pH: 7.2) under on/ 
off of 100 W Xenon lamp. The electrochemical impedance spectrum has 
been recorded in the frequency region of 1 MHz to 1 kHz with an 
amplitude of 10 mV. Room temperature electroluminescent device 
(LED) was characterized under externally applied different bias voltages 
and corresponding emission spectra were recorded using TRIAX-320 
monochromator and Hamamatsu R928 photomultiplier detector. The 
current–voltage (I–V) characteristics of the photodetector devices were 
studied at room temperature using a Keithley 4200 SCS system along 
with two different light sources, 325 nm UV illumination (He-Cd laser, 
240 mW/cm2) and white light illumination (broadband solar simulator 
AM 1.5, 100 mW/cm2). Newport quantum efficiency/IPCE measure­
ment system (QEPVSI-b) equipped with a lock-in amplifier, mono­
chromator and broadband light source, was utilized for the 
measurement of external quantum efficiency (EQE) of the device.
2.4. Theoretical calculation details
Density functional theory (DFT) based first-principles calculations 
were performed utilizing Quantum Espresso [55]. The generalized 
gradient approximation using the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) 
functional was employed for the exchange and correlation effects of the 
electrons. The potentials of the atoms were described by the projected 
augmented wave pseudo-potential method (PAW) [56]. Using the 
optimized g-C3N4 structure, one N vacancy and H substitution at N site 
were created and the defect structures were further optimized. An en­
ergy cut-off of 600 eV and the forces on individual ions in the optimized 
structure were below 0.001 eVÅ−1. As a model, we have considered a 
confined flake with a vacuum of 20 Å along c-axis (to avoid spurious 
interactions) to estimate the work function.
A. Ghosh et al.
Applied Surface Science 556 (2021) 149773

articles.title: Oxygen doping through oxidation causes the main active substance in g-C3N4 photocatalysis to change from holes to singlet oxygen
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental
2.1. Photocatalyst synthesis
Bulk g-C3N4 (CN) was prepared from melamine by heat condensa-
tion (Jiang et al., 2018). Melamine (2.00 g) was heated to 550 °C in a
clean dry corundum crucible at a heating rate of 2.2 °C·min‑1. This poly-
condensation reaction was conducted for 4 h and then allowed to cool
naturally to obtain CN.
Oxidized g-C3N4 (OxCN) was prepared by ultrasonically dispersing
CN in concentrated nitric acid. The degree of oxidation depended on
the ultrasonic oxidation reaction time. CN (2 g) dispersed in concen-
trated nitric acid (30 mL) was subjected to ultrasonic oxidation for 0.5,
2, or 4 h. The oxidized dispersion was slowly diluted by pouring into de-
ionized water (150 mL). After centrifugal washing with ethanol and de-
ionized water to obtain a neutral supernatant, and drying at 60 °C for
12 h, OxCN1, OxCN2, and OxCN3 powders exhibiting different degrees
of oxidation were obtained.
2.2. Characterization of physical and chemical properties
To characterize the physicochemical properties, the catalyst surface
morphology was observed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
using an S-4800 SEM instrument (Hitachi Ltd., Japan). Transmission
electron microscopy (TEM) images were obtained using a JEM-2010F
TEM system with an acceleration voltage of 160 kV (JEOL Ltd., Japan).
To analyze crystal structures, X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were col-
lected using an X'Pert Pro MPD X-ray powder diffractometer
(Panalytical B.V., Netherlands) with Cu radiation between 5° and 80°
