articles.title: Unveiling the origin of boosted photocatalytic hydrogen evolution in simultaneously (S, P, O)-Codoped and exfoliated ultrathin g-C3N4 nanosheets
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental methods
2.1. Preparation of doped g-C3N4
Melamine is used as a precursor for g-C3N4 (referred as CN), and the
doping sulfur or phosphorus is supplied by thiourea and ammonium
phosphate, respectively. First of all, x g of (NH4)2HPO4 (x = 0, 0.5, 1, 2,
3) was dissolved in 50 mL deionized water. Then, 1 g thiourea was
dissolved to the above solution, subsequently, 10 g melamine was dis-
persed. After that, the excess water in the whole slurry was removed via
evaporation. Afterwards, the resultant solids were heated at 550 ℃for
4 h with a heating rate of 2℃/min. The resultant products were suc-
cessively labeled as CN-SP 0.5, CN-SP, CN-SP 2 and CN-SP 3. Similarly,
CN-S and CN-P were fabricated using the same procedure without
adding ammonium phosphate or thiourea, respectively. For preparing
oxygen doped CN-SP sample, CN-SP powders were further heat treated
via the secondary and the third pyrogenation at 550 ℃for 1 h with a
heating rate of 5℃/min and the as-obtained sample was named as CN-
SPM and CN-SPO, respectively.
2.2. Characterization
The powder X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) patterns were obtained using
Bruker D8 advance X-ray diﬀractometer at room temperature using Cu
Kα (λ = 0.15406 nm). Infrared spectrometer (FT-IR) was carried out on
the Nicolet company Nicolet Nexus 470. The speciﬁc surface area was
determined by the multipoint Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method
on NETZSCH NOVA3000e. The morphology of the products was ob-
served via scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL JXA-840A) and
transmission electron microscopic (TEM, Japan JEM-100CX II100 kV).
X-ray photoelectron spectrum (XPS) was characterized by PHI-5000C
system. UV–vis diﬀused reﬂectance spectra were recorded using a
UV–vis spectrophotometer (UV2550, Japan Shimadzu). Fluorescence
spectrophotometer (Hitachi, F-7000) and electrochemical workstation
(Chenhua Instruments, CHI660D) with a three electrode system were
used to record the Photoluminescence (PL) spectra, photocurrent re-
sponse and EIS Nyquist plots. The electron spin resonance (ESR) mea-
surements were carried out at X-band frequency on a Bruker A300
spectrometer with 2,2,6,6-Tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) ra-
dical capture reagent. Typically, the photocatalyst (0.10 g) was added
to a NaHCO3 aqueous solution (for TEMPO-e−signal) or acetonitrile
solution (for TEMPO-h+ signal) containing TEMPO (0.05 mM) within a
container. After deoxidized, the mixture was photoirradiated for 15 min
and then the photocatalyst was recovered by ﬁltration, and the solution
was transferred to ESR analysis.
2.3. Photocatalytic hydrogen production
The photocatalyti C-H2 evolving experiments were conducted in an
on-line photocatalytic hydrogen production system (LabSolar-3AG,
PerfectLight, Beijing). Typically, 10 mg catalysts were suspended in a
mixture solution of 80 mL distilled water, 20 mL triethanolamine and
3 wt.% H2PtCl6. A 300W Xenon lamp (PLS-SXE 300C (BF)), equipped
with a 420-nm cut-oﬀﬁlter was used as the light irradiation source. Gas
evolution was analyzed by an on-line gas chromatograph (GC D7900 P,
TCD detector).
2.4. Density functional theory calculation
Calculations were performed using the CASTEP code [39], based on
density functional theory (DFT) using the plane-wave pseudopotential
method, and the generalized-gradient approximation of Perdew, Burke,
Ernzerhof (PBE-GGA) [40] for exchange correlation. The electron wave
function was expanded in plane waves with a cutoﬀenergy of 340 eV.
For the smallest g-C3N4 supercell, a 7 × 7 × 1 Monkhorst-Pack grid
[41] was used for irreducible Brillouin zone sampling. For the larger
supercells, a 3 × 3 × 1 grid was used. Test calculations show that using
more k-points does not lead to evident changes in the energetic con-
vergence, electronic band structures and density maps for the electronic
states. The total energy is converged to 1.0 × 10−5 eV/atom, and all
the geometries are fully relaxed until the quantum mechanical forces
acting on the atoms become less than 0.03 eV/Å.

articles.title: Confining Single-atom Pd on g-C3N4 with Carbon Vacancies towards Enhanced Photocatalytic NO Conversion
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental Section
2.1. Catalysts preparation
Synthesis of g-C3N4: g-C3N4 was synthesized using urea as precursor. 20 g of urea was put into an
alumina crucible and transferred to a tube furnace. Then, the crucible was heated with 5 oC/min heating rate

and finally held at 600 oC for 2 h under N2 atmosphere. The resultant powder was denoted as CN.
Synthesis of g-C3N4 modified with carbon vacancies: g-C3N4 modified with carbon vacancies was
synthesized using urea as precursor following a protocol previously reported [39]. In a typical run, 20 g of
urea was put into an alumina crucible and transferred to a muffle furnace. Then, the crucible was heated with
5 oC/min heating rate and finally held at 600, 550 or 500 oC for 2 h in the air. The resultant powder was
washed with deionized water to remove the surface salts and followed by drying at -50 oC in a vacuum
Journal Pre-proof
freeze dryer oven overnight. The final product was denoted as Cv-CN, Cv-CN-1 and Cv-CN-2, which
represented the samples heated at 600, 550 and 500 oC, respectively.
Synthesis of single-atom catalyst：0.5 mL aqueous solution of PdCl2 (1 mg/mL) and NaCl (5 mg/mL)
were dissolved in 50 mL deionized water. Then, 0.1 g of g-C3N4 modified with carbon vacancies was added
into the above solution. The mixture was kept stirring in an oil bath at 80 oC for 8 h. After filtration and
washing, the precipitate was dispersed in 50 mL deionized water and irradiated under the light of 420 nm
wavelength by using a cut-off optical filter for 1 h to proceed the reduction of Pd2+. Finally, the resultant
precipitate was washed and then dried in a vacuum freeze dryer at -50 oC overnight. The final product was
denoted as Pd-Cv-CN. The Pd-CN was prepared by the same routine by using CN as support.
Different load amount of Pd modified with Cv-CN was also synthesized, the final samples were
denoted as xPd-Cv-CN, where x was the mass fraction of Pd.
The nanosized Pd particles loaded on Cv-CN (Pdnano –Cv-CN) was obtained by directly photo-reduction
for 3 h.
2.2. Characterization
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observations were obtained using a Titan G260-300
microscope. Aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM characterization and energy-dispersive X-ray
spectroscopy mapping images were performed on a Cs-corrected Titan G2 60-300 electron microscope (FEI,
USA). X-ray diffractions were conducted to identify crystal phases by a D8 Rigaku9000 using a Cu kα

radiation in the 2θ range of 5-800. Fourier transform infrared spectra (FT-IR) of the samples were recorded
on a NICOLET iS10 FT-IR spectrometer. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) study was performed on
a Thermo Scientific K-Alpha+ spectrometer. UV-Vis diffuse reflectance (UV-Vis DRS), photoluminescence
(PL), and time-resolved transient PL decay spectroscopic analyses were achieved on a UV−8000A system,
Edinburgh fls1000 spectrophotometer with an excitation wavelength of 360 nm, respectively. Electron
Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR Bruker, a300) was applied to identify the carbon vacancies and
Journal Pre-proof
photo-induced reactive oxygen species, ·O2- and ·OH-. XAFS spectroscopy of Pd K-edge was recorded at
TPS 44A1 of National Synchrotron Radiation Research Center (NSRRC), the electron storage ring was
operated at 3 GeV with a constant current of 250 mA.
2.3. Computational details
All the calculations in this work were performed using the CASTEP program within the Perdew–
Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional of Generalized Gradient Approximation (GGA) in
Materials Studio software (7.0). The cutoff energy was set as 600 eV. A series of geometrical structures were
built based on a graphitic carbon nitride with the stoichiometric vacancy defects on carbon sites measured by
XPS. The k-points were set as 15×15×1 in order to reveal the 2D properities of Pd-CN. The 2s and 2p
electrons of nitrogen and carbon atoms and 4s, 4d, 4f and 5s electrons of palladium atoms were treated as
valence electrons. Besides, ultrasoft pseudopotentials were used and the relevant representations were
carried out in reciprocal space. The set SCF tolerance was 5.0×10-7 eV/atom. The formation energy is
calculated by the following Eq. (1):
𝐸𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛= 𝐸𝑃𝑑−𝐶𝑁−𝐸tst−C −𝐸𝑃𝑑 (1)
where Eformation is the formation energy of single-atom Pd based on g-C3N4, Epd-CN and Etst are the total
energies of Pd-loaded samples and pure tri-s-triazine g-C3N4, respectively, after geometry optimization.
2.4. Photocatalytic NO conversion

Photocatalytic NO oxidation was conducted under a continuous flow in a column-like reactor of 12.8
cm in diameter, 9.7 cm in height, and mean volume of 4.5 L. 20 mg of the photocatalyst was dispersed by
ultrasonic onto a glass dish with the diameter of 5.8 cm and placed in the middle of the reactor. The NO gas
was provided from a compressed gas cylinder with a concentration of 100 ppm balanced by Argon gas,
which was further diluted to about 2.2 ppm by an air stream with a flow rate of 1.7 L/min. The reaction
temperature was 298 K controlled by a circulating cooling water system and relative humidity was kept
Journal Pre-proof
around 50%. After reaching adsorption-desorption equilibrium, the 300 W Xe lamp was turn on placed
vertically above the reactor. The concentration of NO and NO2 were measured by a NO2/NO/NOx monitor
(2B Technologies, USA). The cycling test was conducted in a similar route: after the first performance test
as mentioned above, the NO stream and light source were turned off, keeping the sample decontaminated by
the remaining air for 30 min for fully desorption. Afterwards, the NO stream was released again to maintain
the normal concentration of NO. After reaching adsorption-desorption equilibrium, the light source was
switched on for about 30 min. The next cycling test followed the same routine.
After the photocatalytic conversion NO experiment was terminated, the off-line sample was
immediately took out from the reactor and mixed with 6 mL of deionized water and kept under stirring for
30 min to ensure complete dissolving of the surface oxidation products in deionized water. Thereafter, the
suspension was filtered with a 0.22 μm membrane. A 2.5 mL solution of the obtained supernatant was added
to 0.2 mL of Griess reagent to attain a colorful product after 20 min [40]. Then, the amount of NO2- was
measured under the wavelength of 520 nm. The amount of NO3- ion in this solution can be determined by
using UV spectrophotometry method under the wavelength of 220 nm and 275 nm [41]. In comparison, the
amount of NO2- /NO3- was also tested of the sample before the reaction.
The removal ratio of NO was calculated according to Eq. (2):
η(NO,%)=(1-[NO]o/[NO]i)×100% (2)
where [NO]o and [NO]i mean the concentration of NO in the outlet and feeding streams, respectively.

P, K co-doped porous g-C3N4 with enhanced photocatalytic activity synthesized in vapor and self-producing NH3 atmosphere

2. Experimental
2.1. Chemicals and reagents
All chemical reagents were commercially sourced and used without
further puriﬁcation. These included dicyandiamide (C2H4N4, AR, 99%,
TianJin Guangfu Co., Ltd), dipotassium hydrogen phosphate (K2HPO4,
AR, 99%, Co., Ltd), phosphoric acid (H3PO4, AR, 85%, Co., Ltd), po-
tassium chloride (KCl, AR, 99%, Tianjin Xinqiao Co., Ltd), rhodamine B
(C28H31ClN2O3, AR, 99%, Co., Ltd), and deionized water.
2.2. Preparation of photocatalysts
The preparation of Bulk and modiﬁed g-C3N4 is illustrated in
Scheme 1. Illustration of the experimental processes of Bulk and modiﬁed g-C3N4.
Scheme 1. Bulk-C3N4 (labeled as BCN) was synthesized by heating di-
cyandiamide at 550 °C for 4 h in a N2 atmosphere.
To synthesize P, K co-doped g-C3N4, 5 g of dicyandiamide and
15 mL of deionized (DI) water, with varied amounts of K2HPO4, were
added to a 50 mL crucible. After being ultrasonicated and stirred for
120 min, the obtained suspension was heated to 90 °C to dissolve
completely and was dried to a paste with constant stirring. Next, the
precursors were heated from room temperature to 550 °C with a heating
rate of 10 °C/min, and were maintained at 550 °C for 240 min in a tube
furnace without the addition of other gases. All the samples were pre-
pared concurrently. Finally, the tube furnace was naturally cooled to
room temperature, following which some yellow products were ob-
tained and grounded. These products, obtained using 0, 20, 40, 60, 80,
and 100 mg of K2HPO4, are denoted as CN-0PK, CN-20PK, CN-40PK,
CN-60PK, CN-80PK, and CN-100PK, respectively. P and K single-doped
g-C3N4 (labeled as CN-P and CN-K) were synthesized by replacing
K2HPO4 with H3PO4 and KCl during the experiment. The doping
amounts were determined by the sample CN-80PK, which includes the
same amount of the P or K in the dopants. Furthermore, to clarify that
the vapor generated from the residual water played an important role in
increasing the speciﬁc surface area of g-C3N4, another undoped g-C3N4
(marked as CN) was synthesized solely by the same process as that for
CN-0PK, except for the complete removal of water before heating in the
tube furnace.
2.3. Characterization
X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) patterns were collected using a D8 advance
(Bruker, Germany). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was per-
formed using the S-4800 (Hitachi, Japan). Additionally, transmission
electron microscopy (TEM) and elemental mapping images were ob-
tained using a Jem-2100F device (Jeol, Japan). UV‐Vis DRS analysis
was performed on a UV2600 instrument (Shimadzu, Japan) with BaSO4
as the reference. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was per-
formed using the ESCALAB 250xi (Thermo, USA). Nitrogen adsorption-
desorption tests were performed using a tri 3020 BET analyzer
(Micromeritics, USA). Photoluminescence (PL) emission spectra were
obtained on a Fluorolog3 ﬂuorescence spectrophotometer (HORIBA
JOBIN YVON, USA) under xenon lamp irradiation at 325 nm. Finally,
the photocurrent (PC) response curves were acquired using the CHI
660E equipment (CH Instruments Inc., USA) with a three-electrode
system (Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode).
2.4. Evaluation of photocatalytic and adsorptive activities
The photocatalytic activities were evaluated under RhB (20 mg/L)
degradation. A 300 W Xe lamp (CEL-HXF300) with a cut-oﬀﬁlter
H. Shen, et al.
Applied Surface Science 507 (2020) 145086

and 3500 cm−1 are derived from NeH stretching. For the other three
modiﬁed samples, a distinct peak at 2347 cm−1 can be detected, which
is ascribed to the CO2 adsorbed from the air [22]. Moreover, a weak
peak at 2162 cm−1 could be observed on CN-80PK and CN-K, which is
attributed to the defects of the cyano group (C^N) stretch formed by
the incomplete polymerization. The K-doped g-C3N4 synthesized by
Zhang et al. also displays the same peak [37]; therefore, we can con-
clude that K atoms may be helpful to create cyano group defects during
polymerization, which is beneﬁcial to improving the photocatalytic
performances.
The morphologies and microstructures of the samples were char-
acterized by SEM and TEM. As clearly seen in Fig. 2a and b, BCN shows
a typical stacked structure. On the contrary, CN-0PK and CN-80PK show
a loosely gathered sheet-like morphology with more porous structures.
The corresponding TEM images (Fig. 2d and f) further conﬁrm the
thinner sheet-like morphology because of the transparency. These re-
sults indicate that the vapor and the self-producing NH3 atmosphere
play an important role in the crystallization process, making the sam-
ples more porous and eﬃcient. Comparing CN-0PK and CN-80PK, we
can conclude that the introduction of P and K has no positive eﬀect on
loosening g-C3N4. Moreover, element mapping was performed to detect
the element distribution. As shown in Fig. 3, C and N are the main
elements, and P, O, and K are uniformly dispersed in the g-C3N4 matrix.
The mapping proﬁles of P and K prove that the doping atoms are suc-
cessfully doped in the g-C3N4 matrix, and the O atoms in our samples
originate from the adsorbed water on the surface of the catalysts [38].
XPS was performed to conﬁrm the surface elemental composition of
the samples and the corresponding chemical states of the elements. The
survey spectra of several representative samples are shown in Fig. S2.
No distinct diﬀerences could be observed because the doping atoms are
low in quantity and hard to detect. The spectra of C 1s, N 1s, P 2p, and K
2p are also displayed for further analysis. The C 1s high-resolution
spectra of CN-0PK and CN-80PK are compared in Fig. 4a. Three distinct
peaks (284.8 eV, 288.1 eV, 288.5 eV) can be easily detected from the
CN-0PK sample, which could be assigned to the typical CeC bonds, sp2-
hybridized N]CeN bonds, and CeNH2 species, respectively, in the g-
C3N4 aromatic structure. Further, we can see that the CN-80PK peaks
undergo a slight shift to a higher energy zone of the C 1s binding en-
ergies compared with CN-0PK. The N 1s high-resolution XPS proﬁles
(Fig. 4b) of CN-0PK can be divided into three peaks located at 398.5 eV,
399 eV, and 400.9 eV. The ﬁrst peak located at 398.5 eV is attributed to
the sp2-bonded nitrogen (CeN]C). The peak at 399 eV is assigned to
the Ne(C)3 groups in the tri-s-triazine rings, while the last peak at
400.9 eV represents the terminal amino functional groups (NeH2 and
NeH). As for CN-80PK, the ratio of the two peak areas located between
398 eV and 400 eV indicates a distinct diﬀerence from CN-0PK.
Meanwhile, a clear positive shift could be detected. The results conﬁrm
(λ ≥420 nm) was used as the light source. The photocatalysts (20 mg)
was transferred into a 100 mL (20 mg/L) RhB aqueous solution. The
mixture was treated under ultrasonication for 20 min and stirred in the
dark for another 20 min to attain adsorption equilibrium. After ex-
posure to light, 3 mL of the suspension was collected at an interval of
20 min and centrifuged, following which the concentration of RhB was
measured on a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (absorption wavelength:
554 nm).
RhB adsorption experiments were employed to reveal the adsorp-
tion capability. Firstly, 50 mg of photocatalysts was transferred into a
100 mL (10 mg/L) RhB aqueous solution, then the suspension was
stirred in the dark. Start from stirring, 3 mL of the suspension was
collected at 0, 10, and 30 min, then centrifuged and measured.
2.5. Trapping experiments
The trapping experiments were almost the same as the above-
mentioned photodegradation processes, the diﬀerence being the addi-
tion of various quenchers. A moderate amount of isopropanol (IPA),
benzoquinone (BQ), or triethanolamine (TEOA) was added to the
mixture solution containing the catalyst and RhB before light exposure.

2.1. Preparation of g-C3N4
All reagents were commercial and used without further pur­
ification, which were supplied by Aladdin Industrial Corporation and 
Sinopharm Chemical Reagents Co., Ltd. g-C3N4 was fabricated 
through heating the melamine in a semi-closed environment ac­
cording to the literature [29]. Briefly, 10 g of melamine was firstly 
placed in a crucible with a cover in static air and then heated to 
823 K with a rate of 5 K/min. After maintained at 823 K for 2 h, the 
resulting yellow agglomerates were ground manually into a powder 
in an agate mortar for further structural characterization and pho­
tocatalytic experiments.
2.2. Synthesis of Pt/g-C3N4 photocatalysts
The Pt/g-C3N4 was firstly prepared by an incipient impregnation 
method using chloroplatinic acid (H2PtCl6) as metal precursor. After 
impregnation, the H2PtCl6/g-C3N4 samples were treated by Ar 
plasma using the enhanced protocols from our previous work [27]. 
200 mg of sample was distributed uniformly in a quartz boat. Then 
the quartz boat was transferred into a radio frequency inductively 
coupled plasma (RF-ICP) chamber. The discharge reactions were 
generated under different powers (20, 50, 100, 150 and 200 W) for 
40 min, and the flow velocity of the discharge gas was 15 sccm under 
the vacuum condition (about 30 Pa). The loading content of Pt was 
set at 0.5 wt%. The obtained samples with different discharge gases 
and powers were labeled as Pt/CN-Ax, where A and x labels re­
present the use of Ar plasma and the value of the discharge power, 
respectively. 
Pristine g-C3N4 was also treated by Ar plasma at 150 W for 
40 min through a similar procedure in the absence of H2PtCl6, and 
was abbreviated as CN-A150. After the plasma treatment, the mass 
of CN-A150 was reduced by 4.4%. As g-C3N4 was prepared by the 
pyrolysis of melamine at 823 K for 2 h, the mass reduction of CN- 
A150 may be caused by the residual melamine because the thermal 
effect of the active species produced by the plasma treatment will 
further decompose the residual melamine. 
For comparison, Pt/g-C3N4 composite was also fabricated using 
the photodeposition reaction. In a typical process, 200 mg of g-C3N4 
was dispersed into 100 mL 20 vol% triethanolamine (TEA) aqueous 
solution containing H2PtCl6 precursor, and then transferred to a top- 
irradiation gas-closed circulation reactor with an outside cooling- 
water jacket. A 300 W Xenon lamp source (PLS-SXE300D, Beijing 
Perfectlight Technology Co., Ltd.) equipped with a UV cutoff filter 
was used as the visible source in the range of 420–750 nm. Before 
visible photoreaction for 3 h under continuous stirring, the sus­
pension was degassed with pure N2 (99.99%). The obtained sample 
was filtered, washed, and dried in vacuum at 333 K overnight. The 
loading content of Pt was also set at 0.5 wt%. The as-prepared sample 
was denoted as Pt/CN-PR.
2.3. Structure characterization
The crystal structure was investigated through the powder X-ray 
diffraction technique using a Rigaku Smartlab 9 kW X-ray dif­
fractometer with a Cu Kα radiation source in the range of 10–90°. 
Raman spectra were explored at room temperature using a Horiba JY 
LabRamHR Evolution spectrometer with a near-IR (1064 nm) ex­
citation. The microstructure was studied using a field-emission 
transmission electron microscope (JEM-2100F). The UV–visible dif­
fuse reflectance spectra were collected using a Solid Spec 3700 UV/ 
vis spectrometer in the range of 200–800 nm using BaSO4 as a re­
ference, and converted to absorption spectra by the Kubella–Munk 
function to estimate the optical bandgap of the samples. The elec­
tronic structure was recorded by an ESCALAB-250 X-ray photoelec­
tron spectroscope (XPS). The photoluminescent (PL) spectra of the 
obtained powder samples were characterized using a fluorospectro- 
photometer (JY Fluorolog-3-Tou). Fourier transform infrared spectra 
were measured on a PerkinElmer Spectrum Two spectrometer.
2.4. Photocatalytic experiments
The photocatalytic performances for hydrogen production were 
measured in the above-mentioned top-irradiation gas-closed circu­
lation reactor and Xenon lamp source. In a typical experiment, 10 mg 
of the photocatalyst was dispersed in 100 mL DI water containing 
20 vol% TEA. Before the photocatalytic reaction, the suspension was 
purged with pure N2 for 30 min to remove the dissolved air. During 
the photocatalytic reaction, 500 μL of the evolved gas was taken
J. Ding, X. Sun, Q. Wang et al. 
Journal of Alloys and Compounds 873 (2021) 159871
intermittently and analyzed using a gas chromatography (Kexiao 
GC1690 gas chromatography equipped with a TDX01 column and a 
thermal conductive detector). After the reaction, the evolved gas in 
the reactor was degassed thoroughly by pure N2, and then cyclic 
experiments were carried out to evaluate the photocatalytic sta­
bility.
shown in Figs. 2 and S4–S7, after the low-temperature plasma re­
duction of H2PtCl6 precursor, ultrafine Pt nanoparticles can be easily 
observed and are found to be uniformly deposited on the surface of 
g-C3N4 nanosheets. The homogenous dispersion of Pt nanoparticles 
can be further confirmed by the STEM image (Fig. 2B). With in­
creasing the discharge power of the plasma source, the average 
diameter of Pt nanoparticles was slightly increased from 1.26 nm to 
1.59 nm (Fig. S8), which indicates that the size of Pt nanoparticles 
can be effectively adjusted by changing the power of the plasma 
source and Pt nanoparticles will not overgrow into large particles on 
g-C3N4 surface. The distance of ~0.23 nm can be attributed to the 
(111) plane of face-centered cubic Pt crystals from the HRTEM 
images of Pt nanoparticles (the insets in Fig. 2A). 
For comparison, Pt/g-C3N4 composite was also synthesized using 
the photodeposition method. When g-C3N4 was irradiated in the 
presence of TEA sacrificial reagent under visible light, the photo­
generated electrons migrated to the active sites on the surface of 
g-C3N4 where the absorbed Pt4+ was reduced in-situ to Pt nano­
particles. From Figs. S8 and S9, Pt nanoparticles with the mean size 
of 3.7 nm were formed in-situ on the surface of g-C3N4 after the 
photodeposition reaction. Several reports confirmed that cocatalysts 
formed on the active sites through the photodeposition reaction 
improved the photocatalytic performance [33–35]. However, the 
larger size of Pt nanoparticles in Pt/CN-PR composite means weaker 
metal-support interaction and low utilization of Pt atoms compared 
to the plasma-treated Pt/g-C3N4 composites. 
The chemical composition and electronic structure of the as- 
prepared samples were studied by XPS analysis. For g-C3N4 in Fig. 3, 
the peak of C 1s was fitted with two peaks located at 288.1 and 
284.7 eV (Fig. 3A). The first peak was assigned to the sp2-bonded 
carbons in the heptazine ring system (NeC]N), while the last peak 
was ascribed to the sp2 C]C bonds [36]. Three main peaks of N 1s 
in g-C3N4 (Fig. 3C) at 398.6, 399.8 and 401.2 eV were the signals of 
the sp2-bonded nitrogen in the triazine rings (C-N), the tertiary 
nitrogen groups (N-C3) and the presence of residue amino functions 
in the melon structures (C-N-H) [37]. The small peak at 404.2 eV 
can be attributed to the charging effect or positive charge locali­
zation in the heterocycles [38]. The O 1s spectrum (Fig. 3E) was 
deconvoluted into two peaks at 531.5 eV for the C-O groups and 
532.5 eV for the absorbed oxygen and water, respectively [39]. After 
the Ar-plasma treatment, the increased intensity of N‒C3 bonds and 
decreased intensity of C‒N bonds (Fig. 3D) can be ascribed to the 
formation of new three-coordinated nitrogen states [40]. For C 1s 
states in the Ar-plasma treated g-C3N4 sample (Fig. 3B), the new 
peaks at 286.5 and 289 eV are related to sp3 hybridized carbons in 
the defect states and trace amount of C‒O or ‒COOH bonds, re­
spectively. The enhancement of sp2 C]C peak at 284.8 eV was 
caused by the unavoidable formation of graphitic carbon atoms, 
indicating that the surface structure of g-C3N4 was affected by the 
plasma treatment [41]. For O 1s of Ar-plasma treated g-C3N4 
(Fig. 3F), the intensity of C-O groups increased and the signal of 
water or oxygen reduced, which means that the pre-absorbed 
oxygen or water were converted into oxygen-containing groups on 
the surface of Ar-plasma treated g-C3N4. 
In addition, the binding energies of C 1s, N 1s and O 1s for Ar- 
plasma treated g-C3N4 were all higher than those of pristine g-C3N4. 
This effect could be caused by the transformation of carbon-con­
taining or nitrogen-containing groups to new active oxygen-con­
taining species on the surface of g-C3N4 by the low-temperature 
plasma treatment, such as –OH and –COOH [42]. These active 
oxygen-containing groups were formed by the reaction between the 
pre-absorbed water or oxygen on the surface of g-C3N4 and the ac­
tive species produced by Ar plasma. The existence of these oxygen- 
containing groups will improve the adsorption of water molecules 
on the surface of g-C3N4 and thus are expected to be favorable for 
photocatalytic decomposition of water [43].
2.5. Electrochemical analysis
The photoelectrochemical properties of the as-prepared photo­
catalysts were recorded on a CHI-760D electrochemical analyzer 
with a three-electrode quartz cell at ambient conditions. An Ag-AgCl 
electrode, a platinum mesh electrode and 1 M Na2SO4 solution were 
used as the reference electrode, counter electrode and electrolyte, 
respectively. A glassy carbon electrode (3 mm in diameter, Tianjin 
Aida) coated with photocatalyst served as the working electrode. The 
glassy carbon electrode was firstly polished with Al2O3 slurry 
(300 nm and 50 nm, respectively), then tested in the mixture solu­
tion of 0.02 M K3Fe(CN)6 and 1 M KCl by cyclic voltammetry with a 
scanning rate of 50 mV/s. After the potential difference between the 
reduction peak and oxidation peak was less than 70 mV, the glassy 
carbon electrode was washed by DI water and anhydrous ethanol, 
respectively. 10 mg of photocatalyst was ultrasonically dispersed in 
1 mL of 1:1 ethanol/water solution to obtain uniformly slurry. 
Subsequently, 10 μL slurry and 3 μL Nafion solution (Dupont 5% 
D520) were dropped onto the surface of the pre-treated glassy 
carbon electrode. All the working electrodes had similar film thick­
ness by controlling the slurry volume and concentration.

articles.title: Strengthening Reactive Metal-Support Interaction to Stabilize High-Density Pt Single Atoms on Electron-deficient g-C3N4 for Boosting Photocatalytic H2 Production
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental and theoretical section
Chemicals.
All of the reagents were of analytical grade, and used without further purification. H2PtCl6,
dicyandiamide and triethanolamine were purchased from Aladdin (Shanghai, China).
Deionized (DI) water was used in all experiments.
Synthesis of g-C3N4.
g-C3N4 photocatalysts were prepared by following a typical thermal polymerization
procedure.[20] Briefly, 5 g of dicyandiamide was put into a covered crucible, heated to 500
°C at a ramp rate of 2 °C min-1 in a tube furnace under air condition and then maintained at
this temperature for additional 2 h. After being cooled down to room temperature, the
resultant powders were grinded and collected.
Synthesis of N-vacancy-riched g-C3N4.
1 g of g-C3N4 was put into a crucible, heated to 400, 560 and 620 °C at a ramp rate of 2 °C
min-1 in a tube furnace under N2 condition, respectively, and maintained at the corresponding
temperature for 2 h. After being cooled down to room temperature, the resultant powders
were collected, noted as CN400, CN560 and CN620, respectively.
Synthesis of PtSA-loaded g-C3N4 (PtSA-CN).
20 mg of CN was dispersed in 10 mL of deionized water containing 4 μmol H2PtCl6 under
magnetic stirring for 30 min. Next, the mixed solution was ultrasonicated for 30 min, and
stirred for 12 h. Then, the mixed solution was rapidly frozen by liquid nitrogen, followed by
irradiating under a 300 W Xe light with the light filter of 420 nm and IR. After 3 min
irradiation, the ice layer was naturally melted. The formed solution was centrifugalized and
separated. The obtained precipitates were further washed with deionized water for two times.
Finally, the precipitates were dried in an oven at 60 oC for 12 h.
Synthesis of PtNP-loaded g-C3N4 (PtNP-CN).
For a comparison, PtNP-loaded C3N4 was synthesized by directly irradiating the mixed
solution of CN620 and H2PtCl6 without the pretreatment of liquid nitrogen. Other procedures
were similar to the above preparation method for making the PtSA-loaded C3N4.
Catalyst characterization.
The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns, obtained on an X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku, Japan)
using Cu Kα radiation at a scan rate of 0.05o 2θ s-1, were used to characterize the crystalline
phase of the samples. The accelerating voltage and applied current were 40 kV and 80 mA,
respectively. The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface area (SBET) of the samples
was measured in a nitrogen adsorption apparatus (Micromeritics ASAP 2020, USA). Before
nitrogen adsorption measurements, all the samples were degassed at 200 oC. The SBET was
determined by a multipoint BET method using adsorption data in the relative pressure (P/P0)
range of 0.05-0.3. The pore-size distributions were determined by the nitrogen adsorption
volume via the Barret-Joyner-Halender (BJH) method assuming a cylindrical pore model.
Aberration-corrected 
HAADF-STEM 
analysis 
was 
conducted 
on 
JEM-ARM200F
transmission electron microscope with an accelerating voltage of 300 kV. X-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were performed on an ESCALAB 250Xi
electron spectrometer with Mg Kα (1253.6 eV) source. All binding energies were referenced
to the C 1s peaks at 284.8 eV from the adventitious carbon. Electron spin resonance (ESR)
experiments were conducted on an ER-200D spectrometer (Bruker, Germany) at a
microwave frequency of 9.5 GHz under room temperature. The content of Pt elements in the
as-prepared samples was analyzed by an inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission
spectrometer (ICP-AES) on PerkinElmer Optima 7300DV. Steady-state and time-resolved
photoluminescence emission spectra (332 nm excitation) were collected on a fluorescence
spectrophotometer (Edinburgh Instruments, FLSP-920) at room temperature.
XAFS measurement and data analysis.
XAFS spectra at the Pt L3-edge were measured at the 1W1B beamline of Beijing Synchrotron
Radiation Facility (BSRF), China. The storage ring of BSRF was working at the energy of
2.5 GeV with a maximum electron current of 250 mA. The hard X-ray was monochromatized
with Si(111) double-crystal monochromator, and the detuning was done by 30% to remove
harmonics. The acquired EXAFS data were processed according to the standard procedures
using the ATHENA module of the IFEFFIT software packages. The k3-weighted χ(k) data in
the k-space ranging from 2.0-11.5 Å-1 were Fourier transformed to real (R) space using a
hanning windows (dk = 1.0 Å-1) to separate the EXAFS contributions from different
coordination shells. To obtain the detailed structural parameters around Pt atom in the as-
prepared samples, the quantitative curve-fittings were carried out for the Fourier transformed
k3χ(k) in the R-space using the ARTEMIS module of IFEFFIT3. Effective backscattering
amplitudes F(k) and phase shifts Φ(k) of all fitting paths were calculated by the ab initio code
FEFF8.0. During the fitting analysis, the amplitude reduction factor S0
fit value of 0.70, which was determined from fitting the reference sample of metal Pt bulk,
PtN2 bulk and PtCl4 bulk. In general, it was difficult to distinguish Pt-O, Pt-C and Pt-N
coordination. Thus the Pt-O coordination was used to describe the Pt-C/N/O coordination. To
fit the data of PtSA-CN400, PtSA-CN560, PtSA-CN620 and PtNP-CN620 samples, the
interatomic distance (R) and the Debye-Waller factor (σ2) were allowed to vary. We have
distinguished Pt-C/N/O and Pt-Cl from Pt-Pt coordination, considering the existing bonding
length difference between them.
Catalytic activity measurements.
The photocatalytic H2 production measurements were conducted in a double layered Pyrex
vessel (inner volume of 200 mL with diameter of 50 mm and height of 100 mm). A 300 W
Xe lamp with the light filters of 420 nm and IR was used as the light source. The focused
intensity on the flask was ∼100 mW·cm−2, measured by a FZ-A visible-light radiometer
2 was fixed to the best-
(made in the photoelectric instrument factory of Beijing Normal University, China) with a
wavelength range of 400-1000 nm. In a typical photocatalytic H2 production experiment, 20
mg of the as-prepared photocatalyst was suspended in 100 mL of 10 vol% triethanolamine
aqueous solution, and then bubbled with Ar through the reactor for 30 min to completely
remove the dissolved oxygen. The suspension solution in the reactor was continuously stirred
by a magnetic stirrer during the experiment. A thermostatic digital controller (HX-205) was
used to control the temperature of reactor (25 oC). The amount of produced H2 was tested
every hour. 1 mL of gas sample was sampled from the headspace of the flask through the
septum and analyzed by gas chromatography (GC-7890B, Agilent, America, TCD, with Ar as
a carrier gas and 5 Å molecular sieve column). The obtained H2 content was used to evaluate
the H2 production activity of different samples. The apparent quantum efficiency (AQE)
measurements were performed under the irradiation of a 420 nm LED light with an
irradiation density of 50 mW cm-2. Others were same with the experiments above. The AQY
of photocatalytic H2 production was calculated by the equation (1):
AQY = 2 × n(H2)/n(photons) ×100 (1)
Where n(H2) and n(photons) denote the number of produced H2 molecules and the number of
incident photons, respectively.
Theoretical simulation.
The geometry structures and electronic properties of PtSA-loaded g-C3N4 were investigated
by the density functional theory (DFT) calculations based on the VASP package using the
PBE exchange-correlation function.[21,22] The interaction between valence electrons and the
ionic core was described by the PAW pseudo-potential. The model of g-C3N4 was simulated
by a periodic atomic layer containing 96 C atoms and 128 N atoms. The N vacancy was built
by removing a N2C atom. The geometry structures of pure and N-vacancy-riched g-C3N4 were
optimized with the cutoff of 400 eV. All the atoms in the model were allowed to adjust until
the magnitude of all residual forces was less than 0.001 eV Å-1. Considering the calculation
cost, the geometry optimization was only performed at Gamma point. After the geometry
optimization, the PDOS was calculated by the cutoff energy of 400 eV and the Monkhorst-
Pack k-point mesh of 2 × 2 × 1. The adsorptions of PtSAs at the low-coordinated C2C and N2C
sites were considered. For a comparison, the PtNP was simulated by a Pt cluster containing
38 Pt atoms.
The adsorption energy (Eads) of PtSA at the C2C and N2C sites was used to evaluate the
stability of coordination structure, which was calculated by the following formula:
Eads = ECN+PtSA - ECN - EPtSA (2)
where ECN+PtSA was the total free energy of PtSA-CN, ECN was the free energy of CN and
EPtSA was the free energy of one PtSA in vacuum.
The Eads of H+ ion on the PtSA or PtNP was used to evaluate the H-reduction ability, which
was calculated by the following formula:
Eads = ECN+PtSA+2H - ECN+PtSA – 2EH (3)
where ECN+PtSA+2H was the total free energy of H-adsorbed PtSA-CN and EH was the free
energy of one H+ ion in the H3O+.
The desorption energy (Edes) of H2 on the PtSA or PtNP was used to evaluate the H2-
evolution ability, which was calculated by the following formula:
Edes = ECN+PtSA + EH2 - ECN+PtSA+2H (4)
where EH2 was the free energy of one H2 molecule in vacuum.
The electronic properties of PtSA-CN and PtNP-CN were also investigated by calculating the
PDOS plots, which were performed with the cutoff energy of 400 eV and the Monkhorst-
Pack k-point mesh of 2 × 2 × 1. The photogenerated electron transfer between PtSA/PtNP
and CN was constructed by calculating the charge density differences (ρdifference(r)) of the
PtSA-CN/PtNP-CN model after and before charging with two electrons:
ρdifference(r) = ρPtSA-CN+2e(r) - ρPtSA-CN(r)
where ρPtSA-CN+2e(r) and ρPtSA-CN(r) were the charge density of PtSA-CN/PtNP-CN after and
before charging, respectively.

3. Materials and Methods
3.1. Synthesis of CNx and CNx-Pt
Thermal polycondensation was utilized for the synthesis of pure g-C3N4. Thiourea
(30 g) (CH4N2S, ≥99%, supplied by Sigma-Aldrich Korea, Seoul, Republic of Korea), as the
precursor, was loaded in an aluminum-foil-covered crucible and then heated in a mufﬂe
furnace to 550 ◦C for 4h at a heating rate of 5 ◦C/min under an air atmosphere. The
as-prepared bulk g-C3N4 sample was designated as CN.
After being dissolved in 100 mL of deionized (DI) water, 1 gram of CN powder was
sonicated for two hours at room temperature. The CNx samples (x = 0, 3, and 9 h, where x is
the hydrothermal period) were placed in a 150 mL TeﬂonTM autoclave, which was heated
to 180 ◦C (heating rate = 5 ◦C/min) in an oven. After being cooled to room temperature,
the resulting materials were repeatedly rinsed with DI water.
A magnetic stirrer was used to dissolve the CNx samples in 1000 mL of DI water for
30 min. The H2PtCl6.6H2O amount added to the mixture was calculated to set the initial
content of Pt at 2 wt.%. Pt on CNx was processed with hydrogen reduction for 60 min under
a 30 rpm H2 ﬂow rate at 60 ◦C. The precipitates were collected, repeatedly washed with DI
water, and freeze-dried for additional characterization in the ﬁnal step. The materials were
CN0-Pt, CN3-Pt, and CN9-Pt, according to their CNx precursors.
3.2. Characterization
The Pt element composition of CNx-Pt samples was validated using an inductively
coupled plasma–optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES) (700-ES; Varian Australia Pty.
Ltd., Mulgrave, Australia). The morphologies of the CNx-Pt samples were investigated
using ﬁeld-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) (Quanta 200 FEG, FEI Corp.,
Hillsboro, OR, USA). A Cu-Kα X-ray source with a wavelength of λ = 1.5415 Å (D/MAZX
2500 V/PC high-power diffractometer; Rigaku, Tokyo, Japan) was used to record the XRD
patterns of the samples at a scan rate of 2◦(2θ)/min. A Fourier transform infrared (FTIR)

Catalysts 2023, 13, 92
8 of 11
transmittance spectrometer (Nicolet™380 spectrometer, Nicolet™iS5 with an iD1 trans-
mission accessory; Thermo Scientiﬁc™, Waltham, MA, USA) was employed to examine
the functional groups of the prepared photocatalysts. Thermo Scientiﬁc’s K-Alpha system
(Waltham, MA, USA) was utilized for XPS. A UV–Vis diffuse reﬂectance spectrometer
(SPECORD®210 Plus spectroscope; Analytik Jena, Jena, Germany) and photoluminescence
(PL) measurements (Cary Eclipse ﬂuorescence spectrophotometer; Agilent, Santa Clara, CA,
USA) were used to analyze the optical properties of the photocatalysts. In PL measurements,
a 473 nm diode laser was used to monitor the PL spectra at ambient temperature.
3.3. Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution Test
For the photocatalytic H2 evolution experiments, a solar simulation system with a
light source consisting of an LED lamp with a light intensity set to 100 mW.cm−2 was
used. Each photocatalyst (30 mg) was then dissolved for 30 min with high-purity Argon
purging in the dark in 100 mL of DI water. As a hole scavenger, 10 mL of triethanolamine
(TEOA) was incorporated into the solution. Argon was used to purge the reactor system
before starting H2 evolution tests. An online gas chromatograph with an installed thermal
conductivity detector was utilized to examine the gas products. The same setup in 5 h
cycles was used for the photocatalyst stability tests. At the beginning of each cycle, an extra
amount of TEOA (10 mL) was added to the solution, and Argon was again used to purge
the reactor system.
3.4. Photoelectrochemical Test
In addition, an impedance analyzer (VSP series; Bio-Logic Science Instruments,
Seyssinet–Pariset, France) was utilized to measure the EIS data. After a 10 min inter-
val under the illumination of a 3 W visible-light bulb, a frequency range of 0.01 Hz to
100 kHz with an amplitude of 10 mV and a direct current potential of +0.8 VSCE were
used in the test. Then, 20 mg of the catalyst powder ground in a mortar was mixed with
2 mg of active carbon for 20 min to produce a ﬁne powder mixture. The powder was then
incorporated into 100 µL of isopropanol 99.7% and 30 µL of Naﬁon 5 wt.% (both from
Sigma-Aldrich Korea, Gyeonggi, Korea). Next, 10 mL of potassium hydroxide 1 M (KOH)
was used as the electrolyte in a 3-electrode setup. The reference and counter electrodes
were a RE-1BP (Ag/AgCl) electrode and a platinum wire. A 6 mm standard-type glassy
carbon electrode with 10 µL of the sample (1 µL of suspension per time by a micro-pipette)
loaded on it was used as the working electrode.

2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
2.1. Sample Preparation. The melamine was heated and
recrystallized in a crucible with a cover to synthesize pristine
C3N4.36 In the typical synthesis of the Cl-modiﬁed C3N4 (C3N4−Cl)
sample, a suspension of melamine (0.01 mol) and NaCl (0.0004 mol)
was dissolved in 150 mL of deionized water, and the as-prepared
suspension was reﬂuxed at 95 °C for 2 h. The above suspension was
then centrifuged and dried at 70 °C after washing by water and
ethanol to obtain the precursor. Finally, the sample was obtained after
calcination at 550 °C for 2 h in air. The modiﬁed C3N4 samples with
diﬀerent NaCl contents (C3N4−Cl0.5, C3N4−Cl2, C3N4−Cl4, C3N4−
Cl5, and C3N4−Cl6) were synthesized by the above method with
diﬀerent molar weights of NaCl (0.05, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, and 0.6 mmol).
Loading Co(OH)2 cocatalyst onto samples: The Co(OH)2−
C3N4−Clx samples were synthesized by the hydrothermal method.
Typically, 500 mg of the above photocatalyst was dispersed in 25 mL
of Co(NO3)2·6H2O solution with diﬀerent concentration. Then, 0.4
mL of ammonium solution (NH3·H2O, 25 wt %) was added into this
suspension, followed by stirring for 15 min. The mixture was
transferred to a 50 mL Teﬂon-lined stainless steel autoclave. After
that, the stainless autoclave was heated at 150 °C for 1 h. The
precipitate was centrifuged, and then washed by deionized water and
ethanol after the stainless autoclave cooled to room temperature.
Lastly, the samples were obtained after drying at 80 °C for several
hours. Various photocatalysts with Co(OH)2 loading weights of 0.1,
0.2, 0.3, and 0.5 wt % were obtained.
2.2. Catalyst Characterization. Systematic characterizations
were performed, including X-ray diﬀraction (XRD), transmission
electron microscopy (TEM), high-resolution transmission electron
microscopy (HRTEM), UV−visible spectra, photoluminescence
(PL), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), electron spin
resonance (ESR) spectra, and X-ray absorption spectroscopy
(XAS). The density functional theory (DFT) calculations were
carried out to analyze the formation energy of nitrogen vacancies in
C3N4. Please refer to the Supporting Information for details.
2.3. Photoelectrochemical Tests. Typically, 5 mg of sample was
dispersed in 300 μL of absolute ethanol and 100 μL if deionized water
to form a suspension, which was spread onto F-doped tin oxide
(FTO) glass. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and
photocurrent of samples were measured in a conventional three-
electrode cell by an electrochemical station (CHI 660e, CH
instruments, China). The electrolyte was 0.1 M Na2SO4 aqueous
solution. The light source was a 300 W xenon lamp. The EIS spectra
were measured at a 1.0 V bias potential versus Ag/AgCl. The
photocurrent measurement was performed with a bias of 1.0 V (vs
Ag/AgCl).
2.4. Photocatalytic Overall Water Splitting Test. Photo-
catalytic overall water splitting was performed in an online gas
chromatography (GC-2014C; Shimadzu Corp., Japan) with a closed
gas circulation under UV−visible light irradiation (λ > 300 nm).37
Typically, 0.02 g of Co(OH)2-C3N4−Clx photocatalyst was dispersed
in 100 mL of water. Then, an appropriate amount H2PtCl6 was added
to load the photocatalysts with Pt (0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4 wt %) by
the photodeposition method.

photocatalytic overall water splitting was performed with a band-pass

2.1. Synthesis of photocatalysts.
Bulk g-C3N4 (BCN) was synthesized according to a previously re-
ported procedure [31]. Porous nitrogen vacancies-modiﬁed g-C3N4
(PNCN) was prepared via SBA-15 template under HPHT. Note that SBA-
15 has been used as template to create porous structure in g-C3N4 at
ambient pressure conditions [11,32,33]. Here, mesoporous SBA-15 was
synthesized by a referenced process, which exhibits the same XRD
patterns and SEM images (Fig. S1 in supplementary data) [34]. 4 g of
dicyandiamide is mixed with 1.5 g of SBA-15, which are dissolved in
22.5 mL of deionized water, followed by stirring at 70 °C for 4 h. The
obtained material is centrifuged, and dried in vacuum oven. The re-
sultant solid is calcined at the same condition as that for the preparation
of bulk g-C3N4.
The above resultant powder is treated in a cubic anvil HPHT ap-
paratus (SPD-6 × 1200) and the detail can be found elsewhere [30,35].
Various HPHT conditions, 2 GPa/250 °C, 2GPa/300 °C and 3 GPa/
300 °C for 10 min are studied, while we found the sample treated at 3
GPa and 300 °C was partially carbonized. Therefore, only the samples
synthesized at 2 GPa were analyzed in this paper. Finally, the quenched
samples are ground into powder, following a 10 wt% HF treatment for
72 h to remove the template, and then centrifuged and washed care-
fully, followed by freeze-dried. The obtained porous g-C3N4 samples
with nitrogen vacancies in this way are designated as PNCN-1 and
PNCN-2, respectively. For comparison, the porous g-C3N4 (PCN) by
directly removing the template (48 h) without HPHT treatment was also
synthesized.
2.2. Characterization
X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) patterns were recorded on a MicroMax-
007HF instrument (Cu Kα, λ = 1.5418 Å). Scanning electron micro-
graph (SEM, Magllan400) installed on an energy-dispersive spectro-
scope (EDS) was carried out for sample characterization. X-ray photo-
electron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were conducted on an
ESCALAB 250 XPS instrument. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR)

analysis for C and N were determined by a Vario EL cube element

were carried out with a JES-FA200 spectrometer at room temperature.

articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental section
2.1 Preparation of C3N4 samples
Approximately 3 g of melamine (Aladdin) and an arbitrary amount KOH were
premixed, ground, and transferred to a crucible with a lid. The thermal polymerization
reaction was performed in a muffle furnace that was heated at 5°C·min-1 to 520°C and
held at that temperature for 4 h. After cooling, the sample was washed three to five
times with deionized water, dried at 80°C, and ground to obtain a compact yellow mass
powder as the final product. According to the vol% x of KOH added to the 3 g of
melamine, the products are labeled g-C3N4-x. Pure g-C3N4 and g-C3N4 modified by
NaOH and KI were prepared in the same way except that KOH was not added or was
replaced by one of the other modifiers.
2.2 Characterization
The crystal structures of the catalysts were determined by XRD measurements
(DX-2007 SSC). TEM images and HAADF scanning transmission electron microscopy
images were obtained using an FEI Talos F200S electron microscope. The UV–vis DRS
spectra were obtained using a UV−vis spectrophotometer (Lambda750S, PerkinElmer,
USA). FT-IR spectroscopy was performed using an FT-IR spectrophotometer
(Spectrum Two Li10014, PerkinElmer). XPS (ESCALAB 250Xi, Thermo Scientific,
USA) was used to analyze the surface chemical composition of the samples. The PL
spectra were obtained using an FLS1000 spectrophotometer (Edinburgh Instruments).
EA was performed using an Elementar Vario EL cube. ESR measurements (JES-FA200,
JEOL) were performed using DMPO as the spin capture agent. A Chenhua 760E three-
electrode electrochemical workstation was used to conduct RDE and EIS analyses.
2.3 Photogeneration of H2O2
Photogeneration of H2O2 using C3N4 was conducted in an OCRSIV photoreactor
system with a 500 W xenon lamp and a cutoff filter. Approximately 30 mg of the
photocatalyst and 30 mL of an aqueous IPA solution (10 vol%) were fed into a 50 mL
quartz tube, and the pH was adjusted to 3 using an arbitrary acid. The light intensity
was changed by adjusting the distance between the tubes and the light source, and was
measured using a CEL-NO2000 illuminance meter. When oxygen adsorption
equilibrium was reached after 30 min of bubbling in the dark, the photocatalytic
reaction was started. Approximately 2 mL of the solution was removed after an
arbitrary time interval, and the H2O2 concentration was determined using the titanium
method34, 35 with a UV-1500PC spectrophotometer.
The performance stability of the photocatalyst was tested by cycling a g-C3N4
sample centrifuged from the reacted solution and washed. A radical capture experiment
and experimental analysis of the mechanism were performed by adding a scavenger to
the photoreaction system.
2.4 Superoxide radical detection
Electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy was used to detect superoxide
radicals (•O2-), and 5,5-dimethyl-l-pyrrole-n-oxide (DMPO) was used as a spin capture
agent. The specific test method was as follows: 30 mg of catalyst is dispersed in a
water/isopropanol mixed solution (9/1 v/v, 30 ml). After bubbling with O2 for 10
minutes, the solution was subjected to light scattering under a 500W fluorescent lamp
(λ > 420 nm) for 3 minutes. The catalyst was recovered by centrifugation, and the
resulting solution was expected to be analyzed.
2.5 Photoelectrochemical experiments
The Rotating disk electrode (RDE) was measured on a Chenhua 760E
electrochemical workstation using a three-electrode battery. The reference electrode
was an Ag/AgCl electrode, and the counter electrode was a Pt sheet electrode. The
working electrode was prepared as follows: 10 mg of the sample was added to ethanol
(2ml) containing 10 μL of nafion solution. After ultrasonication for 30 min, 20 μL of
the suspension was dropped on the glass electrode and dried at room temperature. A
linear scanning voltammetry (LSV) curve test was performed after continuously O2
bubbling for 5 min into a 0.1mol/L phosphate buffer solution (pH = 7), and the scan
rate was 10 mV/s. The number of electrons involved in O2 reduction can be estimated
by linear regression of the graph with the following equation:

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was obtained in a Chenhua 760E

working electrode was prepared as follows: A 10 mg sample was added to ethanol (2

dropwise on FTO conductive glass. The obtained electrode was dried at 80 °C for 12 h.
0.5M Na2SO4 aqueous solution was used as an electrolyte. Electrochemical impedance
spectroscopy (EIS) analysis was performed at a DC voltage of -0.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl, an
AC voltage amplitude of 50 mV and a frequency of 0.1 MHz to 0.01 Hz.
2.6 Theoretical calculations
The electronic densities of g-C3N4 and g-C3N4-0.05 were simulated using the
plane-wave pseudopotential DFT method. The Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof functional of
the generalized gradient approximation was used as the exchange–correlation function.
The ultrasoft pseudopotential was selected to describe the interaction between the
valence electrons and the ionic core. A 3 × 3 × 1 Monkhorst–Pack k-point grid was
adopted, and the energy cutoff was set to 450 eV. A vacuum gap of 20.0 Å in the z
direction was used to avoid interactions between layers.

articles.title: 3D macroporous architecture of self-assembled defect-engineered ultrathin g-C3N4 nanosheets for tetracycline degradation under LED light irradiation
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental
2.1. Materials
Sigma Aldrich (USA) supplied melamine. Ethylene glycol was ac­
quired from Merck (India). Tetracycline was supply obtained from Loba 
Chemie Ltd. (India). Benzoquinone (BQ), isopropanol (IPA), and diso­
dium ethylenediaminetetraacetate dihydrate (EDTA-2Na) were ob­
tained from Merck, India. All the reagents were consumed as purchased. 
Unless specified otherwise, Millipore water was utilized during the 
study.
2.2. Synthesis of defect engineered 3D macroporous g-C3N4
The pristine g-C3N4 (designated as BCN henceforth) was prepared via 
the polycondensation of precursor melamine according to the procedure 
reported elsewhere [38]. Typically, 2 g melamine was kept in a covered 
crucible (alumina) and heated at 550 ◦C for 3 h in a muffle furnace. Upon 
reaching ambient temperature, the yellowish residue was taken out, 
powdered in a mortar pestle, and stored for further use. 
The nitrogen defect engineered 3D macroporous g-C3N4 structure
Materials Research Bulletin 133 (2021) 111074
(denoted as EGCN hereafter) was synthesized following the procedure 
mentioned above with an extra step as the addition of the ethylene 
glycol solvent. Specifically, 2 g melamine was initially taken in an 
alumina crucible, followed by the addition of an appropriate amount of 
ethylene glycol and rigorous mixing using a glass rod. After that, the 
crucible was covered and heated in a muffle furnace at 550 ◦C for 3 h to 
produce EGCN. The as-obtained EGCN with different amounts of 
ethylene glycol was synthesized by adding 1, 2, 3, and 4 mL of ethylene 
glycol and denoted as 1EGCN, 2EGCN, 3EGCN, and 4EGCN.
2.3. Characterization
A Cu kα irradiated Bruker D2 phaser X-ray diffractometer was 
employed to obtain the XRD spectra of the photocatalyst. A Nicolet 6700 
(Thermo Fischer Scientific) FTIR instrument was used to record the 
findings of the FTIR (Fourier transform infrared) analysis. The micro­
structure of the samples was examined with a field emission scanning 
electron microscope (Merlin, Carl Zeiss, Germany) and a JEOL JEM 
2100 transmission electron microscope (Japan). X-ray photoelectron 
spectroscopy (XPS) was employed to explore the chemical composition 
of the samples. An electron spectrometer (ULVAC-PHI5000VersaPro­
beII) was engaged to record the XPS spectra of the materials. A UV–vis 
spectrophotometer (Model-Cary 5000, Agilent Technologies) was used 
to investigate the optical characteristics of the materials. An ESR 
(electron spin resonance) spectrophotometer (Bruker Elexys) was 
engaged to record the spectra. Atomic force microscopy analysis was 
carried out in a 5500 AFM (atomic force microscopy) analyzer (Agilent 
technologies). A Cary Eclipse (Agilent Technologies) Fluorescence 
spectrophotometer was used to capture the photoluminescence spectra 
of the catalysts in the emission range of 400 nm–600 nm, at an excitation 
of 350 nm. The detailed elemental composition investigation was 
executed in a Euro vector EA3000 (Italy) elemental analyzer. The pore 
size distribution and specific surface area of the catalysts were analyzed 
in a surface analyzer (Quantachrome autosorb iQ). The TOC (total 
organic carbon) content of the antibiotics were analyzed in a TOC 
analyzer (Aurora O-I-Analytical).
2.4. Photocatalytic experimentation
Tetracycline (TC) antibiotic was photocatalytically degraded to 
evaluate the efficacy of the EGCN samples using a 50 W LED light 
(Philips India) as an illuminant. The photocatalytic experiments were 
accomplished in a closed reactor, equipped with the light vertically 
above, having a volume of 100 mL. The spectrum of the light is reported 
in Fig. s1 in the supporting information. The intensity of the LED light 
was 60 mW/cm2. The intensity of the LED light was recorded in a digital 
solar power meter (KM-SPM-530, Kusam-Meco, India). Initially, an 
aqueous solution of TC (50 mL; 20 mg/L) was placed in the reactor, and 
50 mg of the catalyst was added and dispersed ultrasonically for 5 min. 
Then, the adsorption-desorption equilibrium was ascertained by stirring 
the solution in absence of light for 30 min. After that, the reactor was 
exposed to the LED light illumination for a stipulated time. Throughout 
the experiment, a 3 mL aliquot was taken out at a regular interim and 
filtered through a 0.22 μm filter paper before measuring the TC con­
centration in a Cary 60 (Agilent Technologies) spectrophotometer.
2.5. Radical scavenging experiment
In order to consolidate the radicals taking part in the degradation, 
sequential active radical species quenching tests were executed with the 
addition of 0.05 mM BQ, 1 mM EDTA-2Na and 10 mM IPA as superoxide 
(⋅O2
−), hole (h+) and hydroxyl radical (⋅OH) radical scavengers, respec­
tively. Additionally, the generation of ⋅OH was ascertained through the 
following method: an aqueous solution (50 mL) dispersed with 50 mg of 
4EGCN, containing terephthalic acid (3 mM) and NaOH (10 mM), was 
stirred in a magnetic stirrer for 30 min in the absence of light, and,
U. Ghosh et al.
thereafter irradiated for 60 min. Afterward, a 3 mL sample was with­
drawn at a definite break, filtered through a 0.22 μm filter paper, and the 
produced 2 hydroxyterephthalic acid concentration was measured using 
a Cary Eclipse fluorescence spectrophotometer, excited at 320 nm 
wavelength.

A conventional g-C3N4 sample was prepared by directly calcining
melamine at 500 °C at a rate of 4 °C/min in air for 2 h. This sample was
labelled g-C3N4. Porous g-C3N4 nanosheets containing nitrogen defects
were synthesized as follows: a quantity of 1.5 g of ammonium persul-

quantity of 0.05 g of catalyst was mixed with 0.05 L of MER solution in

of 1 mL of solution was extracted every 2 min during the photocatalytic

membrane and Nafion solution (D520, 5 wt%) were purchased from 
DuPont.
2.2. Preparation of CN and N-CN
CN was prepared by dicyandiamide two-step annealing synthesis. 
Primarily, dicyandiamide was pretreated by freeze-drying of
Chemical Engineering Journal 419 (2021) 129455
dicyandiamide aqueous solution (mass ratio 1:4) to obtain an assembled 
dicyandiamide. Subsequently, the assembled dicyandiamide was pro­
cessed at 550 ◦C for 2 h in N2 with a heating rate of 1 ◦C/min. The CN 
was finally obtained by the resulting product heated at 500 ◦C for 1 h in 
the air to remove impurities. N-CN was prepared as follows: 0.17 g CN, 2 
g LiCl powder, and 10 mL isopropanol were added into a ball mill tank 
and ball milling at 200 rpm/min for 2 h. The mixed slurry was dried at 
60 ◦C in a vacuum oven and then transferred into an alumina crucible 
and heated at 550 ◦C for 2 h in a vacuum tube furnace. Afterward, the 
processed powder was dispersed into 5 wt% sulfuric acid solution to 
remove the occurring impurities. The mixture was rinsed by deionized 
water several times until the solution pH was neutral and dried at 60 ◦C 
in a vacuum oven to obtain N-CN.
2.3. Preparation of IrO2/N-CN, IrO2/CN and IrO2
IrO2/CN, IrO2/N-CN, and IrO2 were prepared via hydrothermal re­
action followed by heat treatment. IrO2/CN and IrO2/N-CN samples 
were synthesized as follows: 0.21 g H2IrCl6 6 H2O and 0.1 g CN (or N- 
CN) were added into alcohol and deionized water mixture (volume ratio 
9:1) and kept at 80 ◦C for 8 h. The mixture solution was then under the 
hydrothermal condition at 180 ◦C for 4 h. After cooling down, the 
resulting precipitate was collected by vacuum filtration and dried at 
60 ◦C in a vacuum oven. Finally, the achieved IrO2/CN or IrO2/N-CN 
was processed at 400 ◦C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 ◦C⋅min−1. The 
synthesis process of IrO2 was the same as IrO2/CN or IrO2/N-CN but 
without the adding of CN or N-CN.
2.4. Materials characterizations
Phase purity and crystal structure of the prepared samples were 
determined by an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Bruker D8 Advance X-ray 
diffractometer). Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy of the 
samples was recorded using an FT-IR spectrometer (Bruker EQUINOX 
55). Morphological and microstructure features were studied by scan­
ning electron microscopy (SEM, FEI QUANTA250FEG*), transmission 
electron microscopy (TEM), high-resolution transmission electron mi­
croscopy (HRTEM), and high-angle annular dark-field imaging (HAADF) 
(JEOL JEM 2100F microscope equipped with Energy Dispersive X-Ray 
(EDX) instrument). N2 absorption–desorption method was used to 
evaluate the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface area and 
Barrett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) pore size distribution of the sample by 
using Micromeritics ASAP 2020. Elemental analysis (EA) was recorded 
with an elementary (vario MICRO CUBE). Electron paramagnetic reso­
nance (EPR) spectrum was performed by using a Bruker EMXplus. 
UV–vis diffuse reflectance spectrum (UV/Vis DRS) was carried on a 
spectrophotometer (HITACHI UH-4100). The electrical conductivity of 
the sample was recorded on a Van der Pauw method with an Accent 
HL5500. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and XPS valence band 
were analyzed using an X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (AXIS 
UltraDLD). XPS valence band spectrum corrected with Shirley back­
ground was employed to calculate the d-band center by the equation:

where N(ε) represents the XPS intensity with Shirley corrected. The N K- 
edge X-ray absorption near-edge (XANES) spectra were measured at the 
BL12B-a beamline of the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory 
(NSRL), in the total electron yield (TEY) mode by collecting sample 
drain current under a vacuum better than 5 × 10−8 Pa. The details of the 
theoretical calculation are supplied in the supporting information.
2.5. Preparation of MEAs and single PEM cell characterizations
Using 60 wt% Pt/C as cathode catalyst, the as-synthesized samples as
S. Wang et al.

anodic catalysts and Nafion 117 membrane as an electrolyte, and the 
membrane electrode assembly (MEA) was prepared by spray method. 
Before the spray, Nafion 117 membranes were first boiled in 3 wt% H2O2 
solution, 5 wt% H2SO4 solution, and deionized water at 90 ◦C for 1 h, 
respectively, and then dried at 80 ◦C. As for the preparation of catalyst 
ink, a certain amount of catalyst was added into the mixture solution of 
isopropyl alcohol, deionized water, and Nafion solution, and then ul­
trasonic dispersion in an ice water bath for 1 h. The volume ratio of the 
used isopropyl alcohol and deionized water was 9:1 and the amount of 
Nafion used is 25 wt% and 10 wt% of the amount of cathode catalyst 
anode catalyst, respectively. The prepared inks were sprayed onto each 
side of the Nafion 117 membrane. Pt and IrO2 loading mass of each 
MEAs were 0.5 mg cm−2 and 1.5 mg cm−2, respectively. The obtained 
active area of each MEAs was controlled at 4 cm2. MEA formed a 
sandwich structure between a porous sintered titanium plate and carbon 
paper. Titanium plates with flow fields as bipolar plates were situated on 
each side of the sandwich structure. Finally, the housing plates with 
upper and lower holes were placed at both ends and formed a single PEM 
electrolytic cell. 
Prior to the electrochemical characterizations, high purity water 
with a flow rate of 30 mL min−1 flowed into the anode compartment in 
the assembled single PEM cell for 24 h. The activity of MEA was eval­
uated under the current density of 0.01–1.6 A cm−2 powered by a DC 
power supply. The durability of the MEA was examined at the current 
density of 1.6 A cm−2 for 100 h. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves of the 
single PEM cells were observed in the potential range between 0.1 and 
1.38 V vs. RHE with a scan rate of 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, 30, 50, 70, 100 mV 
s−1. During the CV test, the prepared sample (anode catalyst) was acted 
as the working electrode, and the Pt/C catalytic layer (cathode side) kept 
in the H2 atmosphere was used as a reference electrode. 
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) Nyquist plots for the 
single PEM cells were recorded at 1.5 V range from 0.01 Hz to10 kHz 
with an amplitude of 10 mV. The ohmic resistance of the single PEM 
cells was determined at high 10 kHz. CV and EIS tests of the single PEM 
cell were probed by a connection of Solartron 1287 potentiostat and 
1260 frequency response analyzer. All the electrochemical performance 
tests were under the condition of a water temperature of 80 ◦C at a flow 
rate of 30 mL min−1 through the anode chamber in the assembled single 
PEM cell single.

2. Experimental
2.1. Catalyst preparation
All reagents used were of analytical grade and without further 
purification. Urea (99.5%, QRec) was used as g-C3N4 precursor. 
g-C3N4 was synthesized by directly heating urea in a closed system. 
10 g of urea was placed in a covered crucible, subsequently heated at 
550 °C for 2 h with ramping rate of 5 °C/min. The resultant yellow 
powder was obtained and grounded into fine powder. Carbon-doped 
g-C3N4 nanocomposite was synthesized by a two-step polymeriza­
tion technique according to previously reported method [23]. Glu­
cose (Merck, 99.5%) was used as carbon precursor for carbon-doped 
g-C3N4. 10 g of urea and certain amount of glucose was placed into a 
covered crucible. The crucible was heated at 550 °C for 2 h in muffle 
furnace with ramping rate 5 °C/min. Glucose was calcined and 
transformed as carbon doped to g-C3N4 during the polymerization 
process. The sample was then cooled and placed into a covered 
quartz boat before heated at 620 °C for 2 h in the tube furnace under 
nitrogen (N2) flow and the resultant brown powder was collected. 
The same procedures were repeated using different glucose to urea 
weight ratio from 0.05% to 0.5%. The corresponding samples were 
noted as 0.05, 0.2, and 0.5 wt% of C/g-C3N4.
2.2. Characterization
The crystalline structures of the prepared samples were analysed 
using X-ray diffractometer, XRD (Rigaku, Cu Kβ radiation). The 
morphology of the samples was observed by field emission scanning 
electron microscopy, SEM (SEM images and EDX spectra were ac­
quired at 2 kV and 3 kV, respectively, using an FEI Magellan 400 L 
HRSEM coupled to an Oxford Instruments XMax Ultim Extreme EDX 
detection system), HR-TEM (Hitachi, HT7700) operated at 120 kV. 
XPS measurements were performed at room temperature with a 
SPECS PHOIBOS 150 hemispherical analyser (SPECS GmbH, Berlin, 
Germany)) in a base pressure of 5 × 10−10 mbar using monochro- 
matic Al Kalpha radiation (1486.74 eV) as excitation source. The 
surface area Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) and pore size distribu­
tion of samples were examined by nitrogen adsorption (Thermo 
Scientific, SURFAR analyser) operating at −196 °C for 4 h. Diffuse 
reflectance spectra, DR UV-Vis ( Perkin Elmer Lambda), was con­
ducted using barium sulphate as the reference at wavelength 
200─800 nm. Photoluminescence, PL and Raman spectra were con- 
ducted by Raman Spectrophotometer (HORIBA scientific) with laser 
emission of 325 nm and 785 nm, respectively. The photocurrent 
measurement was recorded using source meter (Keithley SMU2450). 
The slurry sample was dropped onto indium titanium oxide (ITO) as 
a coated glass slide and let to dry. Pt wire and Ag/AgCl were used as

counter and reference electrodes, respectively. Solar simulator 
(HAL-C100) was used as the light source.
2.3. Photocatalytic testing
The photocatalytic reduction of CO2 was performed in a slurry 
photoreactor. 0.2 mg photocatalyst, C/g-C3N4, and 1 M (200 mL) of

tracted after the reaction and filtered in order to separate from the 
catalyst residue. The withdrawn solution was analysed using GC-FID

2. Experimental section
2.1. Preparation of photocatalysts
All reagents were analytical grade and used without further pur-
iﬁcation.
2.2. Synthetic of g-C3Nx (X) nanosheets
g-C3Nx (X) nanosheets was prepared by urea pyrolysis according to
a standard literature method. Brieﬂy, 15 g of urea was dissolved with
stirring into aqueous barium hydroxide solution, the barium hydroxide
solution was prepared by dissolving diﬀerent amounts of sodium hy-
droxide in 30 mL ultrapure water, and then the resulting solution eva-
porated to dryness in an oven at 80 °C. The solid mixtures of urea and
barium hydroxide were then calcined at 500 °C in a muﬄe furnace for
2 h at a heating rate of 2 °C min−1, then rise to 520 °C at the same rate
and hold for 6 h. All samples were washed with water to remove any
residual alkali. The obtained products were denoted as g-C3Nx(X),
where X = 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5 g, and corresponds to the mass(g)
of barium hydroxide used.
2.3. Synthetic of g-C3Nx(X)/Ni-Se and g-C3Nx(X)/Ni-Bi-Se nanosheets
In the typical synthesis, the prepared g-C3Nx(X) (X = 0.005, 0.01,
0.05, 0.1, 0.5 g) is added in 100 mL beaker, and then added 30 mL
ethylene glycol dispersed 10 min to form suspension. The diﬀerent
molar ratio of nickel nitrate, bismuth nitrate and selenium are respec-
tively added in the beaker. Thereafter, the mixed suspension is trans-
ferred to a polytetraﬂuoroethylene reactor for 6 h at 120 °C and natu-
rally cooled to room temperature at theend of the reaction. The
precipitate was with deionized water for removed the unreacted pre-
cursor and evaporated to dryness in an oven at 60 °C, then heated in a
tube furnace under a nitrogen atmosphere for an hour. The same
method was used for the synthesis of g-C3Nx(X)/Ni-Se nanosheets ex-
cept that no Bi element was doped.
2.4. Characterization
XRD crystalline structure analysis using Cu Kα radiation (tube
current 40 mA, tube voltage 40 keV). Fourier transform infrared spec-
troscopy (FT-IR) spectrawere performed on Thermo Nicolet Avatar 380
FT-IR spectrometer. UV–vis diﬀuse reﬂectance spectra were carried out
an UV-2550 (Shimadzu) spectrometer by using BaSO4 as the reference.
The microstructure and morphology of the prepared samples were ex-
amined using ﬁeld emission scanning electron microscopy (JSM-
6701F.JEOL) at an accelerating voltage of 5.0 kV. To increase the
conductivity, the sample was dropped onto a copper frame and gold
plated. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) char-
acterization is using a FEI Tecnai TF20 high-resolution transmission
electron microscopy with the accelerated voltage of 300 kV. The ele-
ment composition was detected by X-ray photoelectron spectroscope
(XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi). The nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms
of samples were measured at 77 K with an ASAP 2020 M instrument and
analyzed
by
the
Brunauer–Emmett–Teller
(BET)
equation.
Photoluminescence data (PL) was obtained using a FLUOROMAX-4
spectrophotometer in a mild environment.
H. Wang et al.
Molecular Catalysis 453 (2018) 1–11
2.5. Photocatalytic hydrogen production tests
Photocatalytic hydrogen evolution experiments were conducted in a
quartz reaction ﬂask (62 cm3) with a ﬂat bottom which was irradiated
by a 5W white light lamp under magnetic stirring condition (PCX50A
Discover 5W). In the typical steps, 10 mg of photocatalyst powder and
20 mg dye Eosin Y (EY) powder were suspended in 30 mL 15% (v/v)
triethanolamine (TEOA) aqueous solution as an electronic sacriﬁce re-
agent, disperse ultrasound for 10 min to form a homogeneous solution,
and the reaction system was purged with bubbling N2 for 30 min so as
to clear away the air in the reaction ﬂask and pledged the reactant
mixtures under anaerobic conditions.
The amount of hydrogen evolution was measured using gas chro-
matography (Tianmei GC7900, TCD, 13X column, N2 as carrier). All
glassware was rigorously cleaned and carefully rinsed with distilled
water prior to use.
2.6. Photoelectrochemical measurements
Working electrode preparation: The Fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO)
(1 × 2 cm2) substrate is immersed by cleaning agent, isopropyl alcohol,
acetone solution, ethanol and water under ultrasonic processing for
30 min. Then the catalyst powder (5 mg) was added in 200 μL anhy-
drous ethanol (containing 50 μL 5% Naﬁon solution) and disperse ul-
trasound for 30 min to form a homogeneous solution. Afterwards, the
suspension 150 μL is evenly scribbled to the pre-treated FTO with a drip
coating which area is about 1 cm2. The painted electrode was dried in
room temperature. All PEC measurements were ﬁnished on an elec-
trochemical work-station (VersaStat4-400, Advanced Measurement
Technology, Inc.) in a three-electrode system. The prepared photoanode
was used as the working electrode, a Pt plate as the counter electrode,
and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode. A
300 W xenon lamp equipped with a ﬁlter (λ ≥420 nm) was used as the
irradiation source. 0.1 M Na2SO4 aqueous and hydrogen producing
system solution (containing TEOA and dye EY) was served as the
electrolyte. Photocurrent response testing of the photoanodes with on
and oﬀcycles were carried out at a ﬁxed bias of 0.4 V vs. SCE.

articles.title: Enhancement of photocatalytic hydrogen evolution activity of porous oxygen doped g-C3N4 with nitrogen defects induced by changing electron transition
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental section
2.1 Materials and reagents
Dicyandiamide was purchased from Aladdin Industrial Corporation. (NH4)2S2O8 
was supplied by Tianjin kaitong chemical reagent Co., Ltd, China. Triethanolamine 
(TEOA) was also provided by Aladdin Industrial Corporation. All reagents used in 
this study were at least in analytical grade without further purification. Deionized 
water was used for all experiments.
2.2 
Preparation of photocatalysts
The porous g-C3N4 samples were synthesized by a one-step pyrolysis treatment of 
dicyandiamide and a certain amount of ammonium persulphate. The simple 
preparation method is as follows: dicyandiamide (2 g) and a certain amount of 
ammonium persulphate were uniformly mixed and ground thoroughly. Then the 
powders were put into muffle furnace and heated at 550 °C for 4 h with a heating rate 
of 5 °C/min. When the program was finished, the furnace was cooled to room 
temperature automatically. The samples with mass ratios of ammonium persulphate to 
dicyandiamide of 0.25:1, 0.5:1, and 0.75:1 were signed as p-CN1, p-CN2, and p-CN3, 
respectively. For comparison, a bulk g-C3N4 sample was prepared by the pyrolysis of 
dicyandiamide without adding ammonium persulphate. Following the synthesis, all 
products were collected, grounded and washed repeatedly with deionized water, and 
then dried at 60 °C for 10 h.
2.3 Characterization

Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were performed on a Rigaku 
smartlab system at 45 kV and 200 mA with Cu-Kα radiation (LKα1 = 1.540593 Å, 
LKα2=1.544414 Å). Data were recorded at a scan rate of 0.02◦ in 2θ in the 2 θ. Fourier 
transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were recorded on a Bruker VERTEX 70 
spectrophotometer, and the samples were prepared as KBr pellets. X-ray 
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) data were obtained on a Thermo ESCALAB250 
instrument with a monochromatized Al Kα line source (200 W). The shift of binding 
energy due to relative surface charging was corrected using the C 1s level at 284.6 eV 
as an internal standard. The spectra were fitted using a nonlinear least square fitting 
program (XPSPEAK) with a Shirley background and to the 80% Gaussian/20% 
Lorentzian peak shape. Nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms were collected at a 
Micromeritics ASAP 2020 surface area and porosity analyzer. The sample was 
degassed at 413 K for 5 h and then analyzed at 77 K. The relative pressure (P/P0) 
range used for calculation of BET surface area was from 0.05 to 0.35. The scanning 
emission microscope (SEM) measurements were conducted using a FEI Nova Nano 
SEM 230 Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope. Transmission electron 
microscopy (TEM) image was recorded using a FEI Tecnai F30 at an accelerating 
voltage of 300 kV. UV–vis diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) were performed on a 
UV-Vis spectrophotometer (Lambda 900, PerkinElmer, USA). BaSO4 was used as a 
reflectance standard. The optical properties were evaluated by F(R), and they were 
applied with a Kubelka-Munk correction. Photoluminescence spectra were recorded 
on a LabRAM HR spectrometer (HORIBA Jobin Yvon, France) under the excitation 
wavelength of 325 nm at room temperature. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) 
measurements were carried out on a Bruker model A300 spectrometer. The settings 
for the EPR spectrometer were as follows: center field, 3510.00 G; microwave 
frequency, 9.79 GHz; power, 5.05 mW. The steady-state photoluminescence spectra 
were gained by using LabRAM HR spectrometer (HORIBA Jobin Yvon, France) with 
a laser excitation of 325 nm.
