2.4 Photocatalytic H2 evolution
The photocatalytic H2 production experiments were performed in an online 
photocatalytic hydrogen production system (CEL-SPH2N, CEAULIGHT, Beijing). In 
a typical experiment, 50 mg of photocatalyst powder was suspended in 50 mL 
aqueous solution (40 mL 3 wt.% H2PtCl6·H2O solution and 10 mL triethanolamine). 
Then, the solution was degassed and irradiated by a 300 W Xenon lamp 
(CEAULIGHT CEL-HXF300, Beijing) with a UV cut-off filter (λ > 420 nm). The 
photocatalytic hydrogen evolution rate was quantified by using an online gas 
chromatograph (GC D7860, TCD detector, N2 carrier, 5A molecular sieve column,

as above, 50 mg of photocatalyst was used for the apparent quantum yield (AQY) 
measurement under the wavelengths of 420, 450, 500 and 600 nm band-pass filters, 
respectively. The AQY was calculated by the following equation:

AQY (%) = 2 × number of evolved H2 molecules × 100 /number of incident 
photons

Electrochemical measurements were conducted with a BAS Epsilon Electrochemi-
cal System in a conventional three electrode cell, using a Pt plate as the counter 
electrode and an Ag/AgCl electrode (3 M KCl) as the reference electrode, the active 
area is confined to 0.25 cm2. The electrolyte was 0.1 M Na2SO4 aqueous solution 
without additive (pH 6.9). The working electrode was prepared on indium-tin oxide 
(ITO) glass that was cleaned by sonication in ethanol for 30 min and dried at 353 K. 
The boundary of ITO glass was protected using Scotch tape. The 5 mg sample was 
dispersed in 1 mL of solution containing 980 μL absolute ethanol of and 20 μL of 
Nafion solution, and the mixed solution was under ultrasonication for 30 min to get a 
slurry. The slurry was spread onto pretreated ITO glass. After air-drying, the working 
electrode was further dried at 373 K for 2 h to improve adhesion. Then, the Scotch 
tape was unstuck, and the uncoated part of the electrode was isolated with epoxy 
resin. The transient photocurrent was obtained by using a 30 s on-off light cycle at a 
bias voltage of 0.2 V. Electrochemical impedance spectra were collected in the 
frequency range from 0.01-106 Hz with a 5 mV sinusoidal AC voltage. The Mott-
Schottky plots were measured at the frequency of 1000 Hz. The visible light source 
came from a 300 W Xe lamp with a filter (λ > 420 nm).

2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Materials
Graphite rods (99.99%), urea and sodium hydroxide (Aldrich, 99%) were used
in the preparation of photocatalysts without further purification. Ultrapure (Milli-Q)
water was used to prepare all solutions and in the photocatalytic experiments.
2.2. Carbon dots synthesis
C-dots were synthesized by the typical electrochemical method [26]. Two
graphite rods were inserted into ultrapure water as the cathode and anode in a beaker,
and connected with each other using a direct current power supply providing a voltage
difference of 30 V. The solution became dark black after continuous stirring for 120 h.
After that, the solution was dried at 80 ℃ to get the black powder. The powder
collected was weighted and added to ultrapure water to form the solution with the
required concentration. 30mL of ammonia was mixed with 30 mL of C-dots solution
and stirred to a homogeneous state. The mixed solution was then transferred into a
100 mL Teflon stainless steel autoclave at 150 ℃ for 7 h. After opened to air to
remove the excess ammonia, the C-dots powder could be achieved by centrifugation
and drying. The powder was weighted again and added to form C-dots solution. In our
work, the C-dot solution concentrations were 10 mg/L, 20 mg/L, 30 mg/L, 40 mg/L,
50 mg/L.
2.3. C-dot@ND-g-C3N4 Fabrication

urea was weighted and dissolved with stirring into NaOH solution (0.01 g in 30 mL
H2O) in the alumina crucibles, then 10 mL C-dots solution was added into 50 mL
alumina crucible. The resulting solution evaporated to dryness in a drying oven at 80 ℃
overnight. The solid mixtures were then calcined at 550 ℃ in a muffle furnace for 4 h
(Fig. S1). The resulted light-yellow samples were collected and washed with

2. Experimental section
2.1. Materials
The bulk g-C3N4-MxUy, x and y mean the mass ratios of M to U, were prepared by
thermal condensation as follows: 2 g of mixture of precursors with x:y from 2:1 to 1:3
were added into 20 mL ethanol. The suspension was stirred at ambient temperature for
0.5 h, then the ethanol was removed by a rotary evaporation apparatus. Subsequently,
the mixture powder was put into an alumina crucible with a cover and heated to 773 K
for 2 h at a heating rate of 2 K min-1 in a muffle furnace, then rising the temperature to
793 K at the same heating rate for another 2 h. The resulted product was collected and

grounded into powder for further use.
g-C3N4-MxUy with nanosheet structure were prepared as follows: 0.45 g of bulk g-
C3N4-MxUy was uniformly dispersed into a alumina ark with dimensions of 50×30×
10 mm to make sufficient contact between bulk g-C3N4-MxUy and air, and then heated
to 773 K in an open system at a heating rate of 2 K min-1 for 3 h in a muffle furnace.
Thus g-C3N4-MxUy with nanosheet structure were obtained.
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
For comparison, g-C3N4-M and g-C3N4-U were also prepared separately by using 2 g
of M and 2 g of U under the same calcination conditions. Particularly, the alumina
crucible loaded with 2 g of U was empty after the first step calcination. No g-C3N4-U
was obtained from the same preparation method.
2.2. Characterization of materials
The samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku, Rint-2500, Cu
Kα source), SEM (JEOL JSM-6330FT), and TEM (JEOL JEM-2100, operated at 120
kV). UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra were obtained on a JASCO V-770 UV-vis/NIR
spectrophotometer. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was measured on a JEOL
JPS-9010 MC spectrometer. The Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface areas were
measured using nitrogen sorption (BEL Japan, BELSORP max). The pore volumes and
pore diameter distributions were derived from the adsorption isotherms using the
Barrett–Joyner–Halenda (BJH) model.
2.3. Photocatalytic H2 production
The photocatalytic H2 production experiments were carried out in a tube with a rubber
stopper. Typically, 50 mg samples were dispersed in 50 mL aqueous solution containing
20 vol % TEOA as the sacrificial electron donor. H2PtCl6·6H2O aqueous solution was
added as the precursor for the cocatalyst Pt. Then, the suspension was thoroughly
degassed under Ar gas flow and irradiated by a xenon lamp (Asahi Spectra, LAX-C100)
with magnetic stirring at room temperature. A 400-nm cutoff filter was used to remove
the UV light. After 30 min photodeposition of Pt on g-C3N4-MxUy, the suspension was
degassed again. H2 production was measured by using Shimadzu GC-8A gas
chromatograph equipped with an MS-5A column and a thermal conductivity detector.
The apparent quantum efficiency (AQE) for H2 production at different wavelengths of
the monochromatic light was calculated via the following equation: AQE = (2 × number
of H2 molecules/number of incident photons) × 100 %. The light intensity at λ= 400

nm, 420 nm, 440 nm and 460 nm were 680 μW cm-2, 1.72 mW cm-2, 1.44 mW cm-2 and
1.77 mW cm-2, respectively. The light intensity was measured by an optical power
meter (1916-R, Newport). The irradiation area was 0.785 cm2.
2.3. Photoelectrochemical measurements
Photoelectrochemical measurements were carried out in a standard three-electrode
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
quartz cell with a platinum wire as the counter electrode, Ag/AgCl electrodes as the
reference electrode, g-C3N4-MxUy modified glass carbon electrode as the working
electrode, and 0.5 M Na2SO4 aqueous solution as the electrolyte. The photocurrent
responses and EIS spectra were recorded at an electrode potential of 0.3 V with a scan
rate of 25 mV s-1. The working electrode was irradiated by a xenon lamp (Asahi Spectra,
HAL-320W) with a 400 nm cutoff filters. All measurements were carried out at room
temperature.
2.4. Single-particle PL measurement by confocal microscopy
Sample preparation for single-particle PL experiments was carried out as follows. The
cover glasses were purchased from DAICO MFG CO., Ltd. (Japan) and cleaned by
sonication in a 20 % detergent solution (As One, Cleanace) for 7 h, followed by
repeated washing with warm water 5 times. g-C3N4-MxUy were well dispersed in
ethanol solution and then were spin-coated on the cleaned cover glasses. The cover
glasses were annealed at 100 °C for 1 h to immobilize the particles on the surface.
Single-particle PL images and spectra of samples were recorded by using an objective
scanning confocal microscope system (PicoQuant, MicroTime 200) coupled with an
Olympus IX71 inverted fluorescence microscope. The samples were excited through
an oil-immersion objective lens (Olympus, UplanSApochromat, 100×, 1.4 NA) with a
circular-polarized 405 nm picoseconds pulsed laser controlled by a PDL-800B driver
(PicoQuant). Typical excitation powers for the PL measurements were 120 μW at the
sample. The emission from the sample was collected by the same objective and detected
by a single photon avalanche photodiode (Micro Photon Devices, PDM 50 CT) through
a dichroic beam splitter (Chroma, 405rdc) and long pass filter (Chroma, HQ430CP).
For the spectroscopy, only the emission that passed through a slit entered the imaging
spectrograph (Acton Research, SP-2356) that was equipped with an electron-
multiplying charge-coupled device (EMCCD) camera (Princeton Instruments, ProEM).
All experimental data were obtained at room temperature.

2.5. Time-resolved diffuse reflectance transient absorption measurements
The femtosecond diffuse reflectance transient absorption spectra were measured by the
pump and probe method using a regeneratively amplified titanium sapphire laser
(SpectraPhysics, Spitfire Pro F, 1 kHz) pumped by a Nd:YLF laser (Spectra-Physics,
Empower 15). The second harmonic oscillation of the amplifier (400 nm, 3 μJ per pulse)
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
was used as the excitation pulse. A white light continuum pulse, generated by focusing
the residual of the fundamental light on a sapphire crystal, was directed to the sample
powder coated on the glass substrate, and the reflected lights were detected by using a
linear InGaAs array detector equipped with a polychromator (Solar, MS3504). All
measurements were carried out at room temperature.

2. Experimental
2.1. Catalysts fabrication and naming
All chemicals and reagents used in this work were without further 
purification. The fabrication methods of catalysts were as follows and 
the names were shown in Table S1.
2.1.1. Fabrication of g-C3N4
30.0 g urea in covered crucible was firstly calcined at 500 ◦C for 4 h 
and then calcined at 550 ◦C for 2 h in open crucible. The sample was 
thoroughly washed with ultrapure water and vacuum-dried at 60 ◦C.
2.1.2. Fabrication of g-C3N4-Nvac
0.5 g g-C3N4 was put into 120.0 mL ultrapure water and ultrasoni­
cally dispersed for 5 min. Then, 30.0 mL 1.32 mol/L NaBH4 solution was 
dissolved into mixture drop by drop and magnetically stirred for 15 min. 
The sample was thoroughly washed with ultrapure water and vacuum- 
dried at 60 ◦C.
2.1.3. Fabrication of NiCo2O4/g-C3N4-Nvac
0.24 g g-C3N4-Nvac was added into 40 mL ethanol and ultrasonically 
dispersed for 5 min, followed by the addition of NiCl2.6H2O and 
CoCl2.6H2O (the molar ratio of Co/Ni was 2), Then, 5.0 mmol NH4HCO3
Journal of Hazardous Materials 414 (2021) 125528
was dissolved into above mixture and magnetically stirred for 6 h. The 
samples were obtained via washing with methanol for several times, 
drying at 60 ◦C and finally calcining at 350 ◦C for 2 h.
2.2. Catalytic degradation procedure
10.0 mg catalyst was respectively added into 100.0 mL tetracycline 
hydrochloride (TCH) (25.0 mg/L), carbamazepine (CBZ) (10.0 mg/L), 
tetrachlorophenol (4-CP) (20.0 mg/L), atrazine (ATZ) (5.0 mg/L) and p- 
nitrophenol (PNP) (20.0 mg/L) solution and ultrasound for 5 min. Then, 
the mixture was darkly stirred for 30 min. And 1.0 mM perox­
ymonosulfate (PMS) was rapidly introduced to initiate the sulfate 
radical-photo-Fenton-like reaction with the assistance of visible-light 
illumination. Subsequently, 5.0 mL sample was collected every 5 min 
to filter with 0.22 µm membrane filters and 0.5 mL methanol was 
simultaneously added to quench the oxidation reaction.
2.3. Characterizations
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were detected via a 
JEOL JSM 6700F electron microscope. X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra 
were detected via a Rigaku D/Max-2550 diffractometer. X-ray photo­
electron spectroscopy (XPS) were obtained via a Thermo VG Scientific 
ESCALAB 250 spectrometer. UV-Vis diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) 
were analyzed via a UV-Vis-NIR spectrophotometer (Shimadzu UV- 
3600). Room temperature photoluminescence (PL) spectra were ob­
tained via a FLUOROMAX-4 spectrometer. Electron spin resonance 
(ESR) spectra were analyzed by a Bruker EMX/Plus spectrometer. TCH 
degradation products were detected by UPLC-MS system (Waters UPLC 
Acquity, Quattro Premier XE) composed of the ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 
column (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.7 mm).
2.4. Analytical methods
Some characterization methods of samples were exhibited in Text S1. 
The detection methods for various pollutants were depicted in Text S2. 
The information of PMS concentration measurement was provided in 
Text S3. The toxicity assessment was shown in Text S4.

All the spin-polarized DFT-D2 calculations were carried out in the

bulk CN that includes 56 atoms was ﬁrst relaxed, and subsequently N

2.1.2. Preparation of porous CNNS with N vacancies (CNNS-Nvac)
The porous CNNS-Nvac was prepared by a simple NaBH4 reduction
method. 0.25 g CNNS was added into 60.0 mL water and then sonicated
for 5 min to evenly disperse. Subsequently, 15.0 mL 1.32 M NaBH4
aqueous solution was added dropwise to above suspension. After
vigorous stirring for 15 min, the resulting sample was filtered and dried
at 60 °C for 10 h.
2.1.3. Preparation of porous Fe-POM/CNNS-Nvac
The porous Fe-POM/CNNS-Nvac was prepared by a facile self-as-
sembly method. Different amount of FeCl3
%6H2O (the mass ratio x% of
FeCl3
%6H2O to CNNS-Nvac was 5%, 15 %, 45 % and 65 %) and 28.0 mg
H3PW12O40
%xH2O were added into 100.0 mL water to form aqueous
solution and pH was adjusted to 1.0 with HCl. Subsequently, 0.1 g
CNNS-Nvac was dispersed into above solution and stirred for 15 h to
form Fe-POM/CNNS-Nvac. The obtained samples were filtered and dried
at 60 °C for 10 h under vacuum, which were denoted as xFe-POM/
CNNS-Nvac (x = 5, 15, 45 and 65), respectively. The corresponding Fe-
POM and Fe-POM/CNNS were prepared via the same self-assembly
method by adding nothing and CNNS, respectively.
2.2. Degradation experiment
In the degradation experiment, tetracycline hydrochloride (TCH)
(20.0 mg/L), atrazin (ATZ) (5.0 mg/L), alachor (ALA) (10.0 mg/L),
tetrachlorophenol
(4-CP)
(20.0 mg/L)
and
methyl
orange
(MO)
(20.0 mg/L) were selected as model pollutants to represent the anti-
biotic, pharmaceutical, herbicide, industrial and textile wastewater,
respectively.
Typically,
50.0 mg
photocatalysts
were
added
into
50.0 mL target pollutant solution. After 5 min of ultrasound, the sus-
pension was magnetically stirred for 30 min in the dark to reach the
adsorption/desorption equilibrium. Subsequently, 50.0 μL H2O2 (30 wt
%) was added to initiate the photo-Fenton reaction under visible light
irradiation. The light source was a 300 W Xenon lamp, which was
equipped with a cut-off filter (λ < 420 nm) to remove the UV light.
During the light irradiation, 3.0 mL sample was collected from the
suspension at an interval of 3 min and immediately filtered with
0.22 μm membrane filters.
The concentrations of TCH, ATZ, 4-CP and ALA were detected by
high
performance
liquid
chromatography
(HPLC,
Agilent
1100)
equipped with a 4.6 × 250 mm, 5 μm Venusil HILIC column. The mo-
bile phase (v/v) were acetic acid (1‰)/acetonitrile (90/10, v/v) for
TCH, water/methanol (50/50, v/v) for ATZ, water/methanol (30/70,
v/v) for 4-CP, water/acetonitrile (70/30, v/v) for ALA, respectively.
The flow rate was 0.2 mL/min. The detection wavelength for TCH, ATZ,
4-CP and ALA were 357 nm, 221 nm, 280 nm and 225 nm, respectively.
The concentration of MO was identified by measuring the absorption at
463 nm, using a UV–vis spectrometer (Maya 2000 Pro) at the room
temperature. 1O2 and %OH concentration measurements are exhibited in
Text S2.
In the ROS scavenger experiment, the scavengers used were p-
benzoquinone (p-BQ) (1.0 mM, Sigma) for %O2
−, L-histidine (10.0 mM)
for 1O2, tert-butanol (TBA) (300.0 mM, Sigma) for %OH and formic acid
(10.0 mM, Sigma) for h+, respectively.
2.3. Frontier electron density calculation
The optimized TCH molecular structure parameters were detected
by Gaussian 09 software package with the B3LYP for molecular orbital
calculations. Moreover, the energy of highest occupied molecular or-
bital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of
all the atoms except hydrogen atom in TCH molecule were evaluated to
predict oxidative degradation behavior of TCH.
2.4. Toxicity evaluation of TCH and its degradation products
The acute toxicity and mutagenicity of TCH and its degradation
products were evaluated by quantitative structure activity relationship
(QSAR) predication using Toxicity Estimation Software Tool (T.E.S.T.)
with consensus method. The cytotoxicity assays with S. aureus is shown
in Text S3.

2.1. Preparation of g-C3N4
A diluted glyoxylic acid solution was obtained by adding 1 mL 
glyoxylic acid (50% weight ratio, CAS No. 298-12-4) into 100 mL 
distilled water. 0.01 mol melamine was dissolved in 100 mL 80 ◦C 
distilled water under stirring for 30 min. A certain amount of diluted 
glyoxylic acid solution (0, 0.6, 1, 1.4, 2, 3, 6 and 10 mL, the corre­
sponding molar ratios of glyoxylic acid to melamine are 0%, 3%, 5%, 
7%, 10%, 15%, 30%, and 50%, respectively) was added to the above 
solution with stirring. Then, the solution was placed into an oven and 
dried at 120 ◦C to obtain glyoxylic acid mediated melamine (denoted as 
GM-X (X = 0, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 30, and 50 for 0%, 3%, 5%, 7%, 10%, 15%, 
30%, and 50% molar ratios of glyoxylic acid to melamine). GM-X (X = 0, 
3, 5, 7, 10, and 15) samples were heated in N2 flow (40 mL/min) at 
550 ◦C for 4 h with a heating rate of 5 ◦C/min. The obtained g-C3N4 
samples were denoted as GMN-X (X = 0, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 15). A further 
thermal process in air was used to increase the specific surface area of g- 
C3N4. The GMN-X samples (X = 0, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 15) were calcined at 
550 ◦C in air atmosphere for 2 h in a muffle furnace. The obtained 
products were denoted as GMNA- X (X = 0, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 15).
2.2. Characterization
A scanning electron microscope (SEM, S4800, Hitachi) was used to 
observe the morphology of the obtained products. The structure of the 
samples was characterized by transmission electron microscope (TEM, 
JEOL JEM-2100). The UV–Vis diffuse reflection properties were

evaluated with a Shimadzu UV-2450 spectrophotometer. Electron

Bruker ElEXSYS spectrometer. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the

A gastight cylindrical glass reactor (325 mL) covered with a quartz

syringe. After 2 h, when the liquid IPA evaporated, uniform gaseous IPA 
formation, then turn on the light for photocatalytic reaction. The light

the photodegradation product were detected by a gas chromatography 
with FID detectors.

2.2. Synthesis of photocatalysts
The preparation method of g-C3Nx is as follows: 2 g of melamine was
dissolved in KOH aqueous solution (30 mL H2O, 0.06 g KOH) under
stirring. After drying in an oven at 80 °C overnight, it was placed in a
muffle furnace and calcined at 550 °C for 2 h at a rate of 5 °C/min. After
cooling at room temperature, it was ground to obtain g-C3Nx powder.
All samples were washed with water for three times to remove any
residual base, which is labeled as CNx. Then, the samples were dried in
an oven and collected. For comparison, 2 g of melamine is directly
calcined under the same conditions to obtain pristine g-C3N4, which is
abbreviated as CN.
The DyVO4/g-C3Nx (DVO/CNx) composites were synthesized by a
precipitation-calcination method. Firstly, Dy(NO3)3 and NH4VO3 with
equimolar are added into deionized water and adjusted the pH to 8 by
the introduction of ammonia water, then the precursor dispersion are
aging for 3 h. The precipitates are washed and dried, and placed it in a
muffle furnace at 500 °C for 2 h at a rate of 10 °C/min to obtain the DVO
powder. Secondly, the synthesized DVO powder was mixed with a
certain amount of CNx and ground for 15 min, and then placed in a
muffle furnace at 500 °C for 2 h to obtain DVO/CNx composites with
different proportions. The products with different weight percentages of
DVO in the DVO/CNx composites are labeled as 5 % DVO/CNx, 10 %
DVO/CNx and 20 % DVO/CNx, respectively.

Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded using a

Corporation, Japan). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images

wavelength of 325 nm. Electrochemical analysis was conducted on a

served as the counter electrode, the reference electrode, and the

The photocatalytic activity of the as-synthesized composites was
evaluated by degradation of tetracycline (TC) under visible light irra-

(10 mg/L), and the mixture was stirred for 0.5 h before irradiation to
ensure adsorption/desorption equilibrium at room temperature. At a
given irradiation time interval, 4 mL aliquot was collected and cen-

lyzed by recording the change in the maximum absorption wavelength

spectrophotometer. The degradation rate can be calculated by the fol-

articles.title: Efficient photocatalytic hydrogen evolution on N-deficient g-C3N4 achieved by a molten salt post-treatment approach
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental section
2.1. Chemicals and reagents
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
Melamine, KCl, LiCl, and triethanolamine (TEOA, analytical reagent (AR) grade) were
purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. and were used without further
purification. All other reagents used in this study were analytically pure and used as
received.
2.2 Synthesis of bulk g-C3N4
Bulk g-C3N4 was prepared by thermal polycondensation of melamine. Typically,
melamine (10 g) in an alumina crucible (50 mL) with a cover was heated in air at a
ramping rate of 2 °C min-1 to 550 °C in a muffle furnace for 3 h. After cooling to room
temperature naturally, the yellow product was collected and then ground into powder in
an agate mortar.
2.3 Synthesis of g-C3Nx
The g-C3Nx was synthesized by a molten salt post-treatment method. A eutectic mixture
of KCl and LiCl with the molar ratio of 41:59 had a melting point of about 352 °C and
was used as the high-temperature solvent for the reactions. Typically, bulk g-C3N4 (1 g)
was ground with KCl (8.2 g) and LiCl (11.8 g) in an agate mortar. Then, the mixture
was heated in air at 550 °C in a muffle furnace for 2 hours at a ramping rate of 2 °C
min-1. After cooling to room temperature naturally, the product was boiled and washed
with deionized water thoroughly to remove residual salts. The product was collected by
pumping filtration, following by drying at 60 °C for 12 h.
2.4 Characterization
The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the as-prepared samples were collected on a
powder X-ray diffractometer (Cu Kα radiation source, D8, Bruker). The morphologies
of the samples were investigated by a field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-
SEM, Hitachi S4800). Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra were obtained on a
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
Tensor 27 spectrometer (Bruker). The solid-state 13C NMR experiments were performed
on a Bruker Advance III 500 spectrometer. UV-visible (UV-Vis) diffuse reflectance
spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu UV-2450 spectrophotometer equipped with an
integrating sphere, then converted into absorption spectra by Kubelka-Munk
transformation. Photoluminescence (PL) spectra were measured at room temperature
using a Fluoromax-4 Spectrophotometer (Horiba Jobin Yvon). The excitation
wavelength was 325 nm, and the emission slit was 1.0 nm. Elemental analysis was
carried out on a Thermo-Scientific Flash Smart micro-analyzer. The XPS patterns were
measured on an electronic energy spectrum (AXIS UltraDLD, Kratos group) at 300 W
using Mg Kα X-rays as 
the excitation source. 
Steady-state/time-resolved
photoluminescence emission spectra (365 nm excitation) were measured at room
temperature with a fluorescence spectrophotometer (PTI, DeltaFlex). Electron
paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra were taken using a Bruker model ER200-SRC
spectrometer.
2.5 Photocatalytic H2 Production
The photocatalytic H2 evolution reactions were carried out in a Pyrex reaction cell
connected to a closed gas circulation and evacuation system using a 300 W Xe lamp
with a cut-off filter (λ > 420 nm). 0.2 g of photocatalyst was dispersed in an aqueous
solution (100 mL) containing (20 vol. %) triethanolamine (TEOA) as a sacrificial agent
by sonication. Before irradiation, the reactor was well-evacuated by a vacuum pump to
remove the dissolved air in water. The amount of H2 evolved was analyzed by on-line
gas chromatography with TCD detector (Hua’ai, GC9160, China, MS-5A, argon as
carrier gas). The co-catalyst Pt for the promotion of hydrogen evolution was photo-
deposited in situ on the photocatalyst with H2PtCl6·6H2O as a precursor. The
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
temperature for all photocatalytic reactions was kept at 25 °C ± 5 °C.
2.6 Photoelectrochemical measurements
The photoelectrochemical properties of the samples were examined by electrochemical
impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and photocurrent response measurements on a
PARSTAT 4000 electrochemical workstation using a standard three-electrode cell with
a working electrode, a platinum foil counter electrode, and an Ag/AgCl reference
electrode. Na2SO4 (0.1 M) was used as the electrolyte solution. The working electrode
was prepared by dip-coating photocatalyst slurry on FTO glass electrode (1.0×1.0 cm2)
and heating it at 60 °C overnight. Mott-Schottky plots were obtained under direct
current potential polarization at different frequencies (1.0, 1.2, and 1.5 kHz). For
photocurrent measurements, the applied over-potential was set to be 0.5 V (vs.
Ag/AgCl). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were carried
out with a sinusoidal ac perturbation of 10 mV applied over the frequency range of
0.01-105 Hz.

articles.title: Enhanced peroxymonosulfate activation on dual active sites of N vacancy modified g-C3N4 under visible-light assistance and its selective removal of organic pollutants

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Chemicals
Melamine, alcohol, methanol, tetra-n-butyl, disodium edetate, p-
benzoquinone and furfuralcohol were purchased from Sinopharm
Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.. Oxone (KHSO5·0.5KHSO4·0.5K2SO4) was
purchased from Aladdin. N2 gas (≥99.999%) was purchased from Dalian
Special Gases Co.. All solutions were prepared with ultrapure water (re-
sistivity>18 MΩ·cm, Laikie Instrument Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China).
2.2. Sample preparation
The 1 g melamine was dissolved in 70 mL ultrapure water under vig-
orous stirring and 60 °C heating. After complete dissolution, the solution
was transferred to a 100 mL Teﬂon-lined stainless steel autoclave and
placed in an oven for hydrothermal treatment at 180 °C for 12 h. After
cooled down to the room temperature, the products were obtained by
ﬁltration through 0.45 μm membrane and rinsed by alcohol and water
several times. Then the powders were placed in a ceramic boat and
sintered in a furnace. The heating process was conducted at a certain
temperature (500 °C, 550 °C and 600 °C) for 3 h in N2 atmosphere
with a heating rate of 2.5 °C min−1. After cooled down to the room tem-
perature, the ﬁnal N vacancy modiﬁed g-C3N4 was obtained. In compar-
ison, the bulk g-C3N4 was synthesized by directing heating melamine to
550 °C in mufﬂe furnace for 3 h. For convenient description, the N va-
cancy modiﬁed g-C3N4 obtained at different temperatures was denoted
as VCN-500, VCN-550 and VCN-600, respectively, and the bulk g-C3N4
was named as CN.
2.3. Characterizations
The crystal information of VCNs was obtained using X-ray diffrac-
tometer (XRD, Shimadzu LabX-6100) with Cu-Kα radiation (λ =
1.5418 Å). The surface groups were measured via IRAfﬁnity-1 Fourier
transform infrared (FT-IR). The morphologies of VCNs were observed
through ﬁeld-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) (JSM-
6460LV, JEOL). The element distribution and speciﬁc species of VCN
samples were measured by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
(ESCALAB250). The speciﬁc surface area of samples was calculated
based on the N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms derived at 77 K via a
physical adsorption-desorption analyzer (NOVA 2000e, Quantachrome).
The N vacancy of samples was detected from electron spin resonance
(ESR) spectra recorded on a Brüker A200 spectrometer (JES FA200) at
77 K. The test was operated with the central ﬁeld of 3510 G, microwave
frequency of 9.8 GHz, microwave power of 22.32 mW, sweep width of
100 G and time constant of 10 s. The light absorbance capability of
VCN samples was tested by UV-2450 UV–visible spectrophotometer
(Shimadzu). The separation efﬁciency of photoinduced electron-holes
of VCNs was investigated by photoluminescence (PL) spectra. Both
photoelectrochemical and electrochemical experiments were carried
out on the CHI-660D electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, China). In
detail, the electrochemical measurements were conducted in a three-
electrode system, in which the VCN coated glassy carbon electrode
served as the working electrode, Pt as a counter electrode, and a satu-
rated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode.

2.4. The photo-assisted PMS activation experiment
The 7.5 mg VCN catalysts were dispersed in a Pyrex photocata-
lytic reactor containing 50 mL pollutant solution (0.04 mM). A
350 W xenon lamp was used as the light source (equipped with a
λ > 420 nm optical ﬁlter). Initially, the catalysts were stirred vigor-

values of pollutant were measured using a TOC analyzer (TOC-
VCPH, Shimadzu, Japan). The experiments were conducted in tripli-
cates, and the average values with standard deviations were
presented.
In order to detect the reactive species in the catalytic process, the
methanol (0.8 M), tert-butanol (TBA, 0.8 M), disodium edetate
(EDTA-Na2, 4 mM), ρ-benzoquinone (ρ-BQ, 4 mM), furfuryl alcohol
(FFA, 4 mM) and AgNO3 (0.8 M) were added to the RhB solution to
quench sulfate radical (SO4
•−), hydroxyl radical (•OH), holes, super-
oxide radical (O2
•−), singlet oxygen (1O2) and electron, respectively.
The EPR spectra of reactive species were conducted on a Brüker
A200 spectrometer (JES FA200) in the presence of both light and
PMS, in which the 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine (TMP) was used as
the spin-trapping reagent for
1O2, while the 5,5-dimethyl-1-
pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO) was utilized as the spin trapping agent
for SO4
•−, •OH and O2
•−. The EPR tests were operated with the center
ﬁeld of 3500 G, microwave frequency of 9.7 GHz, microwave power
of 6.35 mW, sweep width of 200 G and time constant of 10 s. The

articles.title: The effect of oxygen on the N2 photofixation ability over N vacancies embedded g-C3N4 prepared by dielectric barrier discharge plasma treatment
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental
N2 molecules, leading to the activation of N2 molecules.
Plasma, diﬀerent from the gas, liquid and solid states, is considered
as the fourth state of matter. Plasma is composed of a large number of
electrons, ions, atoms, molecules, free radicals, and other particles.
Dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) is a common method to produce
plasma, because it does not require vacuum, can be carried out under
atmospheric pressure, and achieves stable discharges. Due to these
advantages, the DBD method is widely used in material synthesis [29],
volatile-organic-compound treatment [30,31] and surface modiﬁcation
[32]. In this work, N vacancies embedded g-C3N4 was prepared by di-
electric barrier discharge plasma treatment. Compared with N2 atmo-
sphere, as-prepared catalyst displays remarkably promoted N2 photo-
ﬁxation ability under mixture of N2 and O2 using methanol as hole
scavenger. The eﬀect of oxygen on the N2 photoﬁxation ability in this
system is proposed.
2.1. Preparation and characterization
The g-C3N4 was prepared by annealing urea at 550 °C for 2 h under
Ar atmosphere (the rate of 5 °C·min−1). The prepared sample was de-
noted as B-GCN. The B-GCN was modiﬁed in a DBD reactor, which was
used in previous work [35,36]. 0.2 g of B-GCN was placed into the
quartz tube. Argon gas is introduced into the quartz tube for 5 min.
Then, a high voltage of ~10 kV was supplied by a plasma generator
with the H2 ﬂow rate of 50 ml·min−1. The discharge was kept for
30 min with the frequency of 10 kHz. The obtained catalyst was de-
noted as VN-GCN.
The XRD patterns were recorded on a Rigaku D/max-2400 instru-
ment using Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.54 Å). UV–Vis spectroscopy of as-
prepared catalyst was measured by a UV–Vis spectrophotometer
(JASCO-V-550). The catalyst morphology was obtained using both
Y. Zhao, et al.
Diamond & Related Materials 94 (2019) 146–154
Fig. 2. Photocatalytic N2 ﬁxation ability of VN-GCN under diﬀerent reaction condition (a) or under mixed gas with diﬀerent N2/O2 content (b).
scanning electron microscope (SEM, JSM 5600LV, JEOL Ltd.). The X-
ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out on a Thermo
Escalab 250 XPS system. Al Kα radiation was used as the excitation
source. Nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherm was measured using a
Micromeritics 2010 analyser. The SBET was calculated according to the
adsorption isotherm. The catalyst component was measured by ICP
(Perkin-Elmer Optima 3300DV). Adsorption capacity of nitrogen,
oxygen or mixture of nitrogen and oxygen on catalyst surface was
measured by TPD (CHEMBET-3000, Quantachrome). Free radical spe-
cies was detected by electron spin resonance (ESR) (EMX-220, Bruker).
The electrons-holes separation rate of catalyst was tested by photo-
luminescence (PL) spectra using a ﬂuorospectrophotometer (FP-6300).
2.2. Photocatalytic reaction
N2 photoﬁxation performance of as-prepared catalyst is evaluated
according to method reported in previous literature [33]. A 250 W high-
pressure sodium lamp (main wavelength 400–800 nm) was used as a
visible light source. Sodium nitrite aqueous solution with concentration
of 0.5 mol·L−1 was used as a sodium lamp cooling circulating water to
ﬁlter the ultraviolet light portion of the light source. 0.1 g of the catalyst
was added to 500 mL of deionized water and stirred for 0.5 h to fully
disperse. 0.2 mL of methanol or ethanol or nothing was added into the
suspension to trap the holes. Under the stirring condition, the suspen-
sion was placed under the light source for irradiation. At the same time,
a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen (or pure nitrogen) was bubbled. 5 mL
of suspension were collected and centrifuged to obtain the liquid
samples at given time intervals. The NH4
+ concentration was obtained
by the Nessler's reagent spectrophotometry method (JB7478-87)
[33,34].
The photocatalytic hydrogen peroxide production ability of as-pre-
pared catalyst was evaluated in the same manner as the nitrogen ﬁxa-
tion reaction [35]. The concentration of hydrogen peroxide was de-
termined by normal iodometric method [36,37].

articles.title: Efficient visible-light-driven hydrogen evolution and Cr(VI) reduction over porous P and Mo co-doped g-C3N4 with feeble N vacancies photocatalyst
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental section
2.1. Materials
Melamine(C3H6N6, 99%), Ammonium molybdate tetrahydrate (H24Mo7N6O24·4H2O, 99%),
and Bis(2-ethylhexyl)phosphate(C3H35O4P, 95%) were all purchased from Shanghai macklin
Biochemical Co.Ltd, and being directly used without further purification.
2.2. Synthesis of (P, Mo)-g-C3Nx
Typical preparation of (P, Mo)-g-C3Nx was prepared by consulting the method being
reported previously with some modifications.[9] Firstly, 12.6 g melamine (C3H6N6), 2.279 mL
C3H35O4P (P204) were added into 80mL of absolute alcohol under the constant stirring for about
4h at 80 ◦C , followed by evaporation(60◦C) under continuous shaking. Then, the white samples
were being further dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C overnight. Secondly, the above white solid
was grinded into powder, and then being dissolved in 40mL of deionized water in the company
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
of 0.529g H24Mo7N6O24·4H2O. The mixture was under constantly stirring until a homogeneous
solution was being obtained. Then the above solution was being poured into the evaporating
dishes placed in an oven at 180◦C to dry out water completely. After a cooling procedure, the
resulted sample was put into a crucible with a cover and being heated in air at 550◦C for 4h at a
ramp rate of 10◦C/min. For the purpose of comparison, P-g-C3Nx, Mo-g-C3N4 and the pristine g-
C3N4 were also fabricated similarly by using P, Mo precursor or in the absence of both
precursors, respectively.
2.3. Characterization
Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the as-prepared samples were recorded on the
X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Y2000, Dandong, China) using Cu kα X-ray irradiation. And the
morphology of the samples was determined by a field-emission scanning electron microscope
(FE-SEM, ZEISS ULTRA 55, Germany) and a transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-
1400PLUS, Japan). The Brunauer Emmett Teller(BET) specific surface areas(SBET) of the as-
prepared samples were analyzed using a nitrogen adsorption apparatus(ASAP 2020, USA) with
all the samples degassed at 150◦C for 8h under flowing N2 prior to measurements. And the pore
size distributions were determined by the Barret-Joyner-Halenda method. The Fourier transform
infrared spectra (FT-IR) were determined by a FT-IR spectroscopy (FT-IR, Nicolet 6700, USA)
using the standard KBr disk technique. And X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
measurements were conducted on a Thermo Scientific spectrometer (XPS, ESCALAB 250,
USA) with Al kα radiation as the excitation source operated at 150W. The UV-Vis diffuse
reflection spectra (UV-Vis, DRS) of the samples were obtained by a UV-Vis spectrophotometer
(UV-3010, Hitachi, Japan) with 100% BaSO4 as the background at room temperature.
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
Photoluminescence spectra were recorded on a fluorescence spectrometer (PL, F-2700, Hitachi,
Japan) at ambient temperature.
2.4. Photocatalytic H2 production activity
Photocatalytic hydrogen production experiments were carried out at ambient temperature in
a 280 mL Pyrex reaction cell with an efficient irradiation area of ca. 15.1 cm2 connected to a
glass closed gas circulation system. A typical photocatalytic reaction was conducted by
dispersing 10 mg of the as-prepared samples in a 100mL aqueous solution containing
triethanolamine (TEOA) (5 Vol.%) and 17.5 mg eosin Y (EY). A 300W xenon Lamp (PLS-
SXE300BF, Beijing, Trustech) equipped with a 420nm cut-off filter was used as the light source,
and the light intensity is 150 mW/cm2. Before the visible light irradiation, the system was
degassed by bubbling N2 gas for 15 min to ensure the anaerobic conditions in the reaction. And
the aqueous temperature was maintained around room temperature upon a flowing of cooling
water during the photocatalytic reaction. Finally, the amount of H2 evolution was measured
every hour using gas chromatography (GC-9560, shanghai, huaai chromatography Technology
Co.,Ltd) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) using Ar gas as the carrier gas.
2.5. Photocatalytic Cr(VI) reduction measurement
The photocatalytic Cr(VI) reduction experiments of the as-prepared catalyst were carried
out in the photocatalytic reactor, the light source was a 300W xenon Lamp (PLS-SXE300BF,
Beijing, Trustech) equipped with a 420nm cut-off filter. In each photocatalytic test, before the
visible light irradiation, the mixture containing 40 mL K2Cr2O7 aqueous solution (100 mg/L) and
0.03 g tartaric acid (hole scavenger agent) as well as 0.05 g of catalyst was being stirred
constantly for 1 h to ensure the adsorption/desorption equilibrium. During the reaction, 3 mL of
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
the suspension was being taken out at given time intervals(0.5h) and then centrifugated to isolate
the photocatalyst, the residual concentration of Cr(VI) was reflected by a UV–vis
spectrophotometer (UV-1800, Shimadzu, Japan), detected at the main characteristic absorption
peak of Cr(VI) (540 nm).
2.6. Photoelectrochemical Measurements
The transient photocurrent responses of the as-prepared samples were measured on an
electrochemical analyzer (CHI660E) in a standard three-compartment cell with a working
electrode. And the working electrodes were prepared as follows: 5 mg of the as-obtained
photocatalyst was suspended in 1 mL of water to form slurry, which was then being dip-coated
onto an indium tin oxide (ITO) glass electrode (1.0cm2). Afterwards, the electrodes were being
placed in air atmosphere for about 12 h to fully eliminate water and subsequently calcined at 200
◦C for 5 h. A platinum wire and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) were used as a counter
electrode and the reference electrode, respectively. And 0.1 M Na2SO4 was served as the
electrolyte solution.

articles.title: The effect of embedding N vacancies into g-C3N4 on the photocatalytic H2O2 production ability via H2 plasma treatment
articles.experimental_text:
2. Experimental
2.1. Preparation and characterization
The g-C3N4 was synthesized by annealing melamine at 520 °C for 2 h
under Ar atmosphere (5 °C·min−1). The obtained catalyst was denoted
as GCN. The modiﬁcation of GCN was carried out in a DBD reactor,
which was used in our previous work [45,46]. For each run, 0.5 g of
GCN was put into the quartz tube. Ar was allowed to pass through the
quartz tube for 5 min to ﬂush out the air. At a constant H2 ﬂow
(40 ml·min−1), a high voltage of ~10 kV was supplied by a plasma
generator. The power input was 50 V × 0.4 A, discharge frequency was
10 kHz, and the discharge was kept for 30 min. After that, the reactor
was cooled down to room temperature. The obtained g-C3N4 was de-
noted as PH-CN. For comparison, N vacancies embedded g-C3N4 was
also prepared by traditional roasting method. GCN was annealed at
500 °C for 2 h under H2 atmosphere (40 ml·min−1). The obtained cat-
alyst was denoted as AH-CN.
The XRD patterns of the samples were recorded on a Rigaku D/max-
2400 instrument using Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.54 Å). UV–Vis spectro-
scopy was carried out on a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (JASCO V-550)
using BaSO4 as the reﬂectance sample. The morphologies of samples
were observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, JSM
5600LV, JEOL Ltd.). Nitrogen adsorption was measured at −196 °C on
a Micromeritics 2010 analyzer. The BET surface area (SBET) was cal-
culated based on the adsorption isotherm. Elemental analysis was
performed using a vario EL cube from Elementar Analysensysteme
GmbH. Temperature programmed desorption (TPD) studies were per-
formed using a CHEMBET-3000 (Quantachrome, U.S.A.) instrument.
Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) was monitored using a digital
X-band spectrometer (EMX-220, Bruker, USA). The photocurrents were
measured using an electrochemical analyzer (CHI 618C Instruments).
TEM images were taken on a Philips Tecnai G220 model microscope.
XPS measurements were conducted on a Thermo Escalab 250 XPS
system with Al Kα radiation as the exciting source. The binding en-
ergies were calibrated by referencing the C 1s peak (284.6 eV) to reduce
the sample charge eﬀect. The photoluminescence (PL) spectra were
measured with a ﬂuorospectrophotometer (FP-6300) using Xe lamp as
the excitation source. Electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) were
performed via an EIS spectrometer (EC-Lab SP-150, BioLogic Science)
in a three-electrode cell.
2.2. Photocatalytic reaction
The photocatalytic H2O2 production was carried out as follow. 0.2 g
of catalyst was added into 200 mL of deionized water under stirring to
form a suspension. Ethanol with a concentration of 0.789 g/L was
added as a hole scavenger. Then, the suspension was exposed to a
250 W high-pressure sodium lamp with main emission from 400 to
800 nm. The UV light portion of the sodium lamp was ﬁltered by
NaNO2 solution (0.5 M). O2 was bubbled (80 mL·min−1) during the
photoreaction process. All runs were conducted at ambient pressure
and 30 °C. At given time intervals, 5 mL aliquots of the suspension were
collected and immediately centrifuged to obtain the liquid samples. The
H2O2 concentration was analyzed by the normal iodometric method
[47,48].

The g‐C3N4 was synthesized in a DBD reactor, which was

The X‐ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the samples were

urements were performed using a Thermo Escalab 250 XPS

sis was performed using a Vario EL cube from Elementar

tion (TPD) studies were conducted using a CHEMBET‐3000 
(Quantachrome, USA) instrument. Photoluminescence (PL)

spectra were measured with a fluorospectrophotometer 
(FP‐6300) using a Xe lamp as the excitation source. Electro‐
chemical impedance spectra (EIS) were acquired with an EIS

The catalyst (0.2 g) was added into 200 mL of deionized

Speciﬁcally, for the Synthesis of pure C3N4, 20 g CH4N2O was

2.1. Preparation of pure g-C3N4
All chemicals applied in this paper were purchased from Sigma-
Aldrich, Inc. at analytical-grade. The pristine g-C3N4 photocatalyst was
synthesized using a calcination method. Typically, 2 g of grounded
dicyandiamide white powder was put into an alumina crucible with

CN and 2.5-AgI/CN powders because of the small amount and (or) high
dispersion. However, the diﬀraction peak at 13.1° gradually broadened
with decreased intensity after the loading of AgI, which was possibly
caused by the decreased order degree of in-plane structural packing due
to the embedding of AgI nanoparticles. In addition, the peak position at
27.5° slightly moved to higher diﬀraction angle after the addition of
AgI, indicating a reduction of the distance between nanosheets [27–29].
This is because the accumulation of g-C3N4 nanosheets after the in-

C3N4 system. The phase of the prepared AgIO3 precursor was displayed
in Fig. S2, which was similar to standard pattern of silver iodate (JCPDS
No. 45-0880). The speciﬁc surface area and pore size of CN and 2.5-
AgI/CN were analyzed by nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms
(Fig. 1b). Both the isotherms were classiﬁed as type IV isotherms with
an obvious H3 hysteresis loop at high relative pressure, indicating the
existence of mesoporous structure [31]. The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller
(BET) surface area of CN and 2.5-AgI/CN was 7.11 and 5.49 m2·g−1,
and the average pore diameters of CN and 2.5-AgI/CN were 10.29 and
15.31 nm, respectively (Table 1). After loading of AgI nanoparticles, the
speciﬁc surface area decreased a little because of the covering of pores
by in-situ formed AgI. The morphology and microstructure of CN, 1.25-
AgI/CN, 2.5-AgI/CN and 5-AgI/CN composites were characterized by
TEM. Some irregular pores formed on the surface of pure g-C3N4 na-
nosheets (Fig. 1c), while there were fewer pores formed in the g-C3N4
nanosheets after loading of AgI, which is consistent with the results of
BET. For 1.25-AgI/CN, 2.5-AgI/CN, and 5-AgI/CN composites in
Fig. 1d-f, they exhibited a sheet-like structure and AgI nanoparticles
were anchored and dispersed in the lamellar nanosheets of g-C3N4.
Notably, the lamellar structure became thicker with increasing the
content of AgI. Excess addition of AgI caused the aggregation and the
accumulation of g-C3N4 sheets [32].
The compositions and chemical states of CN and n-AgI/CN com-
posite was further explored through XPS (Fig. 2). As depicted in Fig. 2a,
the 2.5-AgI/CN was consisted of Ag, I, C, N and O elements with no
other impurity elements founded. The peak of O was originated from
the adsorbed H2O on the surface of the catalyst powder. The binding
energies of carbon and nitrogen for both CN and 2.5-AgI/CN matched
to the typical position in graphitic carbon nitride. Fig. 2b shown the N
1s high-resolution XPS spectra, which is consisted of four binding en-
ergy peaks at 398.5 eV (C]NeC), 399.3 eV (Ne(C)3), 401.1 eV (NeH)
and 404.5 eV (π-excitation). The peak area ratio of (Ne(C)3) to (C]
NeC) increased from 0.22 to 0.97 after the loading of AgI (Fig. 2b and
Table 2), showing the deﬁciency of nitrogen in C]NeC. The C 1 s
region was presented in Fig. 2c, and the binding energies at 284.7,
286.4, and 288.0 eV corresponded to the adventitious carbon residual
CeNHx and the carbon atom of Ce(N)3 in the framework of g-C3N4,
respectively. As presented in Table 2, the peak area ratio of CeNHx to
NeC]N for CN was 0.036, which increased to 0.038 for 2.5-AgI/CN,
further proving the appearance of nitrogen deﬁciency [33]. The peaks
at 368.1 eV and 374.1 eV in the Ag 3d spectrum of 2.5-AgI/CN was
associated with Ag 3d5/2 and Ag 3d3/2, respectively (Fig. 2d) [34].
Furthermore, the peaks of I 3d5/2 and I 3d3/2 were centered at 618.9 eV
and 630.3 eV in I 3d spectrum in Fig. 2d [35,36]. Compared with CN,
the N/C molar ratio of 2.5-AgI/CN decreased from 1.653 to 1.646 ac-
cording to the elemental analysis (Table 2), which further conﬁrmed
the existence of nitrogen vacancies in 2.5-AgI/CN. In order to probe the
formation process of the nitrogen vacancy, TGA and DSC curves of
AgIO3 was acquired in Fig. S3. The DSC curve indicates three en-
dotherms at about 419.2 °C, 479.9 °C and 555.9 °C which correspond to
the melting of AgIO3, decomposition of AgIO3 and sublimation of AgI,
respectively [22]. During the heating process, AgIO3 decomposes to be
AgI as a residue with a 16.7% mass decrease at about 479.9 °C, which
cover and calcined at 823 K for 4 h with a heating rate of 5 K/min under
argon atmosphere in a tube furnace. After cooling down to room tem-
perature, the yellowish agglomerated sample was ground to ﬁne
powder and recalcined at 803 K for 2 h under argon atmosphere. The
ﬁnally obtained sample was marked as CN.
2.2. Preparation of AgIO3
Silver iodate (AgIO3) was synthesized by a wet chemistry method
according to the reported literature [22]. Firstly, 75 mL 0.1 mM silver
nitrate solution was added dropwise (5 mL/min) to 75 mL 0.101 mM
potassium iodate solution under vigorous stirring. Secondly, the ob-
tained white precipitate was collected by centrifugation and then wa-
shed three times with DI water. Finally, the white powder product was
dried at 325 K for 6 h.
2.3. Preparation of AgI modiﬁed g-C3N4 composite
AgI modiﬁed g-C3N4 composite was synthesized by an in-situ de-
composition-thermal polymerization method with dicyandiamide and
AgIO3 as precursors. In a typical procedure, 2 g of dicyandiamide with a
certain amount of AgIO3 was grounded for 30 min carefully and then
calcined under the same condition as that of pure g-C3N4. The weight
percent of AgIO3 to dicyandiamide was controlled as 1.25, 2.5, and 5 wt
%. The corresponding composites were named as n-AgI/CN, and n re-
presents the weight percent of AgIO3 to dicyandiamide.
2.4. Characterization
The crystal phase structure and morphology of CN and n-AgI/CN
composite was studied by powder X-ray diﬀraction and transmission
electron microscope. UV/vis diﬀuse reﬂectance spectra were applied on
a UV/vis spectrophotometer. The elemental compositions and chemical
states were performed on X-ray photoelectron spectrometer. The N2
adsorption-desorption isotherms were acquired on Micromeritics ASAP
2020 apparatus. The photoluminescence spectra were obtained through
ﬂuorescence spectrophotometer with an excitation wavelength of
365 nm. The decomposition property of AgIO3 was measured by TGA/
DSC. The time-resolved PL spectra were determined on Single photon
counting controller. The atomic ratio of carbon to nitrogen was adopted
by elemental analysis. The details of the equipment applied in this work
were listed in the supporting materials.
2.5. Photocatalytic nitrogen ﬁxation
The photocatalytic nitrogen ﬁxation property was evaluated ac-
cording to the previous literatures [15,23]. The photocatalytic experi-
ments were performed in a cooling-water jacketed beaker at atmo-
spheric pressure with a 300 W Xenon-lamp as the light source. Firstly,
20 mg of photocatalyst was dispersed in 30 mL 5 vol% methanol aqu-
eous solution by ultrasound. Secondly, N2 was continuously bubbled
through in dark atmosphere to establish an adsorption–desorption
equilibrium before the irradiation. Thirdly, approximately 2 mL of the
suspension were withdrawn from the system for the subsequent NH3/
NH4
+ concentration analysis, at a given time interval, which was de-
termined by using Nessler's reagent method with UV–vis spectro-
photometer [10,15]. Ion chromatography was conducted to obtain the
ammonia concentration to verify the accuracy of the Nessler's reagent
method.

articles.title: Synthesis of nitrogen vacancies g-C3N4 with increased crystallinity under the controlling of oxalyl dihydrazide: visible-light-driven photocatalytic activity
articles.experimental_text:
2 Experimental
2.1 Photocatalysts synthesis
Urea and ODH were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.
(purity > 99 %) and directly used for the synthesis of photocatalysts without
other treatment. Urea (20 g) and a given mass of ODH were uniformly grinded
in a mortar. The mixture was heated to 550 °C for 4 h in air, at a heating rate of
5 °C min−1. According to the added ODH mass (0.1 g, 0.2 g, 0.3 g, and 0.4 g),
the products were denoted ODH-CNX (X=1, 2, 3 and 4, respectively). By
contrast, pristine carbon nitride (CN) was synthesized by direct calcination of
20 g urea under the same conditions.
2.2 Photocatalyst characterization
The micromorphology of photocatalysts were characterized on SEM
(Hitachi-S4800, Hitachi, Japan), TEM (JEM-2100, JEOL, Japan) and AFM
(SPA-400, Seiko, Japan). The specific surface area of the photocatalysts were
tested 
through 
the 
N2 
absorption-desorption 
method 
and
Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) model (ASAP-2020; Micromeritics, USA). To
observe the chemical constitution variations of photocatalysts, the elemental
Analyzer (vario EL CUBE), FTIR (NICOLET-700, Nicolet, USA), XPS
(ESCALAB 250XI, Thermo, USA), ESR (JES-FA200, JEOL, Japan) and 13C
solid-state MAS NMR (JNM-ECZ600R, JEOL, Japan) were used. The
crystalline phases of the photocatalysts were recorded by XRD (D8 Advance,
Bruker, USA) using Cu Kα = 1.540562 Å radiation at 40 kV and 40 mA. The
optical properties of photocatalysts were assigned through DR-UV-Vis
(Lambda 950 UV/Vis/NIR Perkin-Elmer, USA) using BaSO4 as a reference, PL
(F7000, Hitachi, Japan) at an excitation wavelength of 391 nm. The
photoelectrochemical properties were determined using an electrochemical
workstation (CHI660D, Chenhua, China).
The photoelectrochemical property measurement was performed in a 0.1 M
Na2SO4 aqueous electrolyte with a standard three-electrode conﬁguration.
Fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO) electrodes coated with catalyst, platinum wire
and saturated calomel electrode (SCE) were used under visible-light (λ > 420
nm) as working electrode, pair electrode, and reference electrode, respectively.
The drop coating colloid method was used to prepare the working electrodes.
The homogeneous colloids were obtained by ultrasonic dispersion of 5 mg of
photocatalyst in a mixed solvent containing 0.6 mL water, 0.2 mL isopropanol,
and 0.01 mL Naﬁon.
2.4 Photocatalytic activity
Decomposition of antibiotics (TC-HCl and SMZ), and H2 evolut ion under a
300 W Xe lamp (λ > 420 nm) were used to determine the photocatalytic activity
of the photocatalysts.
Prior to photocatalytic decomposition, 25 mg of photocatalyst was dispersed in
100 mL of a TC-HCl (15 mg L−1) and SMZ (5 mg L−1) solution, which was
then stirred in the dark at a uniform speed for 30 min to eliminate the effects of
adsorption. After turning the 300 W Xe lamp (λ > 420 nm) on, 1.5 mL aliquots
were produced by the suction tube and then filtered by 0.22 nm
polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) syringe ﬁlters to obtain clear aliquots within the
prescribed illumination interval. The concentration of TC-HCl was evaluated at
a 357 nm wavelength by a UV-vis spectrophotometer. The concentration of
SMZ was analysed through high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)
at a wavelength of 270 nm. The eluent was acetonitrile: water (4:6 V/V), and
the ﬂow rate was 1 mL min−1.
The photocatalytic H2 evolution of different photocatalysts (λ > 420 nm) was
implemented in a 500 mL sealed quartz ﬂask with top-irradiation at 5 °C. The
photocatalyst (25 mg) was dispersed in 100 mL deionized aqueous solution,
which contained 10 vol% of the hole sacrificial agent triethanolamine (TEOA)
and co-catalyst Pt (3 wt% H2PtCl6). In a photocatalytic activity experiment (Pt
as co-catalyst), a photocatalyst sample (25 mg) was dispersed in 100 mL of
distilled water for H2 evolution, and in TC-HCl (100 mL, 15 mg L−1) or SMZ
(100 mL, 5 mg L−1) for simultaneous H2 evolution with antibiotics
decomposition. The obtained suspension solution was dispersed by ultrasound
for 30 min. Before photocatalytic H2 evolution, the co-catalyst Pt was in situ
photo-deposited on the photocatalyst surface under a full-spectrum Xenon lamp
irradiation and the sealed quartz ﬂask exhausted air with N2 for several times. A
gas chromatography (Agilent 7890B), with high-purity N2 as the carrier gas,
was used to determine the generated H2.
2.5 Computational details
The density functional theory (DFT) was calculated in the Gauss 09 program
[39] using the m062x/6-31g (d, p) method [40]. It explained the band structure
and electronic distribution of CN and ODH-CNX. All models were constructed
and optimized by the Gview 5.0 program. Then the lowest unoccupied
molecular orbital (LUMO) and the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO)
of the CN, and ODH-CNX models were simulated.

was removed in the synthesis process. Solid-state 13C NMR
further conﬁrmed the heptazine structure. Two strong peaks
at 156.7 and 164.4 ppm are shown in the NMR spectra (Fig. S6),
which can be identiﬁed as the chemical shifts of inner circle
carbons (C1) and external circle carbons (C2) in the heptazine
units, respectively [62].
Elements of C, N and O are observed in the survey XPS
spectra (Fig. S7). The N/C atomic ratio of g-C3N4 surface
decreased from 1.35 to 1.34, 1.26 and 1.19, (Table S2), respec-
tively, with the increase of GO template usage, indicating that
the loss of nitrogen atoms. Thus, nitrogen vacancies were
formed in the framework during the pyrolysis process. The bulk
ratio of N/C showed a similar trend as determined using EA in
Table S3. The N 1s spectrum (Fig. 4a) was obtained to identify
the location of the nitrogen vacancy. Three peaks at 398.5, 399.2,
and 400.7 eV are shown in the CNM sample, corresponding to
bicoordinated, tricoordinated and N-Hx groups, respectively
[64]. The atomic ratio in Table S4 shows a decreased content of
CeN]C from 58.79% for CNM to 52.75% for NS-CNM-0.3,
implying that the nitrogen vacancies are mainly located at
CeN]C sites. Two peaks at 288.0 and 284.6 eV are shown in the
C 1s spectrum of CNM (Fig. 4b), corresponding to carbon in the
form of NeC]N and adventitious hydrocarbons, respectively
[15,65]. With the increase of GO template usage, the area of a
gradually decreased peak of NeC]N was observed (Table S5),
and a new peak at 286.1 eV assigned to CeNHx began to emerge,
which further conﬁrmed the formation of nitrogen vacancies. In
addition, the BEs shift (labeled in Fig. 4) of both N and C ele-
ments in the NS-CNM suggested that the chemical coordination
environment is changed after the nitrogen vacancies were
introduced into the framework.

2. Experimental
2.1 Preparation. The precursor, flower-like melamine-cyanuric acid (MCA)
supramolecular aggregates, for the fabrication of flower-like gCN was prepared
according to literature [52]. Briefly, 200 ml of DMSO solution containing 10.0 g of
cyanuric acid was dropwise added into 400 ml of DMSO solution that has been
dissolved 10.0 g of melamine under magnetic sitrring. Ten minutes later, the resulted
precipitates were collected by filtration. After washed with water and drying in an
electronic oven at 80 oC for 10 h, 7.2 g of the MCA precursor was obtained.
Flower-like gCN was synthesized by calcining 10.0 g of MCA precursor at 500 oC
for certain time (2-14 h). The resulted flower-like gCN sample is denoted as Fx (see
Table 1). F10 sample denotes the flower-like gCN which was obtained by calcination
of MCA precursor at 500 oC for 10 h, while B10 is the bulk gCN that was prepared by

were observed by a field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) (Hitachi,
Japan) and a transmission electron microscope (TEM) (G20, Tecnai, USA). The phase

in a Bruker D8 Advance using monochromatized Cu-Ka radiation with a scanning

spectrometer (NeXUS 470) using the KBr pellet technique. Uv-vis diffuse reflectance

DMPO-O2•- and aqueous dispersion is used for DMPO-•OH) under an LED lample
irradiation (λ> 400 nm). F-700 fluorescence spectrophotometer (Hitachi, Japan) is
used for photoluminescence (PL) spectrum measurement (λex = 380 nm). The
transient-PL spectrum was monitored at FLSP-920 fluorescence spectrophotometer
(λex = 330 nm).
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
2.3. Photoelectrochemical measurements. Transient photocurrent, electrochemical
impedance (EIS) spectroscopy and Mott-schottky plots were performed on an
electrochemical workstation (CHI760e, Shanghai, China) equipped with a standard
there-electrode system, where a Pt wire, ITO/g-C3N4 electrode and Ag/AgCl (in
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
saturated KCl) electrode were used as the counter electrode, working electrode and
reference electrode, respectively. 0.4 molL-1 Na2SO4 aqueous solution was used as
electrolyte solution. The ITO/gCN electrode was prepared by a drip coating method,
and a 3 W LED lamp (λ = 420 ± 10 nm) was used as the light source (Shenzhen
LAMPLIC, China).
2.4. Photocatalytic oxidation of NO. A continuous-flow reactor (30×15×10 cm)
was used for photocatalytic oxidation of NO, and a visible LED lamp (150 W)
equipped with a cut-off filter (λ > 400 nm) was used as the light source. Firstly, 0.2 g
of gCN photocatalyst was homogeneously deposited on the surface of a glass dish
(diameter of 12.0 cm) by sonication and evaporation. Then the dish was moved into
the reactor. After the adsorption-desorption equilibrium of NO over gCN
photocatalyst was achieved, turn on the LED lamp to initiate the photocatalytic
oxidation of NO. The concentration of NO was adjusted to 600 ppb in air before
entering the reactor, and the flow rate was kept at 1.0 Lmin-1. The concentration of
NO after photocatalytic oxidation was online detected by a NOx analyzer (Advanced
Pollution Instrumentation, Model T200).
3. Results and discussion.
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
3.1 Morphology and phase structure of MCA. Fig. 1a shows the digital image of
MCA supramolecular aggregates. It can be seen that the MCA aggregates are
condense white powders. After calcination of MCA at 500 oC for 10 h, loose yellow
powders (F10 sample) were obtained (Fig. 1b), which are flower-like gCN assembly
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
from nanosheets. When compared with flower-like gCN, the color of bulk gCN (B10)
is much lighter (Fig. 1c), reflecting theimproved light-harvesting ability of flower-like
gCN.
SEM images show that these MCA aggregates are relatively monodisperse, which
exhibit flower-like structures in diameters of about 1-2 um with the pedal thickness of
ca. 20 nm (Fig. 2). Strong hydrogen bonds between melamine and cyanuric acid
facilitate the self-assembly, resulting in the formation of stable MCA supermolecular
aggregates (Fig. S1). The structure of MCA supramolecular aggregates is confirmed
by XRD (Fig. S2) and FTIR spectrum (Fig. S3), corresponding to the results in
literatures [52].
3.2 Transformation of MCA aggregates to gCN. After calcination of MCA at 500 oC
in air, flower-like gCN was obtained (SEM in Fig. 3), indicating that the
transformation is a self-templated in-situ transformation process, although the petals
become much thinner. Carefully view shows that the flower-like gCN has hollow
interials (Fig. 4a), and the building-blocks are porous nanosheets (Fig. 4b). The
porous structures may be caused by the emission of the gases such as NH3 in the
polymerization of MCA. Phase transformation (crystallization) usually begins from
the surface of the microsphere. With increase in the reaction time, hollow interials are
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
produced due to redistribution of the mass from core to shell (Ostwald Rippening) [53,
54]. When compared with that of flower-like gCN, the density of bulk gCN is much
larger (Fig. 1b and Fig. 1c), which is mainly due to its dense structure (Fig. S4).
According to AFM image (Fig. 5), the thickness of a petal from F10 sample is
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
about 2-3 nm, further confirming its sheet-like structure. The thickness of a gCN
nanoparticle from bulk gCN (B10) was measured to be 10-20 nm (Fig. S5), about
5-10 times thicker than that of gCN nanosheet from F10.
The hollow interials and porous structures of flower-like gCN not only facilitate the
diffusion of the gas, but also result in multi-reflection of the light within the cave,
which make it a good candidate photocatalyst for air purification.
Fig. 6A illustrates the effect of calcination time on the XRD patterns of the
obtained flower-like gCN. It can be seen that all samples have two peaks at around
27° and 13o, the typical XRD peaks of carbon nitride (gCN). The former intense peak
is identified as the (002) peak of gCN originated from the interplanar stacking of
aromatic systems, while the latter weak peak is attributed to the in-plane structural
packing motif.
When compared with these of bulk gCN sample (B10), both the (002) and (100)
peak intensities of the flower-like gCN (F10) are much weaker (Fig. 6B), which is
possibly due to the fact that flower-like gCN is assembled from nanosheets. It can
also be seen from Fig. 6B that the diffraction angle of the (002) peak for F10 sample
is 27.60o, larger than that of B10 sample (27.36o). That was to say, the polymerization
of MCA aggregates results in a decrease in the interlayer stacking distance from 0.326
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
nm (B10) to 0.323 nm (F10), reflecting the stronger van der Waals attraction between
the neighboring heptazine layers of flower-like gCN. The potential barrier between
the layers were estimated to be 33.2 eV, which makes the electron transfer between
layers very difficult [55]. Reducing the distance of π–π* layer stacking between
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
heptazine layers can improve the transport of lateral charge, beneficial to improve the
photoreactivity. On the contrary, the diffraction angle of the (100) peak for F10
sample decreases from 12.88o to 12.72o, indicating an extended interplanar packing
distance of the flower-like gCN (0.696 nm) to that of bulk gCN (0.687 nm).
Extending the interplanar packing distance can break the hydrogen bonds originate
from the neighbouring melon strands, facilitating the electron transfer within layers
[27].
The structures of flower-like gCN and bulk gCN were further confirmed by FTIR
sepctra (Fig. 7). The absorption peaks in the range of 3000-3300 cm-1 originate from
the stretching vibration of N-H, while the absorption in the range of 1200-1600 cm-1
is attributed to the typical stretching vibration of C-N heterocycles, and the absorption
peak at 810 cm-1 is attributed to the breathing mode of triazine units of gCN [56].
3.3 UV-visible light absorption spectrum and nitrogen sorption. The efficiency of
photocatalysis mainly depends on the following three processes: (1) separation of
photo-generated carriers after absorption of the light, (2) migration of the
photo-generated electrons and holes to the surface of the photocatalyst, and (3)
capture of the carriers by surface adsorption substrates to initiate photoreaction.
Therefore, light-harvesting ability plays an important role on the photoreactivity of
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
the photocatalyst. Fig. 8A shows the UV-vis absorption spectra of the prepared gCN
samples. It can be seen that flower-like gCN photocatalysts exhibit improved
light-harvesting ability compared to bulk gCN both in UV and visible light regions.
Fig. 8B shows the UV-vis absorption spectra for flower-like gCN (F10) and bulk gCN
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
(B10) photocatalysts. From it we can see that the band absorption edge of flower-like
gCN, which is originated from the π–π* electron transition upon irradiation, is 431 nm
(bandgap of 2.88 eV). While the band adsorption edge of B10 is 456 nm,
corresponding to a reduced bandgap of 2.72 eV. The quantum confinement effect of
the building blocks of nanosheets (Fig. 3) is responsible for the blue-shifted
adsorption edge or enlarged bandgap of flower-like gCN when compared with bulk
gCN. In addition, obviously improved visible light absorption of flower-like gCN is
also observed. This is due to the introduction of nitrogen vacancy (Nv), which will be
shown below.
Surface area also plays very important role on the photoreactivity as larger specific
surface area means more active sites can participate in the photocatalytic reaction [57].
Fig. 9 compares the nitrogen adsorption isotherms of MCA, flow-like gCN (F10) and
bulk gCN (B10) photocatalysts. We can see that the adsorption curve of flower-like
gCN shifts upward, indicating its larger surface area. The BET surface area (SBET) of
F10 is as high as 142.8 m2g-1, which is 8.8 and 22.7 times larger than that of bulk gCN
(16.3 m2g-1) and precursor MCA (only 6.3 m2g-1), respectively.
The isotherm of flower-like gCN photocatalyst is type IV with a hysteresis loop at
relative high pressure range of 0.9-1.0. This H3 type mesopores is consistent with its
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
flower-like morphology (Fig. 3) [15, 57]. Inset of Fig. 9 shows the distribution curves
of pore size for flower-like gCN and bulk gCN. It can be clearly seen that flower-like
gCN has much larger pore volume (0.53 cm3g-1), exceeding that of bulk gCN sample
(0.08 cm3g-1) by a factor of 6.6.
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
Table 1 lists SBET and pore structures of all the prepared gCN photocatalysts. It can
be observed that both SBET and pore volume (PV) of the photocatalyst increase with
extending the calcination time of MCA precursor, and all the flower-like gCN sample
possesses much larger SBET and PV than bulk gCN (B10), which benefit the
adsorption and diffusion of the gas, enhancing the photoreactivity [50].
3.4 Photocatalytic NO oxidation. As a typical pollutant in air, NO is mainly
produced from the incineration of fossil fuels and the emission of the vehicle exhaust,
which can cause acid rain even photochemical smog, incurring irritation in respiratory
system [58, 59]. Therefore, removal of NO from the air is of great importance. Then
NO oxidation was used to evaluate the photoreactivity of the gCN photocatalyst.
From Fig. 10A, it can be seen that the NO is very stable even under the irradiation of
visible LED lamp. However, obvious NO decay was observed in illuminated gCN.
With increase in the calcination time from 2 h (F2 sample) to 10 h (F10 sample), the
NO removal rate over flower-like gCN steady increases from 32.16% (F2 sample) to
59.7% (F10 sample) at illumination time of 30 min. Further increase in the calcination
time, the photoreactivity of the prepared flower-like gCN begins to decrease, which is
possibly due to the collapse of the hierarchical structure. Under other identical
conditions, the removal rate of NO over illuminated bulk gCN (B10) is only 45.8%.
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
To evaluate the photo-stability of the gCN [34, 60], recycling use of flower-like
gCN (F10) for NO oxidation was also performed (Fig. 10B). It was found that NO
removal rate reduced from 59.7% to 50.6% after reuse for 5 times, which infers that
flower-like gCN is relatively stable. The decrease in photoreactivity of flower-like
gCN is possibly due to the lost of the photocatalyst during recyle.
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
3.5 XPS and EPR analysis. To account for the high photoreactivity of flower-like
gCN, we also measured the XPS and EPR spectra. Fig.11A compares the XPS spectra
of flower-like gCN and bulk gCN. Both photocatalysts contain C, N and O elements
with binding energies of 288 eV (C 1s), 399 eV (N 1s) and 533 eV (O 1s),
respectively [28, 61].
Fig. 11B is the high resolution XPS spectra in N 1s region for flower-like gCN and
bulk gCN. It can be seen that both samples contain three kinds of N element, namely,
two-coordinated N-C2 (397.7 eV), three-coordinated N-C3 (398.7 eV), and N-H
(400.2 eV), respectively [13, 62]. According to the XPS characterization results, F10
sample contains a C:N molar ratio of 0.75, which is larger than B10 gCN sample (C:N
molar ratio of 0.70). The higher C/N molar ratio of F10 than that of B10 indicates the
introduction of Nv into the flower-like gCN photocatalyst. The peak-area ratio of
N-C2 for F10 sample is 50.1%, much lower than that for B10 sample, indicating that
Nv mainly loactes at the N-C2 sites (Fig. 11 C).
Fig. 11D compares the high resolution XPS spectra of C 1s between bulk gCN
(B10) and flower-like gCN (F10). It can be seen that each spectrum can be fitted with
three peaks corresponding to the sp2 C-C (284.6 eV), C-NH (285.9 eV) and C-N3
(287.6 eV) species, respectively. Further observation shows that the peak intensity of
C-NH species is weakened in F10 when compared with in B10 sample, further
confirming the formation of Nv in flower-like gCN sample.
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
The formation of Nv in flower-like gCN is also confirmed by EPR spectra (Fig. 12).
Generally, if there is no Nv in perfect gCN framework, the ESR signal will be very
weak. However, if there is Nv in gCN framework, we can observe a Lorentzian line
with a g value of about 2 [63]. This is because the presence of Nv is accompanied
with the increase of the number of unpaired electrons [36]. From Fig. 12, we can see
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
that flower-like gCN sample exhibits much stronger EPR signal at g=1.9993
compared to bulk gCN, indicating the higher concentration of Nv in flower-like gCN
photocatalyst. As the intensity of EPR signal is positively related to the concentration
of Nv in the g-C3N4 framework, the much stronger EPR signal in flower-like gCN
than in bulk gCN indicates that F10 sample possesses high concentrated Nv.
It was reported that the presence of Nv in gCN photocatalyst can facilitate the trap
of photo-generated electrons, enhancing the photocatalytic activity [64]. Therefore,
we can predict the high photoreactivity of flower-like gCN sample.
3.6 (Photo)electrochemical measurements and photoluminescence analysis. Not
only the excitation, but also the separation and recombination of photo-generated
carriers can affect the photocatalytic efficiency. Therefore, we compared the
photocurrents, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) spectra, steady and
transient photoluminescence spectra between flower-like gCN and bulk gCN samples.
From Fig. 13A, it can be seen that the photocurrent of flower-like gCN can be as high
as 37.4 nAcm-2, which is 3.5 times larger than that of bulk gCN (10.8 nAcm-2),
reflecting the higher efficient separation of photo-generated carriers over illuminated
flower-like gCN. Careful view shows that the shapes of the photocurrents for
flower-like gCN and bulk gCN are totally different. The photocurrent of bulk gCN
increases smoothly before levelling off upon illumination (Zone 1 in Fig. 13A),
indicating that almost all the holes are injected to the electrolyte. However, no steady
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
Faradaic current, but an obvious anodic photocurrent spike is observed on illuminated
flower-like gCN electrode (Zone 2 in Fig. 13A), which reflects that photo-generated
holes are accumulated at the electrode/electrolyte interface instead of injection to the
electrolyte due to the low potential [65].
The smaller arc radius on the EIS Nyquist plot of flower-like gCN than that of bulk
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
gCN also indicates the effective separation of the carrier and a faster interfacial charge
migration of flower-like gCN (Fig. 13B). The recombination of the photo-generated
carriers is also effectively retarded in flower-like gCN judging from its lower PL
intensity (Fig. 13C) and longer average life time (Fig. 13D).
3.7 Band structures and mehansim. To compare the band structure of flower-like
gCN with that of bulk gCN photocatalyst, Mott-Schottky analysis was employed to
determine the flat band potentials (Efb), which is near the conduction band (CB)
position of the photocatalyst [34]. From the Mott-schottky plots (Fig. 14), the CB
potentials of flower-like gCN and bulk gCN were determined to be -0.93 and -0.76 V
vs Ag/AgCl, or -0.71 and -0.54 V vs NHE, respectively. By combination the band
absorption edge of UV-visible diffuse reflectance spectrum (Fig. 8B), the CB
potentials of F10 and B10 were calculated to be +2.18V and +2.17 V vs. NHE,
respectively. That was to say, flower-like gCN and bulk gCN have similar VB
potenials, while the CB position of flower-like gCN is more negatively shifted
compared to bulk gCN. The negatively shifted CB potential favors for the production
−, an important ROSs that are responsible for the oxidation of NO [51].
of •O2
To account for the increased absorption in visible region of the flower-like gCN to
that of bulk gCN (Fig. 8B), DFT was used to calculate the band structure. It was
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
found that the calculated bandgap of pristine gCN is 0.72 eV, which is smaller than
that of gCN with Nv (0.99 eV). This confirms the enlarged bandgap of flower-like
gCN with Nv (F14). In addition, the introduction of Nv also results in the formation
of defect states. The Nv-induced sub-band excitation from defect states to the CB of
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
gCN therefore significantly changes the optical property of gCN, resulting in an
broadened visible-light-responsive region (Fig. 8B). The calcluated DOS results also
confirm the negatively-shifted CB potential of flower-like gCN with Nv (Fig. 15).
The bandgap of flower-like gCN is 2.88 eV, which is 0.16 eV larger than that of
bulk gCN (2.72 eV), which is originated from the π–π* electron transition in the
conjugated aromatic ring system. However, the Nv-induced electron transition in
flower-like gCN results in the formation of a smaller sub-bandgap (1.76 eV),
benefiting the visible photoreactivity of gCN photocatalyst (Scheme 1).
